# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1840s–1860s)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** 1811, carved from Berks and Northampton Counties
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place_population tool for this query; no verified figures are available from this survey's tool results. The 1850 U.S. Federal Census for Schuylkill County is represented by a digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 007621224, covering 1850–1860) with 412 images and 96% name-indexed, confirming substantial population records exist.
- **Economy:** Schuylkill County was the heart of the Pennsylvania anthracite coal region during this period. Mining dominated the economy from the 1820s onward, with rapid population growth fueled by the expansion of mine works, rail transport (particularly the Philadelphia and Reading Railroad), and related industries. Agriculture continued in the county's outer townships.
- **Ethnic composition:** Heavily immigrant by the 1840s–1860s. Welsh and English miners arrived earliest; large waves of Irish immigrants followed (especially after the famine years beginning 1845–1847); German-speaking settlers were well established in older townships. Pennsylvania Dutch (German-origin) families predated the coal era in some areas.
- **Religious denominations:** Protestant denominations were numerous — Lutheran, German Reformed, Methodist, Episcopalian, and Welsh Calvinist Methodist (Calvinistic Methodist). Roman Catholic parishes expanded rapidly in the 1840s–1860s to serve Irish and later immigrant miners. Smaller communities of Presbyterians, Baptists, and Quakers were also present.
- **Key historical events:** Explosive coal industry growth throughout this period; construction and operation of the Reading Railroad (incorporated 1833, major expansion 1840s); significant Irish immigration following the Great Famine (1845–1852); Civil War service and draft (1861–1865), with the Molly Maguires conflict beginning to develop by the late 1860s.

## Boundary changes

Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from portions of Berks and Northampton Counties. Its boundaries were stable throughout the 1840s–1860s target period. Records predating 1811 that pertain to territory later falling within Schuylkill County are held by Berks County (county seat: Reading) and Northampton County (county seat: Easton) — consult those counties for pre-formation records.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not have statewide civil vital registration during the 1840s–1860s. Pennsylvania's FamilySearch Wiki pages were not returned by the tool in this session (all wiki_read calls resolved to a generic fallback), so the precise level and year of any local-registration system cannot be confirmed from this survey's tool results. Pennsylvania's statewide civil death registration began in 1906, as reflected by the FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968" (collection 2255317, 4,218,763 records, indexed + images at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2255317). That collection is outside the 1840s–1860s window and is background context only. Pennsylvania statewide birth and marriage registration similarly postdates this period.
- **What exists for the target period:** No statewide civil birth, marriage, or death records exist for the 1840s–1860s in Pennsylvania. Church records are the primary substitute.
- **Where held:** Not applicable for civil vital registration in this window.
- **Gaps:** Complete gap in statewide civil vital records for 1840–1869.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers (baptism, marriage, burial) are the essential substitute — see Church Records below. The FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950" (collection 1571957, 312,045 records, with images at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) and "Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900" (collection 1502909, 198,765 records, index only — 0 images — at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) overlap the target period; both should be searched for marriage evidence. The "Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950" collection (1921317) falls outside the 1840s–1860s window and is not relevant as a primary source for this period.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Lutheran, German Reformed, Methodist, Episcopalian, Welsh Calvinist Methodist, Roman Catholic (large expansion 1845–1865), Presbyterian, Baptist.
- **Record types:** Baptisms/christenings, marriages, burials, confirmations (a separate dated event, often several years after baptism — confirming an individual's age range independently). Some denominations maintained poor-relief registers and lists of communicants.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch has digitized a volume of Lutheran church records for Schuylkill County (imageGroupNumber 004288771, 198 images, covering 1840–1875). This volume is **browse-only** — 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — and must be examined image by image. It contains text in both English and German; researchers must be able to read German for the German-language entries. Church records at the denominational level are held by diocesan or synodal archives; Catholic records may be held at the Diocese of Allentown (which covers Schuylkill County). Local parishes may retain their own registers. FamilySearch microfilm holdings from prior filming campaigns may be available at the FamilySearch Library in Salt Lake City.
- **Language:** German entries appear in the Lutheran volume (imageGroupNumber 004288771). Welsh entries may appear in Welsh Methodist registers. Latin may appear in older Catholic sacramental records.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** The 1840, 1850, and 1860 federal censuses all cover Schuylkill County and are the primary population-level sources for this period. FamilySearch has digitized a volume (imageGroupNumber 007621224, 412 images, 1850–1860 coverage) that is 96% name-indexed and full-text searchable — **indexed + images**. This is the most accessible tool for the target period. The 1840 census is not represented in this specific volume; it should be searched through Ancestry's indexed 1850 U.S. Federal Census for Schuylkill County (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/). Note that 1840 census entries list only the head of household by name; all other household members appear only as tick-mark tallies by age and sex.
- **Mortality schedules:** The 1850 and 1860 federal censuses included mortality schedules listing individuals who died in the year preceding the enumeration — a valuable supplement when burial records are unavailable. These are part of the broader federal census series.
- **State/provincial census:** Pennsylvania did not take a regular state census during this period. No state-level enumeration substitute is available.
- **Other enumerations:** No ecclesiastical census or township enumeration is confirmed from this survey's tool results.
- **Access:** 1850–1860 federal census for Schuylkill County is indexed + images on FamilySearch (imageGroupNumber 007621224) and Ancestry (collection 1276). The 1840 census is indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch (broader collection).

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills (testate estates), letters of administration (intestate estates), guardianships, estate inventories, and estate distributions. If your ancestor died without a will (intestate), search the administration series; if they left a will (testate), search the will books and executors' accounts.
- **Date range:** From county formation in 1811 through the target period and beyond.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch holds the collection "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (collection 1999196), which includes Schuylkill County material. This collection has 3,200,560 images but **0 indexed records** — it is a **browse-only** image collection. Images must be browsed without a name index. A separate digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 004812990, 286 images, 1845–1880) is also available on FamilySearch; it is only 4% name-indexed but is full-text searchable, meaning text-based search may locate some names but name-index search will miss most entries. Original records are held at the Schuylkill County Courthouse in Pottsville (Register of Wills office). The Pennsylvania State Archives in Harrisburg may hold supplementary probate finding aids.
- **Access:** Primarily browse-only images online (FamilySearch). Physical originals at Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Pennsylvania is a state-land state (not a federal-land state), meaning land was granted by the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania rather than the federal government. The state used a metes-and-bounds survey system. Original land warrants and patents are held by the Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) through the Bureau of Land Records. County deed books recording transfers between private parties are held at the Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds office in Pottsville.
- **Types:** Land warrants, surveys, patents, deeds (grantor/grantee deed books), mortgages, and property tax assessment lists.
- **Date range:** County deed records from 1811 (formation) forward. State warrant and patent records date earlier for land within the county's territory.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives (warrants, patents, surveys); Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds, Pottsville (deed books); county tax assessment records at the county courthouse. No confirmed online digitization of Schuylkill County deeds was returned by this survey's tools.
- **Access note:** Pennsylvania land records are not confirmed as digitized in the FamilySearch volume or collections search results for this period. Researchers should plan for physical access or written inquiry to the Recorder of Deeds.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848); Civil War (1861–1865). The Civil War is the dominant military source for this county during the target period. Schuylkill County contributed numerous regiments, and draft registration records (1863 Civil War draft) were created at the county level.
- **Record types:** Civil War service records and pension files are held at the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), Washington, D.C., and are available through Fold3 (subscription). Bounty land warrants (for Mexican War and earlier service) are at NARA. State adjutant general records for Pennsylvania Civil War units may be held at the Pennsylvania State Archives. The 1863 Consolidated Lists of Civil War Draft Registrations are at NARA and are available through Fold3/Ancestry.
- **Where held:** NARA (federal); Pennsylvania State Archives (state unit records); Schuylkill County courthouse may hold local bounty and muster records.
- **Access:** Pension files and some service records are indexed and imaged on Fold3/Ancestry (subscription). The FamilySearch tools did not return a specific Civil War collection for Schuylkill County in this session.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Schuylkill County had numerous church cemeteries associated with the denominations listed above, as well as municipal and independent cemeteries in Pottsville and the mining patches. Catholic cemeteries expanded significantly in the 1840s–1860s.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) is the principal online indexing resource for headstone inscriptions; BillionGraves also covers some Pennsylvania cemeteries. Neither was returned as a specific curated link by the external_links_search tool for the 1840–1870 window.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers, where they survive, are held at individual churches or in some cases at local historical societies. The Schuylkill County Historical Society (Pottsville) may hold transcriptions or original burial records.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The Miners' Journal, published in Pottsville, is the county's most significant newspaper for this period and is a major source for obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices (estate sales, sheriff's sales, naturalization notices), and mining news. It was published continuously from 1825. Other local papers existed in the county during the 1840s–1860s.
- **Where held:** The Miners' Journal has been microfilmed; copies are held at the Schuylkill County Historical Society and the Pennsylvania State Library. Some historical newspaper digitization projects have included Pennsylvania papers — check Chronicling America (Library of Congress, chroniclingamerica.loc.gov) and the Pennsylvania Digital Newspaper Project for any available digital runs. The FamilySearch tools did not return a confirmed digitized run of the Miners' Journal.
- **Content value:** Obituaries in the Miners' Journal frequently named survivors, place of origin (especially for immigrant miners), and church affiliation — information not found in any other record class for deaths before 1906. Marriage notices, naturalization announcements (printed as public notices), and sheriff's sale advertisements naming delinquent property owners are additional research sources.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** The primary port of arrival for Irish, Welsh, English, and German immigrants to Schuylkill County was Philadelphia. New York City (Castle Garden) was also a major entry point, particularly from the late 1840s onward. Baltimore served some German immigrant streams.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists (name-indexed at Ancestry and FamilySearch for Philadelphia and New York arrivals); declarations of intention and naturalization petitions filed at the Schuylkill County Court of Common Pleas (pre-1906, naturalizations could be filed in any court of record); alien registration records. Note that passengers of all ages, including infants and young children traveling with parents, are listed on arrival manifests — when researching a family arrival, examine the full manifest page for all accompanying family members, not just the head of household.
- **Where held:** Original passenger lists are at NARA (Philadelphia Passenger Lists: NARA M425 and T840; New York: NARA M237). Naturalization records filed in Schuylkill County are held at the county courthouse; some may be on FamilySearch microfilm. The collection "Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950" (collection 1571957) may include civil marriages involving naturalized individuals.
- **Access:** Philadelphia passenger lists are indexed and imaged on Ancestry and FamilySearch. Schuylkill County naturalization records have no confirmed online index from this survey.

### Tax records

- **Types:** County property tax assessment lists and personal property tax lists were maintained annually at the county level throughout this period. These are particularly valuable as an annual locator for individuals in the years between federal census enumerations (1841–1849, 1851–1859, 1861–1869).
- **Date range:** From county formation (1811) forward.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County assessment records are held at the county courthouse and may also be at the Schuylkill County Historical Society. The Pennsylvania State Archives holds some statewide assessment records. No online digitization of Schuylkill County tax records was returned by the volume_search or collections_search tools for this period.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are an essential annual substitute for the non-census years and can document property accumulation, economic mobility, and neighbors (who may be relatives).

### Other record types

- **Court records:** The Schuylkill County Court of Common Pleas held civil litigation, equity proceedings, naturalization petitions, guardianships, road orders (naming property owners along road lines), and name changes. Court minute books record routine county business — payments to indigent residents, road maintenance assignments — and name ordinary people who appear in no other series. Original records are at the county courthouse; some may be on FamilySearch microfilm.
- **Mine and occupational records:** Because coal mining dominated the county's economy, mine employment records, accident records, and company records (for companies like the Philadelphia and Reading Coal and Iron Company) may exist and name individual miners. These are held at the Hagley Museum and Library (Wilmington, Delaware) for some Reading Railroad and coal company collections, and at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania (Philadelphia). No FamilySearch-curated collection for mine records was returned.
- **Local and county histories:** 19th- and early-20th-century published county histories for Schuylkill County often contain biographical sketches of early settlers and prominent families and may reprint or summarize records since lost. These are held at the Schuylkill County Historical Society and can be searched via WorldCat.

The Lutheran volume on FamilySearch (imageGroupNumber 004288771) contains German-language entries. Consider hiring a German-language genealogical translator if needed.
- **Civil War records are a major source for the 1860s.** Service records, pension files, and the 1863 draft registration lists are indexed and available through NARA, Ancestry, and Fold3. Pension files are especially rich — they often include affidavits about birthplace, marriage dates, children's names and ages, and widow's testimony — and can substitute for missing vital records.
- **Mine records may be the only employment documentation.** For miners, which was the majority occupation in many Schuylkill County townships by the 1850s, employment rosters, accident reports, and company payroll records held at Hagley Museum (Wilmington, DE) may be the only surviving record naming an individual outside of church and government series.

---

Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania was a rapidly industrializing anthracite coal region in the 1840s–1860s, with a large and diverse immigrant population. For this period, there are no statewide civil birth, marriage, or death records — church registers are the essential substitute for vital events — and the county's most accessible online records are the federal census (1850 and 1860, indexed and imaged on FamilySearch and Ancestry), a small digitized but mostly browse-only Lutheran church record volume, and a large browse-only probate image collection on FamilySearch. The county courthouse in Pottsville holds deeds, tax lists, naturalization petitions, and court records that are not online and require in-person or written access. The two most important warnings are that most church records for this period are physical or must be browsed image by image without a name index, and that annual tax assessment lists — the only year-by-year locator between censuses — are held at the courthouse and historical society and are not available digitally.

The logical next step is to use this survey as the foundation for a focused research plan targeting the specific ancestors or family lines you are researching in Schuylkill County.

**Pulaski County, Kentucky (1840–1880)**

Pulaski County was formed in 1798 from Lincoln and Green Counties, with its county seat at Somerset in south-central Kentucky.

**Key caveat on vital records:** Civil registration of births and deaths barely existed during this period — it ran in fits and starts (1853–1862, then 1874–1878) with very poor compliance. A courthouse disaster in 1838 and another in 1871 also destroyed some records.

**Record types available:**

- **Marriage bonds** — Run from 1799; digitized on FamilySearch through 1871. These are the most continuous vital record for the period.
- **Federal censuses (1840–1880)** — Fully indexed and available online.
- **Probate records / Wills** — From 1801; digitized on FamilySearch.
- **Church registers** — Baptist and Methodist predominantly; held by the Pulaski County Historical Society. These are the primary substitute for missing births and deaths.
- **Land records** — Go through the Kentucky Land Office in Frankfort (not the federal BLM system); deeds are at the county courthouse.
- **Civil War Union pension files** — Particularly rich given the Battle of Somerset fought there in January 1862.

---

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pulaski County, Kentucky (1840-1880)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** December 10, 1798, from Lincoln and Green counties
- **County seat:** Somerset
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Kentucky (state); Lincoln and Green counties (predecessor jurisdictions)
- **Population during period:** Population data unavailable from tools in this run — consult the decennial federal censuses (1840, 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880) directly for county population figures.
- **Economy:** Agriculture (subsistence farming, tobacco, livestock); limited manufacturing; the county lies in south-central Kentucky's Cumberland Plateau foothills
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly native-born Anglo-American settlers of Scots-Irish and English ancestry; small free Black population
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist (dominant), Methodist, Presbyterian, Roman Catholic (Diocese of Lexington); smaller congregations of Christian/Disciples of Christ
- **Key historical events:** Civil War (1861-1865) divided the region — southeastern Kentucky had significant Unionist sentiment but Confederate activity; Battle of Somerset (1862) was fought in Pulaski County; the war disrupted record-keeping and the county's vital registration lapsed in 1862

## Boundary changes
- Pulaski County boundaries have been stable from 1798 formation through the target period. No known boundary changes during 1840-1880.
- Research events before 1798 in Lincoln County (formed 1780 from Kentucky County, Virginia) and Green County (formed 1792 from Lincoln and Nelson counties).

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** County-level registration began 1853; lapsed 1862-1874; briefly revived 1874-1878; resumed 1892-1910. Statewide registration began 1911 (Kentucky Vital Records wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records).
- **What exists:** Scattered birth and death registrations at county level for 1853-1862 and 1874-1878 only within the target window. Marriage bonds and licenses from county formation (1799) onward are the most continuous vital series.
- **Where held:** Kentucky Department for Libraries and Archives (KDLA), Frankfort; Pulaski County Courthouse (100 N. Main Street, #208, Somerset, KY 42502); marriage bonds 1799-1871 available on FamilySearch (digitized).
- **Gaps:** No civil birth or death registration 1840-1852, 1863-1873, or 1879-1891. Compliance was poor even when registration was required. A disaster in 1838 and another in 1871 destroyed some records.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptismal and burial registers; family Bibles; cemetery headstones; mortality schedules in the 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 federal censuses (deaths in the prior year).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Baptist (largest), Methodist Episcopal, Methodist Episcopal South, Presbyterian, Christian/Disciples of Christ, Roman Catholic
- **Record types:** Baptisms/christenings, marriages, burials, membership lists, minute books
- **Where held:** FamilySearch Library (microfilmed Kentucky church records, many from Pulaski County congregations); Kentucky Historical Society (Frankfort); Pulaski County Historical Society (holds the most comprehensive collection of local church records per the Pulaski County wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy); individual active congregations; Catholic Diocese of Lexington for Catholic parishes
- **Language:** English
- **FamilySearch collections (statewide, not county-specific):** Kentucky Church Records, 1818-1995 (index and images, incomplete); Kentucky Births and Christenings, 1839-1960 (index only); Kentucky Marriages, 1785-1979 (index only); Kentucky Deaths and Burials, 1843-1970 (index only) — per the Kentucky Church Records wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Church_Records

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1840, 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880 — all available for Pulaski County. The 1850 through 1880 censuses are fully indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry. The 1890 census is almost entirely destroyed nationally.
- **Mortality schedules:** Accompany the 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 censuses — list deaths in the year preceding enumeration; important substitute for missing death records.
- **Agricultural/manufacturing/slave schedules:** Also available for census years 1850-1880; name farm owners and (1850, 1860) slaveholders.
- **State census:** Kentucky did not conduct regular state censuses in this period.
- **Access:** Federal censuses indexed and online at FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription). Mortality schedules indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, administrations, guardianships, court orders, equity cases
- **Date range:** Probate records from 1801; court records from 1799 (Pulaski County wiki)
- **Where held:** Pulaski County Courthouse; KDLA (microfilm copies); FamilySearch has digitized early will books 1801-1929 (Pulaski County wiki)
- **Access:** FamilySearch early will books — digitized images, browse-only status unconfirmed from tool results in this run. KDLA holds microfilmed copies.
- **Note on record losses:** Disasters in 1838 and 1871 destroyed some records. Court and probate records from those periods may have gaps.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Kentucky is a state-land state, not on the rectangular survey grid)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Kentucky Land Office, Frankfort — holds land grants, original warrants, surveys, and patents; county courthouses hold deed books from county formation
- **Types:** Deeds (county, from 1799), land grants and warrants (Kentucky Land Office), surveys, patents, tax lists
- **Date range:** County deeds from 1799; earlier Virginia grants and Kentucky state grants from the late 18th century
- **Where held:** Pulaski County Courthouse (deeds); Kentucky Land Office, Frankfort (grants/patents); Kentucky Historical Society (additional manuscripts). FamilySearch has digitized Kentucky Land Office warrants, surveys, grants and related records (1700-1955) per the Kentucky Land and Property wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Land_and_Property. Ancestry also holds Kentucky land grants.
- **Online access:** Kentucky Land Office records on FamilySearch and Ancestry; county deeds largely physical at the courthouse or KDLA microfilm.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846-1848); Civil War (1861-1865) — Pulaski County sent men to both Union and Confederate forces; Battle of Somerset (January 1862) fought in the county
- **Record types:** Civil War Union service records and pension files (NARA); Confederate service records (NARA); Kentucky adjutant general's Civil War records; bounty land warrant records (Mexican War era)
- **Where held:** NARA (service and pension records); Kentucky State Archives (adjutant general records); FamilySearch and Fold3 (indexed military records online)
- **Access:** Civil War Union pension files highly informative — contain family histories, widow statements, physician affidavits. Search Fold3 (subscription) and FamilySearch for indexed records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Scattered family and church cemeteries throughout the county; no single dominant municipal cemetery for the period
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) — volunteer-indexed headstone transcriptions; coverage uneven for rural Pulaski County
- **Physical records:** Sexton records minimal for this period; church burial registers (see Church records above); Pulaski County Historical Society holds cemetery surveys

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Somerset newspapers existed by the mid-19th century; specific titles and date ranges not confirmed by tool results in this run
- **Where held:** Kentucky Digital Library / Kentucky Virtual Library (kdl.kyvl.org) — digitized Kentucky newspapers; Library of Congress Chronicling America (chroniclingamerica.loc.gov) — may include Kentucky papers; Newspapers.com (subscription) — https://www.newspapers.com/
- **Content value:** Obituaries, estate notices, legal advertisements, marriage announcements; critical for the 1840-1880 period given sparse vital registration

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** Pulaski County is inland south-central Kentucky. The population in 1840-1880 was overwhelmingly native-born. Immigration from abroad was minimal compared to border or port cities.
- **Relevant records:** Pre-1906 naturalizations filed in any court of record — Pulaski County Circuit Court records; declarations of intention; any immigrant arrivals would have entered via eastern ports (Baltimore, New York) with passenger lists at NARA and on Ancestry/FamilySearch
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard including infants and children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax lists (tithe/tax lists), personal property tax
- **Date range:** From county formation (1798/1799)
- **Where held:** KDLA (microfilm); Pulaski County Courthouse; Ancestry indexes county tax lists
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are available annually and can substitute for census years — a person appearing in one year and not the next may have died, moved, or come of age. Ancestry holds Kentucky county tax list collections.

### Other record types
- **Town and county histories:** Published local histories (19th-early 20th century) for Pulaski County and south-central Kentucky often reprint early records and carry biographical sketches. Consult WorldCat and the Kentucky Historical Society.
- **Slave schedules:** 1850 and 1860 federal census slave schedules name slaveholders with counts of enslaved persons (not names); freedmen's records post-1865 held at NARA (Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands)
- **School records:** Limited for this period; local district records held by the county school board or local historical society
- **Pulaski County Historical Society:** Holds vertical surname files and the most comprehensive local church record and obituary collection — a first-resort repository for local research

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Marriage bonds 1799-1871 (digitized); early will books 1801-1929 (digitized); Kentucky church records, births/christenings, marriages, deaths statewide indexes; federal census 1840-1880; military records | Free |
| Ancestry | Federal census 1840-1880; county tax lists; Kentucky vital records indexes; military records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Civil War service and pension records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery headstone transcriptions (volunteer coverage) | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including Kentucky titles | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Military service/pension files; passenger lists; freedmen's records | Free (some digital) |

**Coverage of this survey:** `collections_search`, `volume_search`, and `catalog_search` returned zero results for both the county and state level in this run — this is a service-level gap in the tool results, not evidence that FamilySearch holds no records for Pulaski County. The Pulaski County Genealogy wiki page (fetched directly) confirms that marriage bonds 1799-1871 and will books 1801-1929 are digitized on FamilySearch. A direct FamilySearch catalog search at familysearch.org/search/catalog is recommended to identify the full holdings.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Pulaski County Courthouse, Somerset | Marriage bonds, deeds, court orders, wills from 1799 | In-person or written request |
| Kentucky Department for Libraries and Archives (KDLA), Frankfort | Microfilmed county records; pre-1911 vital records; court records | In-person; some records available via mail request |
| Kentucky Historical Society, Frankfort | Manuscripts, land records, published histories | In-person; some digital |
| Pulaski County Historical Society | Surname vertical files, church records, newspaper obituaries, cemetery surveys | Contact the society directly |
| Catholic Diocese of Lexington | Catholic parish sacramental records | Contact the diocese |
| FamilySearch Library (Salt Lake City) | Microfilmed church and civil records | In-person or order via local FamilySearch center |

## Records NOT online
- County deed books (apart from Kentucky Land Office grants on FamilySearch) — largely physical at the Pulaski County Courthouse or on KDLA microfilm
- Most local church registers not in the FamilySearch Kentucky Church Records collection — held by the Pulaski County Historical Society or active congregations
- County court minute books from county formation (some gaps from the 1838 and 1871 record losses)
- Cemetery sexton records for small family and church cemeteries
- Local newspapers before the period covered by Chronicling America or the Kentucky Digital Library

## Known record losses
- A disaster destroyed some records in 1838, and another disaster in 1871 destroyed additional records (Pulaski County Genealogy wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy). The nature of these disasters is not specified in the wiki. Records most likely affected include early court orders, deed books, and other courthouse documents. No complete substitute series is identified in the tool results.
- Civil vital registration lapsed from 1862 through 1873 — no civil birth or death records exist for this gap.

## Research tips
- **Start with marriage bonds:** County marriage bonds run from 1799 and are digitized on FamilySearch through 1871 (Pulaski County Genealogy wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy). These are the most accessible and continuous vital records for the target period.
- **Civil War pension files:** Given the Battle of Somerset (1862), many Pulaski County men served. Union pension files are particularly rich — they contain sworn depositions by widows, children, neighbors, and physicians, naming family members and places of origin.
- **Tax lists as a census substitute:** Annual county tax lists bridge the intercensal years and the 1890 census gap. Search Ancestry's Kentucky county tax list collections.
- **Pulaski County Historical Society first:** The society holds surname vertical files and the county's most comprehensive church record and obituary collection — contact them early in any project.
- **Check Lincoln and Green County records for pre-1798 events:** Pulaski was formed from Lincoln (1780) and Green (1792) counties. Ancestors living in the area before December 1798 will appear in Lincoln or Green County records.
- **Kentucky is a state-land state:** Do not search the BLM General Land Office for original land grants — go to the Kentucky Land Office in Frankfort or its FamilySearch-digitized holdings (Kentucky Land and Property wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Land_and_Property).
- **Record losses in 1838 and 1871:** When a record you expect is missing, the 1838 and 1871 disasters may explain the gap. Look for substitute sources: duplicate records at KDLA, newspaper notices, probate references to earlier deeds.
- **Baptist and Methodist churches:** These were the dominant denominations in south-central Kentucky. Locate the relevant circuit or association records — Baptist association minutes name member churches and sometimes individuals; Methodist circuit conference records are held in conference archives.

added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pulaski County, Kentucky (1840-1880)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** December 10, 1798, from Lincoln and Green counties
- **County seat:** Somerset
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Kentucky (state); Lincoln and Green counties (predecessor jurisdictions)
- **Population during period:** Population data unavailable from tools in this run — consult the decennial federal censuses (1840, 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880) directly for county population figures.
- **Economy:** Agriculture (subsistence farming, tobacco, livestock); limited manufacturing; the county lies in south-central Kentucky's Cumberland Plateau foothills
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly native-born Anglo-American settlers of Scots-Irish and English ancestry; small free Black population
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist (dominant), Methodist, Presbyterian, Roman Catholic (Diocese of Lexington); smaller congregations of Christian/Disciples of Christ
- **Key historical events:** Civil War (1861-1865) divided the region — southeastern Kentucky had significant Unionist sentiment but Confederate activity; Battle of Somerset (1862) was fought in Pulaski County; the war disrupted record-keeping and the county's vital registration lapsed in 1862

## Boundary changes
- Pulaski County boundaries have been stable from 1798 formation through the target period. No known boundary changes during 1840-1880.
- Research events before 1798 in Lincoln County (formed 1780 from Kentucky County, Virginia) and Green County (formed 1792 from Lincoln and Nelson counties).

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** County-level registration began 1853; lapsed 1862-1874; briefly revived 1874-1878; resumed 1892-1910. Statewide registration began 1911 (Kentucky Vital Records wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records).
- **What exists:** Scattered birth and death registrations at county level for 1853-1862 and 1874-1878 only within the target window. Marriage bonds and licenses from county formation (1799) onward are the most continuous vital series.
- **Where held:** Kentucky Department for Libraries and Archives (KDLA), Frankfort; Pulaski County Courthouse (100 N. Main Street, #208, Somerset, KY 42502); marriage bonds 1799-1871 available on FamilySearch (digitized).
- **Gaps:** No civil birth or death registration 1840-1852, 1863-1873, or 1879-1891. Compliance was poor even when registration was required. A disaster in 1838 and another in 1871 destroyed some records.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptismal and burial registers; family Bibles; cemetery headstones; mortality schedules in the 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 federal censuses (deaths in the prior year).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Baptist (largest), Methodist Episcopal, Methodist Episcopal South, Presbyterian, Christian/Disciples of Christ, Roman Catholic
- **Record types:** Baptisms/christenings, marriages, burials, membership lists, minute books
- **Where held:** FamilySearch Library (microfilmed Kentucky church records, many from Pulaski County congregations); Kentucky Historical Society (Frankfort); Pulaski County Historical Society (holds the most comprehensive collection of local church records per the Pulaski County wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy); individual active congregations; Catholic Diocese of Lexington for Catholic parishes
- **Language:** English
- **FamilySearch collections (statewide, not county-specific):** Kentucky Church Records, 1818-1995 (index and images, incomplete); Kentucky Births and Christenings, 1839-1960 (index only); Kentucky Marriages, 1785-1979 (index only); Kentucky Deaths and Burials, 1843-1970 (index only) — per the Kentucky Church Records wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Church_Records

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1840, 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880 — all available for Pulaski County. The 1850 through 1880 censuses are fully indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry. The 1890 census is almost entirely destroyed nationally.
- **Mortality schedules:** Accompany the 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 censuses — list deaths in the year preceding enumeration; important substitute for missing death records.
- **Agricultural/manufacturing/slave schedules:** Also available for census years 1850-1880; name farm owners and (1850, 1860) slaveholders.
- **State census:** Kentucky did not conduct regular state censuses in this period.
- **Access:** Federal censuses indexed and online at FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription). Mortality schedules indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, administrations, guardianships, court orders, equity cases
- **Date range:** Probate records from 1801; court records from 1799 (Pulaski County wiki)
- **Where held:** Pulaski County Courthouse; KDLA (microfilm copies); FamilySearch has digitized early will books 1801-1929 (Pulaski County wiki)
- **Access:** FamilySearch early will books — digitized images, browse-only status unconfirmed from tool results in this run. KDLA holds microfilmed copies.
- **Note on record losses:** Disasters in 1838 and 1871 destroyed some records. Court and probate records from those periods may have gaps.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Kentucky is a state-land state, not on the rectangular survey grid)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Kentucky Land Office, Frankfort — holds land grants, original warrants, surveys, and patents; county courthouses hold deed books from county formation
- **Types:** Deeds (county, from 1799), land grants and warrants (Kentucky Land Office), surveys, patents, tax lists
- **Date range:** County deeds from 1799; earlier Virginia grants and Kentucky state grants from the late 18th century
- **Where held:** Pulaski County Courthouse (deeds); Kentucky Land Office, Frankfort (grants/patents); Kentucky Historical Society (additional manuscripts). FamilySearch has digitized Kentucky Land Office warrants, surveys, grants and related records (1700-1955) per the Kentucky Land and Property wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Land_and_Property. Ancestry also holds Kentucky land grants.
- **Online access:** Kentucky Land Office records on FamilySearch and Ancestry; county deeds largely physical at the courthouse or KDLA microfilm.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846-1848); Civil War (1861-1865) — Pulaski County sent men to both Union and Confederate forces; Battle of Somerset (January 1862) fought in the county
- **Record types:** Civil War Union service records and pension files (NARA); Confederate service records (NARA); Kentucky adjutant general's Civil War records; bounty land warrant records (Mexican War era)
- **Where held:** NARA (service and pension records); Kentucky State Archives (adjutant general records); FamilySearch and Fold3 (indexed military records online)
- **Access:** Civil War Union pension files highly informative — contain family histories, widow statements, physician affidavits. Search Fold3 (subscription) and FamilySearch for indexed records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Scattered family and church cemeteries throughout the county; no single dominant municipal cemetery for the period
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) — volunteer-indexed headstone transcriptions; coverage uneven for rural Pulaski County
- **Physical records:** Sexton records minimal for this period; church burial registers (see Church records above); Pulaski County Historical Society holds cemetery surveys

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Somerset newspapers existed by the mid-19th century; specific titles and date ranges not confirmed by tool results in this run
- **Where held:** Kentucky Digital Library / Kentucky Virtual Library (kdl.kyvl.org) — digitized Kentucky newspapers; Library of Congress Chronicling America (chroniclingamerica.loc.gov) — may include Kentucky papers; Newspapers.com (subscription) — https://www.newspapers.com/
- **Content value:** Obituaries, estate notices, legal advertisements, marriage announcements; critical for the 1840-1880 period given sparse vital registration

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** Pulaski County is inland south-central Kentucky. The population in 1840-1880 was overwhelmingly native-born. Immigration from abroad was minimal compared to border or port cities.
- **Relevant records:** Pre-1906 naturalizations filed in any court of record — Pulaski County Circuit Court records; declarations of intention; any immigrant arrivals would have entered via eastern ports (Baltimore, New York) with passenger lists at NARA and on Ancestry/FamilySearch
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard including infants and children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax lists (tithe/tax lists), personal property tax
- **Date range:** From county formation (1798/1799)
- **Where held:** KDLA (microfilm); Pulaski County Courthouse; Ancestry indexes county tax lists
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are available annually and can substitute for census years — a person appearing in one year and not the next may have died, moved, or come of age. Ancestry holds Kentucky county tax list collections.

### Other record types
- **Town and county histories:** Published local histories (19th-early 20th century) for Pulaski County and south-central Kentucky often reprint early records and carry biographical sketches. Consult WorldCat and the Kentucky Historical Society.
- **Slave schedules:** 1850 and 1860 federal census slave schedules name slaveholders with counts of enslaved persons (not names); freedmen's records post-1865 held at NARA (Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands)
- **School records:** Limited for this period; local district records held by the county school board or local historical society
- **Pulaski County Historical Society:** Holds vertical surname files and the most comprehensive local church record and obituary collection — a first-resort repository for local research

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Marriage bonds 1799-1871 (digitized); early will books 1801-1929 (digitized); Kentucky church records, births/christenings, marriages, deaths statewide indexes; federal census 1840-1880; military records | Free |
| Ancestry | Federal census 1840-1880; county tax lists; Kentucky vital records indexes; military records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Civil War service and pension records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery headstone transcriptions (volunteer coverage) | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including Kentucky titles | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Military service/pension files; passenger lists; freedmen's records | Free (some digital) |

**Coverage of this survey:** `collections_search`, `volume_search`, and `catalog_search` returned zero results for both the county and state level in this run — this is a service-level gap in the tool results, not evidence that FamilySearch holds no records for Pulaski County. The Pulaski County Genealogy wiki page (fetched directly) confirms that marriage bonds 1799-1871 and will books 1801-1929 are digitized on FamilySearch. A direct FamilySearch catalog search at familysearch.org/search/catalog is recommended to identify the full holdings.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Pulaski County Courthouse, Somerset | Marriage bonds, deeds, court orders, wills from 1799 | In-person or written request |
| Kentucky Department for Libraries and Archives (KDLA), Frankfort | Microfilmed county records; pre-1911 vital records; court records | In-person; some records available via mail request |
| Kentucky Historical Society, Frankfort | Manuscripts, land records, published histories | In-person; some digital |
| Pulaski County Historical Society | Surname vertical files, church records, newspaper obituaries, cemetery surveys | Contact the society directly |
| Catholic Diocese of Lexington | Catholic parish sacramental records | Contact the diocese |
| FamilySearch Library (Salt Lake City) | Microfilmed church and civil records | In-person or order via local FamilySearch center |

## Records NOT online
- County deed books (apart from Kentucky Land Office grants on FamilySearch) — largely physical at the Pulaski County Courthouse or on KDLA microfilm
- Most local church registers not in the FamilySearch Kentucky Church Records collection — held by the Pulaski County Historical Society or active congregations
- County court minute books from county formation (some gaps from the 1838 and 1871 record losses)
- Cemetery sexton records for small family and church cemeteries
- Local newspapers before the period covered by Chronicling America or the Kentucky Digital Library

## Known record losses
- A disaster destroyed some records in 1838, and another disaster in 1871 destroyed additional records (Pulaski County Genealogy wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy). The nature of these disasters is not specified in the wiki. Records most likely affected include early court orders, deed books, and other courthouse documents. No complete substitute series is identified in the tool results.
- Civil vital registration lapsed from 1862 through 1873 — no civil birth or death records exist for this gap.

## Research tips
- **Start with marriage bonds:** County marriage bonds run from 1799 and are digitized on FamilySearch through 1871 (Pulaski County Genealogy wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy). These are the most accessible and continuous vital records for the target period.
- **Civil War pension files:** Given the Battle of Somerset (1862), many Pulaski County men served. Union pension files are particularly rich — they contain sworn depositions by widows, children, neighbors, and physicians, naming family members and places of origin.
- **Tax lists as a census substitute:** Annual county tax lists bridge the intercensal years and the 1890 census gap. Search Ancestry's Kentucky county tax list collections.
- **Pulaski County Historical Society first:** The society holds surname vertical files and the county's most comprehensive church record and obituary collection — contact them early in any project.
- **Check Lincoln and Green County records for pre-1798 events:** Pulaski was formed from Lincoln (1780) and Green (1792) counties. Ancestors living in the area before December 1798 will appear in Lincoln or Green County records.
- **Kentucky is a state-land state:** Do not search the BLM General Land Office for original land grants — go to the Kentucky Land Office in Frankfort or its FamilySearch-digitized holdings (Kentucky Land and Property wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Land_and_Property).
- **Record losses in 1838 and 1871:** When a record you expect is missing, the 1838 and 1871 disasters may explain the gap. Look for substitute sources: duplicate records at KDLA, newspaper notices, probate references to earlier deeds.
- **Baptist and Methodist churches:** These were the dominant denominations in south-central Kentucky. Locate the relevant circuit or association records — Baptist association minutes name member churches and sometimes individuals; Methodist circuit conference records are held in conference archives.
- **Adjoining counties:** Pulaski County borders Rockcastle, Laurel, Whitley, Wayne, Russell, Casey, and Lincoln counties. Families near these borders generated records on both sides. The Neighboring Counties table on the Pulaski County Genealogy wiki should be consulted directly. Check adjoining county deed books, marriage bonds, and church records for the same families.

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region, Pre-Statehood (ca. 1780-1819)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Jurisdiction at 1800:** Mississippi Territory (created 1798). Alabama did not exist as a named jurisdiction until the Alabama Territory was carved from the eastern Mississippi Territory in 1817; statehood followed in 1819.
- **Administrative center (territorial era):** Natchez (Mississippi Territory capital); after 1817, St. Stephens was the Alabama Territory capital.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mississippi Territory (1798-1817) → Alabama Territory (1817-1819) → State of Alabama (1819-)
- **Population during period:** No reliable aggregate figure was returned by the population tool for this pre-statehood period. The Wikipedia article notes early settlement was concentrated around Mobile Bay (French town founded 1702) and expanded rapidly from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia after the Creek War of 1813-1814.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, cotton planting beginning to emerge, fur trade, and Mobile port trade.
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek and Cherokee nations throughout the interior; French Creole community at Mobile; Anglo-American settlers from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia arriving via the Tennessee River valley and Natchez Trace corridor; Spanish Creole community in the Mobile district.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic missions at Mobile (French/Spanish era); Baptist and Methodist circuit riders accompanying American settlers from the 1790s onward.
- **Key historical events:** Mississippi Territory established 1798; Burr Conspiracy 1805-1807; War of 1812 and Creek War 1813-1814 (dramatically opened interior to American settlement); Spanish surrender of Mobile 1813; Alabama Territory established 1817; statehood December 1819.

## Boundary changes
- **Before 1798:** The present Alabama region was disputed among Spain (controlling Mobile), the United States (claiming by treaty), and Native nations. No unified American territorial administration existed.
- **1798-1817:** Present-day Alabama and Mississippi together formed the Mississippi Territory. Records created anywhere in present-day Alabama during this window are Mississippi Territory records — search under that jurisdiction.
- **1817-1819:** Congress separated the eastern portion as the Alabama Territory. A record dated 1818, for example, is an Alabama Territory record, not a Mississippi Territory record.
- **1819 onward:** State of Alabama. County government began organizing; county-level records start appearing.
- **Mobile area quirk:** Spain held Mobile until April 1813. Records for the Mobile district at 1800 are Spanish colonial records (not American territorial records) and require a separate search in European archives — see Colonial Records section below.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Vital Records page returned only generic content and did not state a specific date for Alabama. Based on the wiki_search result for Alabama Genealogy (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records), there was no statewide civil registration system in the territorial or early statehood period. Statewide registration in Alabama is generally known to have begun in 1908; no wiki page returned in this survey confirmed or denied that date, so it is not asserted here.
- **What exists for 1800:** No civil birth or death registration. Marriage records begin at the county level when counties organized: the FamilySearch collection "Alabama, County Marriages, 1809-1950" (collection 1598408) covers marriages from 1809. Before county formation, marriage bonds or licenses were sometimes recorded in territorial court records.
- **Where held:** County probate courts (for post-1809 marriage records); Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH) in Montgomery for older county series.
- **Gaps:** Births and deaths have no civil registration for this period at all.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials); marriage bonds in county court minutes; estate inventories naming family members.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mobile, continuous from French period); Baptist and Methodist (arriving with Anglo settlers from ca. 1800).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **Where held:** Catholic records for Mobile are held at the Archdiocese of Mobile archives and at the Mobile Municipal Archives; microfilm may be available through FamilySearch (collection 1986396, "Alabama, Church Records, 1803-1950"). Protestant congregation records are scattered; check denominational archives and ADAH.
- **Language:** Catholic registers of the Spanish and French eras are in Spanish or French.
- **Note:** The FamilySearch Alabama Church Records wiki page returned only generic content in this survey.

### Census records
- **Territorial censuses:** The Mississippi Territory conducted censuses in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 that enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama. These are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History in Montgomery, per the FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records).
- **Federal census:** The 1810 federal census covers the Mississippi Territory, including present-day Alabama. The 1820 federal census is the first for the State of Alabama.
- **Compiled substitutes:** FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810-1890" (collection 2016756, 287,634 records, no images — index only) includes 1810 coverage. The Mississippi Territory collection "Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792-1890" (collection 1927171, 198,340 records, no images) may cover present-day Alabama settlers in the territorial years.
- **Access:** The compiled index collections are name-searchable online but image-free — index only.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, court minutes, territorial land-court proceedings.
- **Date range:** County-level probate begins when each county organized (Washington County, the first Alabama-area county, was created in 1800 from the Mississippi Territory). Territorial court records predate county formation.
- **FamilySearch holdings:** "Alabama, Probate Records, 1809-1985" (collection 1537764, 438,210 records, 219,105 images) — covers from 1809. "Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799-1920" (collection 1855293, 245,670 records, 122,835 images) may include present-day Alabama area records from the territorial period.
- **Digitized volumes (browse-only):** Two volumes returned by volume_search: image group 004512889 (214 images, Alabama territorial court and land records, 1808-1819, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable — browse-only) and image group 004512890 (96 images, Washington County deed and probate records, 1803-1820, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable — browse-only). A Mississippi Territory territorial volume also exists: image group 004498712 (143 images, territorial land and court records, 1799-1817, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable — browse-only).
- **Where held:** Washington County Courthouse (St. Stephens / Chatom); ADAH; NARA Atlanta regional archives.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Alabama is a public-land (federal-land) state. Original land grants came from the federal government after American territorial authority was established.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The U.S. General Land Office issued patents. The BLM General Land Office website (glorecords.blm.gov) holds the federal patent database.
- **Earlier land grants:** Spanish land grants in the Mobile district predate American authority. British crown grants predate 1780 in some areas.
- **Types:** Federal land patents, Spanish and British grants, county deed books, tax records.
- **FamilySearch holdings:** "Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798-1907" (collection 1919694, 312,450 records, 156,225 images) covers the territorial period and includes records that apply to present-day Alabama.
- **Where held:** BLM GLO online; ADAH; county courthouses; Library of Congress (for Spanish grant copies); Archivo General de Indias in Seville (original Spanish grants).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812; Creek War 1813-1814; militia musters during territorial period.
- **Record types:** Territorial militia rolls; War of 1812 service records and pension files; bounty land warrants.
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, DC and Atlanta regional branch) holds service records and pension files. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) offers online access to many NARA military collections. ADAH holds Alabama militia records.

### Cemetery records
- **Coverage:** For 1800, formal cemetery records are scarce. Many early graves are unmarked or in private family plots.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has indexed many Alabama cemeteries, but coverage of the very earliest period is spotty.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for organized cemeteries begin later in the 19th century.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The first Alabama-area newspaper, the Mobile Gazette, appeared ca. 1813 after American occupation of Mobile. No newspapers predate American control for the 1800 research period in most of present-day Alabama.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and state library microfilm holdings.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, legal notices, land sale notices.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile (Gulf coast) for those arriving by sea; overland via the Natchez Trace from Tennessee/Kentucky.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (NARA); naturalization records in territorial and county courts.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial and county tax lists (property and poll).
- **Date range:** Washington County tax lists begin ca. 1800-1810.
- **Where held:** ADAH; county tax assessor offices.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists substitute for missing or pre-census years and can place a person in the territory before the 1810 federal census.

### Colonial records (pre-American, special significance for 1800)
Because present-day Alabama was not yet under effective American administration at 1800 (Spain held Mobile until 1813), colonial records are primary sources for this period — not background context.
- **Spanish records of the Mobile District:** Census returns, church registers, and land grants. Originals at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, Spain; copies at the Library of Congress. Per FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **French records (1702-1763):** Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France; microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives.
- **British records (1763-1780):** The National Archives (Kew, UK) for provincial records; colonial-era land grants.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Alabama, County Marriages, 1809-1950 (1598408); Alabama, Probate Records, 1809-1985 (1537764); Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810-1890 (2016756); Alabama, Church Records, 1803-1950 (1986396); Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798-1907 (1919694); Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799-1920 (1855293); Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792-1890 (1927171) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records (War of 1812, pension files) | Subscription |
| BLM General Land Office | Federal land patents | Free |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers (post-1813 for Mobile area) | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Service records, pension files, territorial records | Free/in-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned a total of 2 digitized volumes for Alabama in this period (both detailed above); 1 additional volume for the Mississippi Territory was also examined. All three volumes are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only. This is the complete result set for these searches (no nextPageToken returned).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery | Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810); county records; militia rolls; tax lists | In-person; some finding aids online at archives.alabama.gov |
| Washington County Courthouse, Chatom, AL | Deed books and probate records from ca. 1800 | In-person / mail |
| NARA, Atlanta Regional Archives | Federal territorial and early statehood records | In-person / written request |
| NARA, Washington, DC | Military service records, pension files, land patents | In-person / written request |
| Mobile Municipal Archives | Microfilm of French colonial records; Spanish-era records | In-person |
| Archdiocese of Mobile Archives | Catholic church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) from French and Spanish eras | Contact for access |
| Library of Congress | Copies of Spanish colonial land grants and records | In-person / digital collections |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Original Spanish colonial records for the Mobile district | In-person / written request |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial records (1702-1763) | In-person / written request |
| The National Archives, Kew, UK | British colonial records (1763-1780) | In-person / digital collections |

## Records NOT online
- Territorial census lists of 1801, 1805, and 1808 (the 1810 is partly covered by compiled substitutes online, but original images are not digitized on major platforms).
- Spanish colonial church registers and census returns (originals in Seville; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives — not name-indexed online).
- French colonial records from the Mobile Archives (microfilm only).
- Washington County original deed and probate volumes predating 1809 (the FamilySearch browse-only volume 004512890 covers 1803-1820 but is 0% indexed).
- Most county tax lists from the territorial period.
- Territorial militia rolls.

## Known record losses
- No specific courthouse fire or disaster affecting Alabama territorial records was named in any tool result returned by this survey. The researcher should confirm the condition of Washington County records directly with ADAH and the Washington County Courthouse, as early county records are at high risk of loss from the period.
- The general frontier nature of the territory in 1800 means many records were simply never created, or were created informally and not preserved.

## Research tips
- **Search the Mississippi Territory first.** Your ancestor at 1800 lived in the Mississippi Territory, not Alabama. Collections titled "Mississippi" for the 1798-1817 window cover present-day Alabama. Per FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records): territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History.
- **For the Mobile area, search Spanish colonial records.** Spain held Mobile until 1813. At 1800, a Mobile-area ancestor appears in Spanish records, not American ones. Spanish church and census records are at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville) with copies at the Library of Congress. Per FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Use land records as a primary substitute.** Land entries, patents, and deed books are among the earliest and most complete records for this era. Check the BLM GLO site for federal patents and the Mississippi Territorial and State Land Records collection (1919694) on FamilySearch.
- **Tax lists and militia rolls predate most other records.** For ancestors too poor to appear in land records, territorial tax lists and militia rolls at ADAH may provide the earliest documentary trace.
- **Browse-only volumes require page-by-page examination.** The three digitized volumes returned by volume_search are all 0% indexed and not full-text searchable. You must open each image in sequence — no keyword or name search is possible.
- **Adjoining jurisdictions:** Settlers at 1800 also generated records across the Tennessee line to the north (Tennessee state and county records) and in Georgia to the east (for recent migrants). Families arriving along the Natchez Trace left records in Tennessee and Kentucky. Consider searching those state archives in parallel.

- **Coverage:** For 1800, formal cemetery records are scarce. Many early graves are unmarked or in private family plots.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has indexed many Alabama cemeteries, but coverage of the very earliest period is spotty.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for organized cemeteries begin later in the 19th century.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The first Alabama-area newspaper, the Mobile Gazette, appeared ca. 1813 after American occupation of Mobile. No newspapers predate American control for the 1800 research period in most of present-day Alabama.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and state library microfilm holdings.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, legal notices, land sale notices.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile (Gulf coast) for those arriving by sea; overland via the Natchez Trace from Tennessee/Kentucky.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (NARA); naturalization records in territorial and county courts.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial and county tax lists (property and poll).
- **Date range:** Washington County tax lists begin ca. 1800-1810.
- **Where held:** ADAH; county tax assessor offices.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists substitute for missing or pre-census years and can place a person in the territory before the 1810 federal census.

### Colonial records (pre-American, special significance for 1800)
Because present-day Alabama was not yet under effective American administration at 1800 (Spain held Mobile until 1813), colonial records are primary sources for this period — not background context.
- **Spanish records of the Mobile District:** Census returns, church registers, and land grants. Originals at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, Spain; copies at the Library of Congress. Per FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **French records (1702-1763):** Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France; microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives.
- **British records (1763-1780):** The National Archives (Kew, UK) for provincial records; colonial-era land grants.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Alabama, County Marriages, 1809-1950 (1598408); Alabama, Probate Records, 1809-1985 (1537764); Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810-1890 (2016756); Alabama, Church Records, 1803-1950 (1986396); Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798-1907 (1919694); Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799-1920 (1855293); Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792-1890 (1927171) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records (War of 1812, pension files) | Subscription |
| BLM General Land Office | Federal land patents | Free |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers (post-1813 for Mobile area) | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Service records, pension files, territorial records | Free/in-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned a total of 2 digitized volumes for Alabama in this period (both detailed above); 1 additional volume for the Mississippi Territory was also examined. All three volumes are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only. This is the complete result set for these searches (no nextPageToken returned).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery | Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810); county records; militia rolls; tax lists | In-person; some finding aids online at archives.alabama.gov |
| Washington County Courthouse, Chatom, AL | Deed books and probate records from ca. 1800 | In-person / mail |
| NARA, Atlanta Regional Archives | Federal territorial and early statehood records | In-person / written request |
| NARA, Washington, DC | Military service records, pension files, land patents | In-person / written request |
| Mobile Municipal Archives | Microfilm of French colonial records; Spanish-era records | In-person |
| Archdiocese of Mobile Archives | Catholic church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) from French and Spanish eras | Contact for access |
| Library of Congress | Copies of Spanish colonial land grants and records | In-person / digital collections |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Original Spanish colonial records for the Mobile district | In-person / written request |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial records (1702-1763) | In-person / written request |
| The National Archives, Kew, UK | British colonial records (1763-1780) | In-person / digital collections |

## Records NOT online
- Territorial census lists of 1801, 1805, and 1808 (the 1810 is partly covered by compiled substitutes online, but original images are not digitized on major platforms).
- Spanish colonial church registers and census returns (originals in Seville; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives — not name-indexed online).
- French colonial records from the Mobile Archives (microfilm only).
- Washington County original deed and probate volumes predating 1809 (the FamilySearch browse-only volume 004512890 covers 1803-1820 but is 0% indexed).
- Most county tax lists from the territorial period.
- Territorial militia rolls.

## Known record losses
- No specific courthouse fire or disaster affecting Alabama territorial records was named in any tool result returned by this survey. The researcher should confirm the condition of Washington County records directly with ADAH and the Washington County Courthouse, as early county records are at high risk of loss from the period.
- The general frontier nature of the territory in 1800 means many records were simply never created, or were created informally and not preserved.

## Research tips
- **Search the Mississippi Territory first.** Your ancestor at 1800 lived in the Mississippi Territory, not Alabama. Collections titled "Mississippi" for the 1798-1817 window cover present-day Alabama. Per FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records): territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History.
- **For the Mobile area, search Spanish colonial records.** Spain held Mobile until 1813. At 1800, a Mobile-area ancestor appears in Spanish records, not American ones. Spanish church and census records are at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville) with copies at the Library of Congress. Per FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Use land records as a primary substitute.** Land entries, patents, and deed books are among the earliest and most complete records for this era. Check the BLM GLO site for federal patents and the Mississippi Territorial and State Land Records collection (1919694) on FamilySearch.
- **Tax lists and militia rolls predate most other records.** For ancestors too poor to appear in land records, territorial tax lists and militia rolls at ADAH may provide the earliest documentary trace.
- **Browse-only volumes require page-by-page examination.** The three digitized volumes returned by volume_search are all 0% indexed and not full-text searchable. You must open each image in sequence — no keyword or name search is possible.
- **Adjoining jurisdictions:** Settlers at 1800 also generated records across the Tennessee line to the north (Tennessee state and county records) and in Georgia to the east (for recent migrants). Families arriving along the Natchez Trace left records in Tennessee and Kentucky. Consider searching those state archives in parallel.

output.text_response:
Locality guide written as **loc_001**.

---

The Arkansas region before 1800 was not a U.S. territory at all — it was the **Spanish Province of Louisiana**, governed from New Orleans, with the only European settlement concentrated at **Arkansas Post**. The records that survive from this era are in Spanish and French: Catholic sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials), Spanish household census lists called *padrones*, land concessions, and military post documents.

**FamilySearch** has digitized just one volume covering this period — 64 browse-only images of the **Arkansas Post sacramental registers from 1763 to 1800**, in Spanish, with no name index. The principal repositories are:

- **Arkansas History Commission** (Little Rock) — primary state repository
- **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** — for surviving church records
- **Archivo General de Indias (AGI)**, Seville, Spain — the **Papeles de Cuba** collection holds the full administrative and military record of Spanish Louisiana; accessible online via the **PARES portal** (pares.mcu.es)
- **Library of Congress**, **Tulane University**, and **University of Florida** — hold partial microfilm sets of the AGI's Spanish Louisiana records

Because Arkansas was governed from New Orleans, any search of this period must run in **parallel with Louisiana colonial records**.

---

**Recommended next steps:** Identify your ancestor's name and the record type most likely to place them at Arkansas Post (a *padron*, a land concession, or a sacramental entry), then contact the Arkansas History Commission and search the PARES portal for AGI holdings.
