The only FamilySearch digitized volume covering this period is image group 008814402: 64 images of Spanish colonial sacramental registers at Arkansas Post, 1763-1800, entirely in Spanish, 0% name-indexed — browse-only.
Spanish padrones (census-like household lists) and land concessions survive at the Arkansas History Commission (Little Rock) and in the Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Spain).

Catholic sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) from the French missionary period and the Spanish period are held by the Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock and in transcribed form at the Arkansas History Commission — per the FamilySearch Wiki Arkansas Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records).
Spanish colonial records are in Spanish; French colonial records are in French. Researchers must be able to read both languages or obtain translations.

The territory ceded secretly from Spain back to France in 1800, then passed to the United States via the Louisiana Purchase in 1803 — records created in 1800-1803 fall under French, then U.S. territorial administration.

FamilySearch's three indexed Arkansas collections (marriages 1837-1957, census index 1819-1870, Freedmen's Bureau 1865-1872) all postdate the colonial period and are not directly relevant to pre-1800 research.

The Archivo General de Indias in Seville holds the administrative backbone of Spanish Louisiana — military records, land grants, and colonial correspondence — and must be searched alongside domestic repositories.

Civil registration (births, marriages, deaths required by the state government) did not exist in this territory before 1800. Church records and colonial administrative records are the only vital-event substitutes.
The Library of Congress holds microfilm copies of some Spanish colonial Louisiana records — consult their Hispanic Division.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Arkansas (Spanish Colonial Period, pre-1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Arkansas Post established 1686 (French); Spanish colonial rule began 1763 under the Treaty of Paris; territory secretly retroceded to France 1800; transferred to the United States via the Louisiana Purchase 1803.
- **Administrative center:** Arkansas Post (present-day Arkansas County, Arkansas)
- **Parent jurisdiction (Spanish period):** Province of Louisiana, administered from New Orleans under the Viceroyalty of New Spain
- **Population during period:** Extremely sparse. European settlement was concentrated at Arkansas Post. FamilySearch population data returns no figures for this pre-statehood period; Arkansas was not enumerated in any U.S. federal census until 1810 (as part of Missouri Territory).
- **Economy:** Fur trade, subsistence farming, and military garrison activity. Arkansas Post functioned primarily as a trading and military outpost.
- **Ethnic composition:** French Canadian and French Creole settlers, Spanish colonial soldiers and officials, Native American populations (Quapaw and others), and a small enslaved African population.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (the only organized denomination present; served by French missionaries under Spanish colonial authority).
- **Key historical events:** French establishment of Arkansas Post (1686); transfer to Spain under the Treaty of Paris (1763); brief British occupation during the American Revolutionary War period; return to full Spanish control; secret retrocession to France (1800); Louisiana Purchase (1803).

## Boundary changes
- **1686-1762:** French colonial territory — Arkansas Post was part of French Louisiana.
- **1763-1800:** Spanish colonial territory — transferred to Spain by the Treaty of Paris (1763). Administered as the Province of Louisiana under the commandant at Arkansas Post, reporting to the governor in New Orleans.
- **1800:** Secretly retroceded to France by the Treaty of San Ildefonso (October 1800), though Spanish officials remained in effective control until American arrival in 1803.
- **1803:** Louisiana Purchase — U.S. territorial administration began.
- **Records follow the colonial administration, not modern state boundaries.** Arkansas was not a separate governmental entity before 1819 (Arkansas Territory). For this period, records are tied to the military post at Arkansas Post and the colonial government centered in New Orleans.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration existed in the colonial period. The State of Arkansas did not require civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths until after statehood (1836). The FamilySearch Wiki's Arkansas-specific vital records page returned only generic content in this survey, so no specific statewide registration start date for the later period is confirmed here from that page — consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly for post-statehood dates.
- **What exists for pre-1800:** None. Church sacramental registers are the only vital-event source.
- **Where held:** N/A for civil registration.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic sacramental registers (see Church records below).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic exclusively. French Recollect and Jesuit missionaries served the post from the early 1700s; Spanish Capuchin missionaries served during the colonial period.

Locality guide written as **loc_001**.

---

The Arkansas region before 1800 was not a U.S. territory at all — it was the Spanish Province of Louisiana, governed from New Orleans, with the only European settlement concentrated at Arkansas Post. The records that survive from this era are in Spanish and French: Catholic sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials), Spanish household census lists called padrones, land concessions, and military post documents. The Library of Congress, Tulane University, and the University of Florida hold partial microfilm sets of those Seville records. Because Arkansas was governed from New Orleans, any search of this period must run in parallel with Louisiana colonial records.

The logical next step is to identify your specific ancestor's name and the record type most likely to place them at Arkansas Post (a padron, a land concession, or a sacramental entry), then contact the Arkansas History Commission and consult the PARES online portal (pares.mcu.es) for the AGI's holdings.

Here is what the locality-guide agent found:

---

## Ohio circa 1790 — Locality Guide

### Jurisdictional Context: Northwest Territory, Not Ohio

Researching ancestors in Ohio around 1790 means working entirely within the **Northwest Territory**, not the state of Ohio, which did not exist until **1803**. The territory was governed under the **Northwest Ordinance of 1787**, and counties were organized rapidly as settlers arrived:

- **Washington County** — established 1788, covering a vast swath of territory from the Ohio River
- **Hamilton County** — established 1790 in the southwest
- County boundaries shifted *constantly* as new counties were carved from older ones

> **Critical first step:** Determine which county held jurisdiction at the date and place of your ancestor's event — not which county exists there today.

The **Ohio History Connection** in Columbus is the central archive for this pre-statehood era, holding early territorial court records, land entry records, and county tax lists.

---

### Vital Records Gap

**No civil vital records exist for this period.** Ohio did not require county-level registration of births and deaths until 1867, and statewide registration didn't begin until 1908. This means:

- **Church records are the only documentary source** for baptisms, marriages, and burials in 1790
- FamilySearch holds a county marriages collection beginning in 1789 and a church records collection from 1787, but survival for the territorial period is thin — many early congregations were served by itinerant ministers who kept no systematic registers

---

### Best Available Sources

**Land records are the most reliable substitute** for missing vitals — they can establish a person's presence, approximate age, and neighbors. However, Ohio used **three different survey systems simultaneously**, each at a different repository:

| Survey System | Repository |
|---|---|
| Congress Lands | BLM General Land Office (GLO) patent database |
| Virginia Military District | Virginia Military District warrants held in **Richmond, VA** |
| Connecticut Western Reserve | Separate repository from FamilySearch |

> **Warning:** Searching only FamilySearch will miss the Virginia Military District records held in Richmond.

---

### Recommended Next Steps

1. Identify the specific county and land district that applied to your ancestor's location in 1790
2. Search the **Ohio History Connection** finding aids
3. Search the **BLM General Land Office** patent database
4. For Virginia Military District warrants, check Richmond, VA sources
5. Check the FamilySearch collections for county marriages (from 1789) and church records (from 1787)

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Ohio (Northwest Territory Era) (1780-1803)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The Northwest Territory was established 13 July 1787 by the Northwest Ordinance. Ohio became a state on 1 March 1803 — the first state carved from the Territory.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Territorial government centered at Marietta (seat of Washington County, organized 1788); Cincinnati grew as center of Hamilton County (organized 1790).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Northwest Territory, United States (1787-1803), which itself was administered under the authority of the U.S. Congress.
- **Population during period:** Population data tools returned no results for this period. According to Wikipedia, the region was sparsely settled by American colonists in 1790, with the first federal census (1790) covering only limited settler populations in the Territory. Native peoples — Shawnee, Delaware, Wyandot, and Miami — were the predominant inhabitants.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, fur trade, military garrison economy around forts (Fort Washington at Cincinnati). Land speculation was a major economic driver.
- **Ethnic composition:** Early American settlers were predominantly of English, Scots-Irish, German, and Virginia background. Significant Virginia veteran presence in the Military District. Connecticut settlers in the Western Reserve.
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist circuit riders, Presbyterian, Baptist, and Quaker congregations were among the earliest organized. Catholic presence at some French trading posts. Many settlers in 1790 had no organized church affiliation yet.
- **Key historical events:** Northwest Ordinance (1787) established territorial government and banned slavery; Treaty of Greenville (1795) ended major Native resistance and opened most of Ohio to settlement; statehood 1803.

## Boundary changes
- **1787:** Entire Ohio country becomes part of the Northwest Territory under the Ordinance of 1787.
- **1788:** Washington County organized — the first county in the Territory, covering all of present Ohio east of the Scioto River and beyond.
- **1790:** Hamilton County organized, covering the southwestern portion of what is now Ohio.
- **1796:** Adams, Trumbull, Jefferson, and other counties organized as settlement expanded.
- **1788-1803:** County boundaries changed extremely frequently as population grew and new counties were carved from parent counties. A location in one county in 1790 could be in a differently named county by 1795 and yet another by 1803.
- **Implication for researchers:** You must determine the specific county in which your ancestor's event occurred *at the date of that event*, not based on modern boundaries. The Ohio History Connection maintains boundary histories. Records follow the county that held jurisdiction at the time — not the county that exists today.
- **Note on geographic splits:** Because county formation was a geographic division (not a simple renaming), when a county was divided the records of events before the split remained with the original county, while later events in the newly created area went to the new county. Which side holds a given record depends on exactly where within the original county the event occurred.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed in Ohio territory in 1790. Ohio did not require vital registration even at the county level until 1867 (county-level births and deaths), and statewide registration did not begin until 1908. The FamilySearch Wiki-specific Ohio Vital Records page did not return distinct content; this dating is drawn from the generic repository guidance and general knowledge of Ohio registration history — researchers should verify at the Ohio History Connection.
- **What exists:** No civil birth, marriage, or death records for 1790. County marriage bonds and registers began in some Ohio counties in the 1790s — FamilySearch has indexed the collection 'Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2013' (collection 1803785), which begins in 1789 and covers 1,523,678 records with images. This is the earliest civil marriage documentation available.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (indexed + images for marriages from 1789): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1803785. Original registers at county courthouses and the Ohio History Connection.
- **Gaps:** Births and deaths in 1790 have no civil record. Coverage in the 1789-1803 period is sparse — only the earliest organized counties (Washington, Hamilton) would have any records, and recording was inconsistent.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the primary vital-event source. Family bibles, letters, and land records naming family members are also essential.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Quaker were the earliest organized denominations reaching the Ohio frontier by the 1790s. Catholic at some early settlements. Many settlers in 1790 were unchurched or served only by itinerant circuit riders who may not have maintained written registers.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials. Confirmation records where applicable. Methodist circuit records may survive.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch has an 'Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950' collection (collection 2246917, 678,234 records with images): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2246917. Denominational archives (Methodist archives, Presbyterian historical society, Quaker repositories) hold additional records. Ohio History Connection holds some church record microfilm.
- **Language:** English.
- **Caveat:** Church record survival for 1790 is thin. Many early Ohio congregations did not maintain systematic registers, or those registers have not survived or been digitized.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The first federal census (1790) covered the Northwest Territory, but Ohio-area settlers were so few that coverage is minimal. The 1800 census enumerated the Territory more fully. FamilySearch and Ancestry hold indexes and images of both. The 1790 census did NOT enumerate Native peoples.
- **State/territorial census:** No Ohio territorial census is known to have been conducted between federal enumerations for this period.
- **Access:** 1790 and 1800 federal censuses are indexed and available on FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription). The generic wiki pages returned by the tools note that federal census records are available from 1790.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, guardianships, letters of administration. Territorial court records (civil and criminal). Naturalization filings (territorial courts had this authority).
- **Date range:** Washington County court records from 1788; Hamilton County from 1790.
- **Where held:** Ohio History Connection (Columbus) holds territorial-era court and probate records. Some county courthouses retain originals. The FamilySearch Catalog (catalog_search) and the Ohio History Connection finding aids are the best starting points for identifying specific volumes.
- **Digitization:** The FamilySearch-specific Ohio Probate Records page returned only generic content. No probate volumes for the 1780-1803 window appeared in volume_search results (only 2 volumes total were returned for the period: territorial land records and Washington County tax records).

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Ohio is a federal-land state (public-domain), but THREE different survey systems applied simultaneously in this period:
  1. **Congress Lands** (most of Ohio): rectangular township-and-range system, the first federal public land survey in the US. Patents available at the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM GLO) website: https://glorecords.blm.gov/
  2. **Virginia Military District** (between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers): metes-and-bounds system for Virginia Revolutionary War land warrants. Records at the Virginia State Library (Richmond), not Ohio repositories.
  3. **Connecticut Western Reserve** (northeastern Ohio): separate survey system. Records at the Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland.
- **Types:** Land grants, patents, warrants, deeds, entries. For Congress Lands, the BLM GLO database is the primary index. For Virginia Military District, Virginia warrant records must be consulted.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch has 'Ohio, Land Records, 1787-1840' (collection 1542187, 234,567 records with images): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542187. This begins at 1787 and covers the early territorial period.
- **Where held:** BLM GLO online (Congress Lands patents); Virginia State Library (Virginia Military District); Western Reserve Historical Society (Connecticut Western Reserve); Ohio History Connection; county courthouses (deed books from county formation).
- **Source from wiki_search:** The wiki_search result specifically names the Virginia Military District and Connecticut Western Reserve distinctions (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Northwest Indian War (1785-1795), culminating in the Battle of Fallen Timbers (1794) and Treaty of Greenville (1795). Militia musters and continental/federal service records.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (a major reason veterans settled in the Virginia Military District). These are held at the National Archives (NARA) in Washington, D.C., and on Fold3 (subscription): https://www.fold3.com/
- **Where held:** NARA; FamilySearch has pension and bounty land warrant indexes. Revolutionary War pension files are on Fold3.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Pioneer-era cemeteries in the Ohio country were small farm or community plots, often unmarked or with wooden markers that have not survived. Organized municipal and church cemeteries came later.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes what survives. Coverage for 1790 burials is very sparse.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records were uncommon for 1790 Ohio; most burial information, if it survives, comes from church registers or family records.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The first Ohio newspaper, the Centinel of the North-Western Territory, began publication in Cincinnati in 1793. Coverage before 1803 is minimal.
- **Where held:** Early Ohio newspapers are held at the Ohio History Connection and are partially available through Chronicling America (Library of Congress): https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/
- **Content value:** Marriage notices, legal notices, death notices begin to appear from the mid-1790s, but survival and coverage are thin.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Settlers in 1790 Ohio typically arrived overland (via the Ohio River from Pittsburgh) or through Virginia, not directly through seaports. Port of entry records are less directly applicable than overland migration records.
- **Record types:** Naturalization declarations were filed in territorial courts (any court of record). Pre-1906 naturalizations can appear in county court minutes. NARA holds consolidated indexes.
- **Where held:** Territorial court minute books at the Ohio History Connection. NARA for consolidated indexes.
- **Content note:** The Ohio River was the main migration corridor — look for records in Pennsylvania and Virginia counties the settler passed through (Allegheny County PA; Ohio County VA/WV) as well as Ohio territory records.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial and early county tax lists (property and poll tax).
- **Date range:** FamilySearch has 'Ohio, Tax Records, 1800-1850' (collection 1987542, 345,890 records with images): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987542. This begins at 1800 — not 1790. Pre-1800 tax records exist only in manuscript form.
- **Where held:** Ohio History Connection; county auditors. Washington County tax records 1799-1803 appear in volume_search (imageGroupNumber 005112240, 73 images, 12% name-indexed — most must be browsed).
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the primary substitute for the very limited 1790 census coverage and for events not recorded in church or court records.

### Other record types
- **Territorial court records:** County court minute books record a wide range of business — road assignments, poor relief, payments, petitions — naming ordinary settlers not party to any formal suit. These are among the most important early Ohio sources and are held at the Ohio History Connection.
- **Town and county histories:** 19th-century published local histories for early Ohio counties frequently transcribe or abstract early records (court minutes, land entries, pioneer biographies). Search WorldCat for county history titles.
- **Ohio History Connection finding aids:** The Ohio History Connection (formerly Ohio Historical Society) in Columbus is the central repository for territorial-era records and maintains finding aids: https://www.ohiohistory.org/

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Ohio, County Marriages 1789-2013 (1,523,678 records); Ohio, Church Records 1787-1950 (678,234 records); Ohio, Land Records 1787-1840 (234,567 records); Ohio, Tax Records 1800-1850 (345,890 records); Territorial Land Records 1788-1799 (browse-only, 51 images); Washington Co. Tax Records 1799-1803 (12% indexed, 73 images) | Free |
| BLM General Land Office | Congress Lands patents from 1787 | Free (https://glorecords.blm.gov/) |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (1790, 1800); military records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military service and pension records | Subscription (https://www.fold3.com/) |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free (https://www.findagrave.com/) |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers (very sparse for 1790) | Subscription (https://www.newspapers.com/) |
| Chronicling America | Early Ohio newspapers from 1793 | Free |
| NARA | Military, naturalization, immigration | Free in-person; some online |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume_search returned 2 digitized volumes matching this place and period (totalResults: 2) — both are detailed above. This is the complete result set for the pre-1803 window.

**External links note:** The external_links_search returned 6 general-category links (Ancestry census, FamilySearch Wiki, FindAGrave, Newspapers.com, Fold3, NARA) — these are generic U.S. resources, not Ohio-specific curated collections. totalForPlace did not indicate Ohio-specific curated links beyond these for the 1780-1803 window.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Ohio History Connection (Columbus) | Territorial court records, county records, land records, newspaper microfilm, county histories | In-person; some online finding aids at ohiohistory.org |
| Virginia State Library (Richmond, VA) | Virginia Military District land warrants and patents | In-person / online |
| Western Reserve Historical Society (Cleveland) | Connecticut Western Reserve land and local records | In-person |

Locality guide written as `loc_001`.

---

Researching ancestors in Ohio around 1790 means you are working entirely within the Northwest Territory, not the state of Ohio, which did not exist until 1803. The territory was governed under the Northwest Ordinance of 1787, and counties were organized rapidly as settlers arrived: Washington County came first in 1788, covering a vast swath of the territory from the Ohio River, followed by Hamilton County in the southwest in 1790. County boundaries shifted constantly throughout this period as new counties were carved from older ones, so the most important first step is pinning down which county held jurisdiction at the date and place of your ancestor's event, not which county exists there today. Early territorial court records, land entry records, and county tax lists are held at the Ohio History Connection in Columbus, which is the central archive for this pre-statehood era.

The single most important caution for 1790 Ohio research is that no civil vital records exist at all. Ohio did not require county-level registration of births and deaths until 1867, and statewide registration did not begin until 1908, so church records are the only documentary source for baptisms, marriages, and burials in 1790. FamilySearch holds a county marriages collection beginning in 1789 and a church records collection from 1787, but survival for the territorial period is thin because many early congregations were served by itinerant ministers who kept no systematic registers. Land records are the most reliable source for establishing a person's presence, approximate age, and neighbors: Ohio used three different survey systems simultaneously (Congress Lands, the Virginia Military District, and the Connecticut Western Reserve), and each has its records at a different repository, so searching only FamilySearch will miss the Virginia Military District warrants held in Richmond. The next step is to identify which specific county and land district applied to your ancestor's location, then search the Ohio History Connection finding aids and the BLM General Land Office patent database alongside the FamilySearch collections already noted.

# Locality Guide: Ohio (Northwest Territory Era) (1780-1803)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The Northwest Territory was established 13 July 1787 by the Northwest Ordinance. Ohio became a state on 1 March 1803 — the first state carved from the Territory.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Territorial government centered at Marietta (seat of Washington County, organized 1788); Cincinnati grew as center of Hamilton County (organized 1790).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Northwest Territory, United States (1787-1803), which itself was administered under the authority of the U.S. Congress.
- **Population during period:** Population data tools returned no results for this period. According to Wikipedia, the region was sparsely settled by American colonists in 1790, with the first federal census (1790) covering only limited settler populations in the Territory. Native peoples — Shawnee, Delaware, Wyandot, and Miami — were the predominant inhabitants.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, fur trade, military garrison economy around forts (Fort Washington at Cincinnati). Land speculation was a major economic driver.
- **Ethnic composition:** Early American settlers were predominantly of English, Scots-Irish, German, and Virginia background. Significant Virginia veteran presence in the Military District. Connecticut settlers in the Western Reserve.
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist circuit riders, Presbyterian, Baptist, and Quaker congregations were among the earliest organized. Catholic presence at some French trading posts. Many settlers in 1790 had no organized church affiliation yet.
- **Key historical events:** Northwest Ordinance (1787) established territorial government and banned slavery; Treaty of Greenville (1795) ended major Native resistance and opened most of Ohio to settlement; statehood 1803.

## Boundary changes
- **1787:** Entire Ohio country becomes part of the Northwest Territory under the Ordinance of 1787.
- **1788:** Washington County organized — the first county in the Territory, covering all of present Ohio east of the Scioto River and beyond.
- **1790:** Hamilton County organized, covering the southwestern portion of what is now Ohio.
- **1796:** Adams, Trumbull, Jefferson, and other counties organized as settlement expanded.
- **1788-1803:** County boundaries changed extremely frequently as population grew and new counties were carved from parent counties. A location in one county in 1790 could be in a differently named county by 1795 and yet another by 1803.
- **Implication for researchers:** You must determine the specific county in which your ancestor's event occurred *at the date of that event*, not based on modern boundaries. The Ohio History Connection maintains boundary histories. Records follow the county that held jurisdiction at the time — not the county that exists today.
- **Note on geographic splits:** Because county formation was a geographic division (not a simple renaming), when a county was divided the records of events before the split remained with the original county, while later events in the newly created area went to the new county. Which side holds a given record depends on exactly where within the original county the event occurred.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed in Ohio territory in 1790. Ohio did not require vital registration even at the county level until 1867 (county-level births and deaths), and statewide registration did not begin until 1908. The FamilySearch Wiki-specific Ohio Vital Records page did not return distinct content; this dating is drawn from the generic repository guidance and general knowledge of Ohio registration history — researchers should verify at the Ohio History Connection.
- **What exists:** No civil birth, marriage, or death records for 1790. County marriage bonds and registers began in some Ohio counties in the 1790s — FamilySearch has indexed the collection 'Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2013' (collection 1803785), which begins in 1789 and covers 1,523,678 records with images. This is the earliest civil marriage documentation available.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (indexed + images for marriages from 1789): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1803785. Original registers at county courthouses and the Ohio History Connection.
- **Gaps:** Births and deaths in 1790 have no civil record. Coverage in the 1789-1803 period is sparse — only the earliest organized counties (Washington, Hamilton) would have any records, and recording was inconsistent.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the primary vital-event source. Family bibles, letters, and land records naming family members are also essential.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Quaker were the earliest organized denominations reaching the Ohio frontier by the 1790s. Catholic at some early settlements. Many settlers in 1790 were unchurched or served only by itinerant circuit riders who may not have maintained written registers.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials. Confirmation records where applicable. Methodist circuit records may survive.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch has an 'Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950' collection (collection 2246917, 678,234 records with images): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2246917. Denominational archives (Methodist archives, Presbyterian historical society, Quaker repositories) hold additional records. Ohio History Connection holds some church record microfilm.
- **Language:** English.
- **Caveat:** Church record survival for 1790 is thin. Many early Ohio congregations did not maintain systematic registers, or those registers have not survived or been digitized.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The first federal census (1790) covered the Northwest Territory, but Ohio-area settlers were so few that coverage is minimal. The 1800 census enumerated the Territory more fully. FamilySearch and Ancestry hold indexes and images of both. The 1790 census did NOT enumerate Native peoples.
- **State/territorial census:** No Ohio territorial census is known to have been conducted between federal enumerations for this period.
- **Access:** 1790 and 1800 federal censuses are indexed and available on FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription). The generic wiki pages returned by the tools note that federal census records are available from 1790.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, guardianships, letters of administration. Territorial court records (civil and criminal). Naturalization filings (territorial courts had this authority).
- **Date range:** Washington County court records from 1788; Hamilton County from 1790.
- **Where held:** Ohio History Connection (Columbus) holds territorial-era court and probate records. Some county courthouses retain originals. The FamilySearch Catalog (catalog_search) and the Ohio History Connection finding aids are the best starting points for identifying specific volumes.
- **Digitization:** The FamilySearch-specific Ohio Probate Records page returned only generic content. No probate volumes for the 1780-1803 window appeared in volume_search results (only 2 volumes total were returned for the period: territorial land records and Washington County tax records).

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Ohio is a federal-land state (public-domain), but THREE different survey systems applied simultaneously in this period:
  1. **Congress Lands** (most of Ohio): rectangular township-and-range system, the first federal public land survey in the US. Patents available at the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM GLO) website: https://glorecords.blm.gov/
  2. **Virginia Military District** (between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers): metes-and-bounds system for Virginia Revolutionary War land warrants. Records at the Virginia State Library (Richmond), not Ohio repositories.
  3. **Connecticut Western Reserve** (northeastern Ohio): separate survey system. Records at the Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland.
- **Types:** Land grants, patents, warrants, deeds, entries. For Congress Lands, the BLM GLO database is the primary index. For Virginia Military District, Virginia warrant records must be consulted.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch has 'Ohio, Land Records, 1787-1840' (collection 1542187, 234,567 records with images): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542187. This begins at 1787 and covers the early territorial period.
- **Where held:** BLM GLO online (Congress Lands patents); Virginia State Library (Virginia Military District); Western Reserve Historical Society (Connecticut Western Reserve); Ohio History Connection; county courthouses (deed books from county formation).
- **Source from wiki_search:** The wiki_search result specifically names the Virginia Military District and Connecticut Western Reserve distinctions (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Northwest Indian War (1785-1795), culminating in the Battle of Fallen Timbers (1794) and Treaty of Greenville (1795). Militia musters and continental/federal service records.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (a major reason veterans settled in the Virginia Military District). These are held at the National Archives (NARA) in Washington, D.C., and on Fold3 (subscription): https://www.fold3.com/
- **Where held:** NARA; FamilySearch has pension and bounty land warrant indexes. Revolutionary War pension files are on Fold3.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Pioneer-era cemeteries in the Ohio country were small farm or community plots, often unmarked or with wooden markers that have not survived. Organized municipal and church cemeteries came later.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes what survives. Coverage for 1790 burials is very sparse.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records were uncommon for 1790 Ohio; most burial information, if it survives, comes from church registers or family records.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The first Ohio newspaper, the Centinel of the North-Western Territory, began publication in Cincinnati in 1793. Coverage before 1803 is minimal.
- **Where held:** Early Ohio newspapers are held at the Ohio History Connection and are partially available through Chronicling America (Library of Congress): https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/
- **Content value:** Marriage notices, legal notices, death notices begin to appear from the mid-1790s, but survival and coverage are thin.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Settlers in 1790 Ohio typically arrived overland (via the Ohio River from Pittsburgh) or through Virginia, not directly through seaports. Port of entry records are less directly applicable than overland migration records.
- **Record types:** Naturalization declarations were filed in territorial courts (any court of record). Pre-1906 naturalizations can appear in county court minutes. NARA holds consolidated indexes.
- **Where held:** Territorial court minute books at the Ohio History Connection. NARA for consolidated indexes.
- **Content note:** The Ohio River was the main migration corridor — look for records in Pennsylvania and Virginia counties the settler passed through (Allegheny County PA; Ohio County VA/WV) as well as Ohio territory records.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial and early county tax lists (property and poll tax).
- **Date range:** FamilySearch has 'Ohio, Tax Records, 1800-1850' (collection 1987542, 345,890 records with images): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987542. This begins at 1800 — not 1790. Pre-1800 tax records exist only in manuscript form.
- **Where held:** Ohio History Connection; county auditors. Washington County tax records 1799-1803 appear in volume_search (imageGroupNumber 005112240, 73 images, 12% name-indexed — most must be browsed).
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the primary substitute for the very limited 1790 census coverage and for events not recorded in church or court records.

### Other record types
- **Territorial court records:** County court minute books record a wide range of business — road assignments, poor relief, payments, petitions — naming ordinary settlers not party to any formal suit. These are among the most important early Ohio sources and are held at the Ohio History Connection.
- **Town and county histories:** 19th-century published local histories for early Ohio counties frequently transcribe or abstract early records (court minutes, land entries, pioneer biographies). Search WorldCat for county history titles.
- **Ohio History Connection finding aids:** The Ohio History Connection (formerly Ohio Historical Society) in Columbus is the central repository for territorial-era records and maintains finding aids: https://www.ohiohistory.org/

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848-1870)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** California was admitted as the 31st state on September 9, 1850, bypassing territorial status entirely.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Sacramento (state capital); San Francisco was the dominant commercial port and entry point.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Before statehood, California was a Mexican territory (ceded to the United States under the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, 1848); briefly under U.S. military government 1848-1850.
- **Population during period:** Approximately 92,597 in the 1850 federal census; roughly 380,000 by 1860 (driven by the Gold Rush influx of ~300,000 migrants from 1848 onward, per Wikipedia/California Gold Rush).
- **Economy:** Placer and hard-rock gold mining dominated 1848-1855; agriculture, ranching, and commerce expanded through the 1860s. Mining supply towns (Sacramento, Stockton, San Francisco) served as commercial hubs.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Anglo-American male migrants from the eastern United States; also significant numbers from Chile, Mexico, China, France, Australia, and the British Isles. A pre-existing Hispanic (Californio) and Native Californian population was already present.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (dominant pre-Gold Rush, through the Mission system); Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, Presbyterian, and other Protestant denominations arrived with Anglo migrants in the late 1840s-1850s. Chinese immigrants brought Buddhist and other non-Christian traditions.
- **Key historical events:** Discovery of gold at Sutter's Mill, January 24, 1848; California statehood September 9, 1850; peak Gold Rush migration 1849-1852; Comstock Lode silver rush (Nevada) drew some Californians away after 1859.

## Boundary changes
- California had no prior U.S. territorial period — it jumped directly from Mexican territory to U.S. statehood. Records before 1848 are Mexican or Spanish colonial.
- County boundaries shifted considerably in the early 1850s as the legislature created new counties out of large original ones. If researching a specific mining county, check when it was formed and which county held records before it.
- The state was stable as a unit from 1850 onward; no boundary changes affected California's external borders during this period.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** County-level marriage registration began at statehood (1850). The FamilySearch California Vital Records wiki page returned only generic content — the California-specific start date for statewide birth and death registration was not confirmed by a fetched wiki page. Based on the generic page's guidance that many U.S. states did not require statewide registration until the early 1900s, do not assume statewide birth and death registration existed in the 1850s. Consult the [California Vital Records FamilySearch Wiki page](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Vital_Records) directly for exact dates.
- **What exists:** County birth records from 1850, indexed on FamilySearch (collection 2017276, 789,456 records). County marriage records from 1850 (collection 1452832, 567,890 records). Death registration for this period is sparse — civil death registration at the county level was inconsistent before 1905.
- **Where held:** County courthouses (original); FamilySearch has digitized county births and marriages.
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth or death registration during the 1850s-1860s. Many miners left no vital record at all.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (see below); cemetery sexton records; newspaper obituaries and death notices.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mission system, pre-dating Gold Rush); Methodist, Episcopal, Presbyterian, Baptist, and Congregationalist (arriving with Anglo migrants from late 1840s onward).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and confirmations. Catholic mission registers (1769-1850) are indexed on FamilySearch (collection 1804372, 98,765 records) but predate the Gold Rush migration and document the Hispanic/Native population, not Anglo 49ers.
- **Where held:** Diocesan archives (Roman Catholic Diocese of Monterey and later Diocese of San Francisco archives); individual congregation records vary widely. FamilySearch holds microfilm of some California church records.
- **Language:** Catholic mission records are in Spanish and Latin. Anglo Protestant records are in English.
- **Note:** For Gold Rush-era Anglo migrants, Protestant church records are the most relevant vital substitute but coverage is uneven — many mining camps had no established church.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1850 federal census was California's first but was partially destroyed — some county returns are missing ([California Genealogy, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records)). The 1860 and 1870 federal censuses are complete and fully indexed.
- **State census:** California conducted a state census in 1852, which is the primary substitute for missing 1850 county returns. This volume (DGS 006601001) covers 1850-1852, has 522 images, is 88% name-indexed, and is full-text searchable — the most accessible census substitute for this period.
- **Mortality schedules:** The 1850, 1860, and 1870 federal censuses included mortality schedules listing persons who died in the twelve months preceding enumeration — a valuable death record substitute.
- **Access:** 1852 state census: indexed + full-text searchable (FamilySearch DGS 006601001). Federal censuses 1860, 1870: indexed + images (FamilySearch and Ancestry).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, and estate distributions. Because Gold Rush migrants were often transient and single men, intestate administration (dying without a will) is more common than testate (with a will) — search administration files, not just the will indexes, when the person died in California.
- **Date range:** From 1850 at the county level.
- **Where held:** County courthouses (originals); some have been microfilmed by FamilySearch but specific California probate volumes were not confirmed in the volume_search results for this period.
- **Court records:** Naturalizations before 1906 could be filed in any court of record — county district courts, state courts, and federal courts. Check all three. County court minute books also recorded road maintenance responsibilities, poor relief recipients, and other business naming ordinary residents.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** California is a federal-land (public-domain) state — the U.S. General Land Office (GLO) administered land distribution after 1848. Metes-and-bounds descriptions are used for private land grants (ranchos) from the Mexican era.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM GLO) records portal (glorecords.blm.gov) holds federal land patents for California. The California State Archives holds Mexican-era land grant case files adjudicated under the Land Act of 1851.
- **Types:** Federal land patents (GLO), Mexican rancho grant confirmations, county deed books, mining claim registers, tax records.
- **Mining claim registers:** Held at county recorders' offices. FamilySearch has digitized a volume of San Francisco mining claim registers (DGS 006601002, 340 images, 1849-1855) — browse-only, no name index, no full-text search. Researchers must browse image by image.
- **Date range:** Federal patents from 1850; Mexican-era grant records predate statehood.
- **Where held:** BLM GLO website (federal patents, online free); California State Archives (land grant case files); county recorders (deed books); FamilySearch (some volumes, browse-only).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The Mexican-American War (1846-1848) immediately preceded the Gold Rush; some veterans settled in California. The Civil War (1861-1865) saw California raise volunteer regiments for Union service.
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files at NARA (Washington, D.C.); California volunteer regiment records at the California State Archives; draft registrations (Civil War-era) at NARA.
- **Where held:** NARA (national records); California State Archives (state militia/volunteer records); Fold3 (online, subscription) for digitized service and pension records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Gold Hill, Coloma, Sonora, and other mining-camp cemeteries; urban cemeteries in San Francisco, Sacramento, and Stockton. Many mining-camp graves are unmarked or lost.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) and BillionGraves hold transcriptions for many California cemeteries, but mining-era graves in remote camps are underrepresented.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records where they survive are held by county archives or local historical societies. Coverage is uneven.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Alta California (San Francisco, from 1849) is the most significant Gold Rush-era paper. Sacramento, Stockton, and mining-county papers appeared through the early 1850s.
- **Where held:** California Digital Newspaper Collection (cdnc.ucr.edu, free online); California State Library (microfilm); Newspapers.com (subscription).
- **Content value:** Death notices, obituaries, legal notices (mining claim disputes, probate notices), letters from miners, and arrival notices name individuals not found in formal records.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** San Francisco was the primary Pacific entry point. Panama (overland crossing to the Pacific), Cape Horn, and Valparaiso (Chile) routes all funneled through San Francisco. Overland migrants arrived via the California, Oregon, and Gila trails.
- **Record types:** Ship passenger manifests (arrivals at San Francisco, held at NARA Pacific Region, San Bruno, CA; digitized on Ancestry and FamilySearch). Port arrival registers for Sacramento (FamilySearch DGS 006601003, 298 images, 1849-1858) — browse-only, no name index. Overland migrants are largely undocumented in official arrival records.
- **Where held:** NARA Pacific Region, San Bruno (original passenger manifests); Ancestry.com and FamilySearch (digitized manifests).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with families. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members. Note that many '49ers came overland and will not appear in any ship manifest — look for trail diaries and journals at the Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley) and the California State Library.
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record. Declarations of intention and petitions for naturalization are scattered across county district courts and federal courts in California.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax and personal property tax records, beginning at county formation (1850 and onward as new counties were created).
- **Date range:** From 1850 at the county level.
- **Where held:** County archives and some state archives. Tax records are a valuable substitute for missing census years and can place a person in a specific county when other records do not.
- **Substitute value:** Because the 1850 federal census has gaps, county tax records from 1850-1852 can confirm a person's presence in a specific county during the height of the Gold Rush.

### Other record types
- **Great Registers (voter registration):** California's Great Registers began in 1866 (FamilySearch collection 1923340, 1,345,678 records, 1866-1910). They do not cover 1848-1865 but are invaluable for tracking men who remained in California after the Gold Rush. Each entry typically gives name, age, occupation, physical description, nativity, and county of registration.
- **County histories and local histories:** 19th-century county histories (often published in the 1880s) frequently include biographical sketches of Gold Rush-era pioneers — often the only narrative account of a miner who left no probate or land record. The Bancroft Library and California State Library hold extensive collections.
- **Manuscript collections:** The Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley) and the California State Library hold Gold Rush-era diaries, letters, journals, and organizational records not available anywhere online — essential for locating overland migrants and miners who left no documentary trail in formal records.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | County Births 1850-1919 (789,456 records); County Marriages 1850-1952 (567,890 records); Great Registers 1866-1910 (1,345,678 records); Mission Records 1769-1850 (98,765 records); 1852 State Census (DGS 006601001, 88% indexed, full-text); Mining Claim Registers SF (DGS 006601002, browse-only); Sacramento Port Arrivals (DGS 006601003, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (1850, 1860, 1870); San Francisco passenger manifests | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records and headstone transcriptions | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including Alta California | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military service records and pension files | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Passenger manifests, naturalization records, military records | Free finding aids; some records online |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents from 1850 | Free |
| California Digital Newspaper Collection (cdnc.ucr.edu) | Digitized California newspapers from 1849 | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** 14 digitized volumes match this place and period in volume_search; the 3 detailed above are the first page (nextPageToken present). Further volumes were not examined and may include additional county-level record sets.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| NARA Pacific Region, San Bruno, CA | Original ship passenger manifests, federal court naturalization records | In-person; some records microfilmed/digitized |
| California State Archives, Sacramento | State census (1852), land grant case files, state military records, county records transferred to state | In-person; some records online |
| California State Library, Sacramento | County histories, newspapers, manuscript collections, Gold Rush-era materials | In-person; some digitized |
| Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley | Extensive Gold Rush manuscript collections, diaries, journals, overland trail accounts | In-person by appointment |
| County courthouses | Deed books, probate files, court records, tax records, marriage registers | In-person or mail request; varies by county |
| Local historical and genealogical societies | Local histories, transcribed records, surname files | Contact individual societies |

## Records NOT online
- Most county-level tax records (pre-1870)
- Many county probate and court case files
- Mining claim records beyond the single San Francisco volume on FamilySearch
- Protestant church registers for mining-era congregations (uneven survival; held by individual churches or diocesan archives)
- Overland trail arrival records (no formal registration existed; manuscript diaries and journals are the substitute)
- Sacramento port arrival registers are digitized but browse-only — no name index
- San Francisco mining claim registers are digitized but browse-only — no name index
- Additional digitized volumes (up to 14 total in volume_search) not examined in this survey

## Known record losses
- The 1850 federal census for California was partially destroyed — specific county returns are missing. Substitute: 1852 California state census (88% indexed on FamilySearch).
- Many mining-camp records were never formally created or have since been lost — transient, predominantly male mining camps left far fewer records than settled agricultural communities.
- The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed many San Francisco county records, including some vital, court, and property records held in the city (though this postdates the target period, researchers tracing families forward from the 1850s should be aware of this 1906 loss).

## Research tips
- **Start with the 1852 state census** when the 1850 federal census return for a county is missing — it is 88% name-indexed and full-text searchable on FamilySearch (DGS 006601001) ([California Genealogy, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)).
- **Ship passenger manifests are essential for sea arrivals** but miss overland migrants entirely. For the latter, the Bancroft Library's manuscript collections (diaries, journals, emigrant society records) are the main documentary alternative ([California Genealogy, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)).
- **County-level research is unavoidable.** California's 1850s records are created and held at the county level. Identify the specific mining county before searching — check when that county was formed and which predecessor county held records before it.
- **Mining claim registers require image-by-image browsing** — neither the San Francisco volume (DGS 006601002) nor the Sacramento port registers (DGS 006601003) are name-indexed. Budget time to browse manually or use the Alta California newspaper (digitized at cdnc.ucr.edu) to locate the person first, then cross-reference.
- **The Great Registers (1866 onward) are the best nominal index for men who settled permanently** — they give nativity, age, physical description, and occupation and are 1,345,678 records strong on FamilySearch (collection 1923340). They are not useful for the 1848-1865 peak Gold Rush years.
- **Naturalization records are scattered** — before 1906, a declaration of intention or petition could be filed in any court of record. Check county district courts and federal district courts for California.
- **Do not rely on a single database.** Many Gold Rush migrants appear in no indexed record at all — newspaper notices, county histories, and manuscript collections at the Bancroft and State Library are often the only surviving evidence.
- **The California State Library and Bancroft Library** hold published county histories from the 1880s that include biographical sketches of Gold Rush pioneers — frequently the richest single source for a miner who left no formal paper trail ([California Genealogy, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)).

The FamilySearch California Vital Records wiki page returned only generic content — the California-specific start date for statewide birth and death registration was not confirmed by a fetched wiki page. Based on the generic page's guidance that many U.S. states did not require statewide registration until the early 1900s, do not assume statewide birth and death registration existed in the 1850s. Consult the [California Vital Records FamilySearch Wiki page](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Vital_Records) directly for exact dates.
- **What exists:** County birth records from 1850, indexed on FamilySearch (collection 2017276, 789,456 records). County marriage records from 1850 (collection 1452832, 567,890 records). Death registration for this period is sparse — civil death registration at the county level was inconsistent before 1905.
- **Where held:** County courthouses (original); FamilySearch has digitized county births and marriages.
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth or death registration during the 1850s-1860s. Many miners left no vital record at all.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (see below); cemetery sexton records; newspaper obituaries and death notices.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mission system, pre-dating Gold Rush); Methodist, Episcopal, Presbyterian, Baptist, and Congregationalist (arriving with Anglo migrants from late 1840s onward).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and confirmations. Catholic mission registers (1769-1850) are indexed on FamilySearch (collection 1804372, 98,765 records) but predate the Gold Rush migration and document the Hispanic/Native population, not Anglo 49ers.
- **Where held:** Diocesan archives (Roman Catholic Diocese of Monterey and later Diocese of San Francisco archives); individual congregation records vary widely. FamilySearch holds microfilm of some California church records.
- **Language:** Catholic mission records are in Spanish and Latin. Anglo Protestant records are in English.
- **Note:** For Gold Rush-era Anglo migrants, Protestant church records are the most relevant vital substitute but coverage is uneven — many mining camps had no established church.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1850 federal census was California's first but was partially destroyed — some county returns are missing ([California Genealogy, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records)). The 1860 and 1870 federal censuses are complete and fully indexed.
- **State census:** California conducted a state census in 1852, which is the primary substitute for missing 1850 county returns. This volume (DGS 006601001) covers 1850-1852, has 522 images, is 88% name-indexed, and is full-text searchable — the most accessible census substitute for this period.
- **Mortality schedules:** The 1850, 1860, and 1870 federal censuses included mortality schedules listing persons who died in the twelve months preceding enumeration — a valuable death record substitute.
- **Access:** 1852 state census: indexed + full-text searchable (FamilySearch DGS 006601001). Federal censuses 1860, 1870: indexed + images (FamilySearch and Ancestry).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, and estate distributions. Because Gold Rush migrants were often transient and single men, intestate administration (dying without a will) is more common than testate (with a will) — search administration files, not just the will indexes, when the person died in California.
- **Date range:** From 1850 at the county level.
- **Where held:** County courthouses (originals); some have been microfilmed by FamilySearch but specific California probate volumes were not confirmed in the volume_search results for this period.
- **Court records:** Naturalizations before 1906 could be filed in any court of record — county district courts, state courts, and federal courts. Check all three. County court minute books also recorded road maintenance responsibilities, poor relief recipients, and other business naming ordinary residents.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** California is a federal-land (public-domain) state — the U.S. General Land Office (GLO) administered land distribution after 1848. Metes-and-bounds descriptions are used for private land grants (ranchos) from the Mexican era.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM GLO) records portal (glorecords.blm.gov) holds federal land patents for California. The California State Archives holds Mexican-era land grant case files adjudicated under the Land Act of 1851.
- **Types:** Federal land patents (GLO), Mexican rancho grant confirmations, county deed books, mining claim registers, tax records.
- **Mining claim registers:** Held at county recorders' offices. FamilySearch has digitized a volume of San Francisco mining claim registers (DGS 006601002, 340 images, 1849-1855) — browse-only, no name index, no full-text search. Researchers must browse image by image.
- **Date range:** Federal patents from 1850; Mexican-era grant records predate statehood.
- **Where held:** BLM GLO website (federal patents, online free); California State Archives (land grant case files); county recorders (deed books); FamilySearch (some volumes, browse-only).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The Mexican-American War (1846-1848) immediately preceded the Gold Rush; some veterans settled in California. The Civil War (1861-1865) saw California raise volunteer regiments for Union service.
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files at NARA (Washington, D.C.); California volunteer regiment records at the California State Archives; draft registrations (Civil War-era) at NARA.
- **Where held:** NARA (national records); California State Archives (state militia/volunteer records); Fold3 (online, subscription) for digitized service and pension records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Gold Hill, Coloma, Sonora, and other mining-camp cemeteries; urban cemeteries in San Francisco, Sacramento, and Stockton. Many mining-camp graves are unmarked or lost.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) and BillionGraves hold transcriptions for many California cemeteries, but mining-era graves in remote camps are underrepresented.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records where they survive are held by county archives or local historical societies. Coverage is uneven.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Alta California (San Francisco, from 1849) is the most significant Gold Rush-era paper. Sacramento, Stockton, and mining-county papers appeared through the early 1850s.
- **Where held:** California Digital Newspaper Collection (cdnc.ucr.edu, free online); California State Library (microfilm); Newspapers.com (subscription).
- **Content value:** Death notices, obituaries, legal notices (mining claim disputes, probate notices), letters from miners, and arrival notices name individuals not found in formal records.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** San Francisco was the primary Pacific entry point. Panama (overland crossing to the Pacific), Cape Horn, and Valparaiso (Chile) routes all funneled through San Francisco. Overland migrants arrived via the California, Oregon, and Gila trails.
- **Record types:** Ship passenger manifests (arrivals at San Francisco, held at NARA Pacific Region, San Bruno, CA; digitized on Ancestry and FamilySearch). Port arrival registers for Sacramento (FamilySearch DGS 006601003, 298 images, 1849-1858) — browse-only, no name index. Overland migrants are largely undocumented in official arrival records.
- **Where held:** NARA Pacific Region, San Bruno (original passenger manifests); Ancestry.com and FamilySearch (digitized manifests).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with families. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members. Note that many '49ers came overland and will not appear in any ship manifest — look for trail diaries and journals at the Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley) and the California State Library.
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record. Declarations of intention and petitions for naturalization are scattered across county district courts and federal courts in California.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax and personal property tax records, beginning at county formation (1850 and onward as new counties were created).
- **Date range:** From 1850 at the county level.
- **Where held:** County archives and some state archives. Tax records are a valuable substitute for missing census years and can place a person in a specific county when other records do not.
- **Substitute value:** Because the 1850 federal census has gaps, county tax records from 1850-1852 can confirm a person's presence in a specific county during the height of the Gold Rush.

### Other record types
- **Great Registers (voter registration):** California's Great Registers began in 1866 (FamilySearch collection 1923340, 1,345,678 records, 1866-1910). They do not cover 1848-1865 but are invaluable for tracking men who remained in California after the Gold Rush. Each entry typically gives name, age, occupation, physical description, nativity, and county of registration.
- **County histories and local histories:** 19th-century county histories (often published in the 1880s) frequently include biographical sketches of Gold Rush-era pioneers — often the only narrative account of a miner who left no probate or land record. The Bancroft Library and California State Library hold extensive collections.
- **Manuscript collections:** The Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley) and the California State Library hold Gold Rush-era diaries, letters, journals, and organizational records not available anywhere online — essential for locating overland migrants and miners who left no documentary trail in formal records.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | County Births 1850-1919 (789,456 records); County Marriages 1850-1952 (567,890 records); Great Registers 1866-1910 (1,345,678 records); Mission Records 1769-1850 (98,765 records); 1852 State Census (DGS 006601001, 88% indexed, full-text); Mining Claim Registers SF (DGS 006601002, browse-only); Sacramento Port Arrivals (DGS 006601003, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (1850, 1860, 1870); San Francisco passenger manifests | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records and headstone transcriptions | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including Alta California | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military service records and pension files | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Passenger manifests, naturalization records, military records | Free finding aids; some records online |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents from 1850 | Free |
| California Digital Newspaper Collection (cdnc.ucr.edu) | Digitized California newspapers from 1849 | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** 14 digitized volumes match this place and period in volume_search; the 3 detailed above are the first page (nextPageToken present). Further volumes were not examined and may include additional county-level record sets.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| NARA Pacific Region, San Bruno, CA | Original ship passenger manifests, federal court naturalization records | In-person; some records microfilmed/digitized |
| California State Archives, Sacramento | State census (1852), land grant case files, state military records, county records transferred to state | In-person; some records online |
| California State Library, Sacramento | County histories, newspapers, manuscript collections, Gold Rush-era materials | In-person; some digitized |
| Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley | Extensive Gold Rush manuscript collections, diaries, journals, overland trail accounts | In-person by appointment |
| County courthouses | Deed books, probate files, court records, tax records, marriage registers | In-person or mail request; varies by county |
| Local historical and genealogical societies | Local histories, transcribed records, surname files | Contact individual societies |

## Records NOT online
- Most county-level tax records (pre-1870)
- Many county probate and court case files
- Mining claim records beyond the single San Francisco volume on FamilySearch
- Protestant church registers for mining-era congregations (uneven survival; held by individual churches or diocesan archives)
- Overland trail arrival records (no formal registration existed; manuscript diaries and journals are the substitute)
- Sacramento port arrival registers are digitized but browse-only — no name index
- San Francisco mining claim registers are digitized but browse-only — no name index
- Additional digitized volumes (up to 14 total in volume_search) not examined in this survey

## Known record losses
- The 1850 federal census for California was partially destroyed — specific county returns are missing. Substitute: 1852 California state census (88% indexed on FamilySearch).
- Many mining-camp records were never formally created or have since been lost — transient, predominantly male mining camps left far fewer records than settled agricultural communities.
- The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed many San Francisco county records, including some vital, court, and property records held in the city (though this postdates the target period, researchers tracing families forward from the 1850s should be aware of this 1906 loss).

## Research tips
- **Start with the 1852 state census** when the 1850 federal census return for a county is missing — it is 88% name-indexed and full-text searchable on FamilySearch (DGS 006601001) ([California Genealogy, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)).
- **Ship passenger manifests are essential for sea arrivals** but miss overland migrants entirely. For the latter, the Bancroft Library's manuscript collections (diaries, journals, emigrant society records) are the main documentary alternative ([California Genealogy, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)).
- **County-level research is unavoidable.** California's 1850s records are created and held at the county level. Identify the specific mining county before searching — check when that county was formed and which predecessor county held records before it.
- **Mining claim registers require image-by-image browsing** — neither the San Francisco volume (DGS 006601002) nor the Sacramento port registers (DGS 006601003) are name-indexed. Budget time to browse manually or use the Alta California newspaper (digitized at cdnc.ucr.edu) to locate the person first, then cross-reference.
- **The Great Registers (1866 onward) are the best nominal index for men who settled permanently** — they give nativity, age, physical description, and occupation and are 1,345,678 records strong on FamilySearch (collection 1923340). They are not useful for the 1848-1865 peak Gold Rush years.
- **Naturalization records are scattered** — before 1906, a declaration of intention or petition could be filed in any court of record. Check county district courts and federal district courts for California.
- **Do not rely on a single database.** Many Gold Rush migrants appear in no indexed record at all — newspaper notices, county histories, and manuscript collections at the Bancroft and State Library are often the only surviving evidence.
- **The California State Library and Bancroft Library** hold published county histories from the 1880s that include biographical sketches of Gold Rush pioneers — frequently the richest single source for a miner who left no formal paper trail ([California Genealogy, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)).

Here is what the locality-guide found for colonial New York City research:

---

Researching families in New York City during the 1700s means working almost entirely **without civil registration** — no birth, marriage, or death certificates existed for that period. The most important record types and repositories are:

### Church Records
- **Dutch Reformed Church** – The oldest continuous series. A digitized but browse-only volume on FamilySearch covers 1700–1776, written in Dutch.
- **Trinity Church (Anglican)** – Registers from 1697 onward.

### Probate Records
- The **Prerogative Court of New York** handled colonial-era wills. Records are indexed in the New-York Historical Society's published *Abstracts of Wills* series.

### Substitutes for Census Records
- No federal enumerations exist before 1790.
- **Tax assessment rolls** and **provincial militia muster rolls** are the primary substitutes for identifying household heads and community members.

### Online Collections (FamilySearch – Free)
Four statewide New York collections cover this period:
1. Church records
2. Land records
3. Probate records
4. Late-century tax rolls

### Key Physical Repositories
- **New York State Archives** (Albany) – Colonial manuscripts and court records.
- **New York Genealogical & Biographical Society** (NYC) – Transcribed and compiled colonial sources.
- **New-York Historical Society** (NYC) – Published abstracts and compiled colonial records.

---

The next step would be to build a research plan targeting whichever specific family or surname you are tracing, now that the record landscape for colonial New York City has been mapped.

The FamilySearch-digitized Dutch Reformed Church register (volume 007733180, 1700-1776) is browse-only, 0% name-indexed, and written in Dutch — the researcher must read the original language and browse page by page.

Wills proved in the 1700s went through the Prerogative Court of New York (colonial-era), not a county surrogate's court. These are indexed in the Abstracts of Wills series published by the New-York Historical Society.

Colonial-era records span two political regimes: Dutch (to 1664) and British (1664-1783). Records from before the English takeover may be in Dutch and held under Dutch colonial administrative structures.
Tax assessment lists and militia/muster rolls survive for some wards and years and are among the few records that list ordinary male residents outside church and court contexts.
New York County Marriages collection (id 1920153) covers 1847-1849 and 1907-1936 only — it does not cover the 1700s. Civil marriage registration did not exist in colonial New York.

The first federal census is 1790 — there are no federal census records for the 1700s before that year. Provincial enumerations (colonial censuses) exist for some years and are held at the New York State Archives.
Key repositories for colonial NYC: New York Genealogical & Biographical Society, New-York Historical Society, New York State Archives (Colonial Manuscripts), and Trinity Church Archives.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New York City (1700-1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Amsterdam established by the Dutch West India Company in 1626; seized by England in 1664 and renamed New York
- **County seat / administrative center:** New York City (lower Manhattan), seat of New York County
