| New-York Historical Society | Colonial church register transcriptions; Abstracts of Wills; colonial newspapers on microfilm; manumission records | In-person; some digitized collections |
| New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYG&B) | Extensive colonial-era record transcriptions; published finding aids; local histories | Membership or in-person; some databases at newyorkfamilyhistory.org |
| Trinity Church Archives | Anglican parish registers from 1697; burial records | Written request or in-person appointment |
| National Archives (NARA), Northeast Region | Federal-era records from 1789; Revolutionary War pension files | In-person or through NARA online order; Fold3.com |

## Records NOT online
- Colonial-era ward tax lists (before 1799): physical only at New York State Archives and NYC Municipal Archives
- Mayor's Court records (civil court proceedings): physical at New York State Archives
- Most colonial ship/passenger arrival records pre-1789: fragmentary; held at New York State Archives and New-York Historical Society
- Trinity Church and other individual congregation burial registers in full: contact respective church archives
- Prerogative Court original will packets (as opposed to abstracts): New York State Archives
- Provincial militia and muster rolls: New York State Archives

## Known record losses
- No major courthouse fire is documented for colonial-era New York City records in the tool results returned for this survey. However, the British military occupation of New York City (1776-1783) is known to have disrupted civic record-keeping, and some records from that period are incomplete or missing.
- The African Burial Ground records were largely unrecorded during the colonial era; the burial ground itself was lost and only rediscovered in 1991.
- Many colonial ship arrival records were never systematically compiled or have not survived.

## Research tips
- **Church registers are the vital records for this period.** There was no civil vital registration in New York City in the 1700s. Begin with church records for any baptism, marriage, or burial event. The wiki search result "New York City Genealogy" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records) names the Dutch Reformed Church (from 1639) and Trinity Church Anglican registers as the two most important series for the colonial city.
- **The Dutch Reformed register on FamilySearch is browse-only and in Dutch.** Volume 007733180 (1700-1776, 211 images) has 0% name-indexing and is not full-text searchable. It must be reviewed image by image, and the researcher must read 18th-century Dutch script.
- **For colonial-era wills, start with the Abstracts of Wills.** The New-York Historical Society's published *Abstracts of Wills* series indexes the Prerogative Court of New York wills — this is the standard finding aid for 1700s probate and is available in major research libraries.
- **Tax lists and militia rolls substitute for census records.** The first federal census is 1790. For earlier years, ward tax assessment rolls and provincial militia muster rolls are among the best resources for placing a man in a specific ward and year. The wiki search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records confirms these records survive for some periods.
- **Identify the denomination before searching church records.** New York City in the 1700s had Dutch Reformed, Anglican, Presbyterian, Lutheran, Quaker, and Jewish congregations, each keeping separate registers. Knowing or hypothesizing the family's religious affiliation narrows the search considerably.
- **Dutch surnames were often anglicized after 1664.** Families with Dutch surnames (van, de, ten prefixes) may appear under anglicized or shortened variants in English-language records after the English takeover. Search variant spellings.
- **Research the New York Genealogical & Biographical Society's online databases.** NYG&B (newyorkfamilyhistory.org) has published transcriptions of many colonial-era New York records — church registers, wills, deeds — not available on FamilySearch or Ancestry.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content** for all four place-specific sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) in this survey — the New York City Genealogy wiki page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy should be consulted directly for more specific research guidance.

**Locality Guide: Virginia During the American Revolutionary War (1775–1783)**

Here's what the research turned up:

---

### Key Challenge: Virginia's Record Gaps

There are no statewide civil records for births, marriages, or deaths during this period. Crucially, **Virginia's 1790 federal census was destroyed** when the British burned Washington in 1814, leaving a major gap in early American research.

---

### Most Important Record Types & Repositories

#### 1. **Military Pension Files** *(National Archives / Fold3)*
- Often the richest genealogical source — pension applications frequently name a soldier's wife, marriage date, and children
- Search on [Fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com) for digitized pension files and compiled service records

#### 2. **Compiled Service Records**
- FamilySearch collection: **"Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783"** — searchable by name
- Also available on Fold3

#### 3. **County Personal Property Tax Lists (1782+)**
- Virginia began taxing personal property in 1782; these lists substitute for the missing census
- Available through FamilySearch and the Library of Virginia

#### 4. **County Court Marriage Bonds**
- Virginia kept marriages at the county level via bonds and ministers' returns
- County-specific; held at the Library of Virginia and on FamilySearch

#### 5. **Anglican/Episcopal Parish Registers**
- Baptism and burial records for the colonial/Revolutionary era
- Survival varies by parish; many are on FamilySearch or microfilm at the Library of Virginia

#### 6. **Revolutionary War Land Bounty Warrants**
- A digitized FamilySearch volume exists but is **unindexed** — browse-only, image by image

---

### Key Repositories

| Repository | What They Hold |
|---|---|
| **National Archives (NARA)** | Pension files, compiled service records, bounty warrants |
| **Fold3.com** | Digitized NARA military records |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Virginia military records 1775–1783, tax lists, parish registers |
| **Library of Virginia** | County records, marriage bonds, tax lists, muster rolls |

---

### Recommended Next Step

Since Virginia kept nearly **all records at the county level**, the most effective next step is to identify the specific county (or counties) where your ancestors lived, then build a research plan around that county's surviving records. If you'd like help with that, just let me know the county or a specific ancestor's name!

quirks: Virginia's 1790 federal census was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814 — use the 1782-1785 county personal property tax lists as the primary substitute; they survive for nearly all counties.

Virginia was a state-land state: land grants and patents were issued by the colonial governor and then the Commonwealth, not the federal government. The Bureau of Land Management GLO site does not cover Virginia.

Church records for the colonial and Revolutionary era are overwhelmingly Anglican (Church of England / Protestant Episcopal). After disestablishment in 1776, church record-keeping became uneven; many parish registers were lost or transferred to county courthouses or the Library of Virginia.

Civil statewide registration of births, marriages, and deaths in Virginia did not begin until 1853 at the county level, and was not reliable until the early twentieth century. For 1775-1783, look to church registers and county court marriage bonds rather than civil vital records.

Virginia granted post-war bounty lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio; warrant and survey records at the Library of Virginia and State Archives connect veterans to those claims and are a valuable collateral source.

Continental Line service records (NARA Record Group 93) and pension/bounty-land warrant files (NARA Record Group 15) are the primary federal military records — search both, as a veteran might appear in one but not the other.

The FamilySearch-digitized volume of Revolutionary War land bounty warrants (image group 005301447, 341 images, 1779-1800) is browse-only — it has 0% name-indexing and is not full-text searchable; it must be browsed image by image.

Augusta County court order books (image group 005301448, 1775-1795, 61% name-indexed) are partially searchable by name — a useful example of the county-level military and civil activity recorded in court minutes.

Virginia Loyalists (Tories) who sided with the Crown may appear in confiscation records, escheat records, and British claims commission files — an often-overlooked source for families on both sides of the conflict.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775-1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Virginia was one of the original Thirteen Colonies; it ratified the U.S. Constitution in 1788, but its county-level record-keeping infrastructure dates to the 1630s.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Richmond (state capital from 1780; Williamsburg before that)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Colony of Great Britain until independence declared July 4, 1776; Commonwealth of Virginia thereafter
- **Population during period:** Virginia was the most populous of the original states; the 1790 federal census (which survived only partially, as the Virginia schedules were destroyed) documented approximately 747,000 free persons plus an enslaved population of roughly 293,000 — the Revolutionary-era population was somewhat smaller.
- **Economy:** Tobacco planting, mixed farming, maritime trade (especially in the Tidewater), iron works, and frontier land speculation in the western counties
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English colonial stock; substantial Scots-Irish and German settlers in the Shenandoah Valley and western Piedmont; significant enslaved African population throughout
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican/Church of England (established church, disestablished 1776 and reorganized as Protestant Episcopal); Presbyterian (especially Scots-Irish settlers); Baptist (growing rapidly through the Revolution); Methodist; Quaker (particularly in the Northern Neck and Piedmont); Lutheran and German Reformed (Valley counties)
- **Key historical events:** Declaration of Independence 1776; Virginia's colonial government disestablished the Anglican Church 1776; Dunmore's Proclamation (1775) offered freedom to enslaved persons who joined the British, creating complex records; battles at Great Bridge (1775) and Guilford Court House (just across the NC border, 1781); siege of Yorktown (1781) ended major fighting

## Boundary changes
- Virginia's county boundaries were fluid throughout this period. New counties were carved from existing ones regularly. Always identify the specific county that existed at the event date.
- Kentucky County was created from Fincastle County in 1776; Kentucky District was organized in 1780. Records for families in what is now Kentucky before those dates are held under the parent Virginia counties.
- West Virginia did not separate until 1863; families in that territory in 1775-1783 were Virginia residents.
- The Virginia Military District of Ohio (post-war bounty lands) lies entirely outside Virginia's current borders but produces Virginia-created warrant and survey records.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki does not return a specific Virginia Vital Records page, so the following is based on general knowledge and the wiki_search results: Virginia did not have statewide civil registration during 1775-1783. Statewide registration began at the county level in 1853.
- **What exists for 1775-1783:** No civil birth, marriage, or death registers at the state level exist for this period. County court marriage bonds and consents survive for many counties and are the closest civil equivalent to marriage registration.
- **Where held:** County courthouses and the Library of Virginia, Richmond. Many have been microfilmed by FamilySearch.
- **Gaps:** Extensive — civil vital registration simply did not exist in this period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Anglican/Episcopal parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the primary substitute; county court marriage bonds are the main marriage source.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican/Protestant Episcopal (dominant; the established church through 1776), Presbyterian, Baptist, Methodist, Quaker, Lutheran, German Reformed
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, vestry minutes, tithe lists (Anglican vestries also administered poor relief and produced tithe lists that name householders)
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929" (collection ID 1598230) covers this period and is searchable by name. Original registers are held at the Library of Virginia, individual parishes, and diocesan archives. Many Anglican registers were transferred to county courthouses after disestablishment.
- **Language:** English throughout
- **Note:** After Anglican disestablishment in 1776, many dissenting congregations began their own record-keeping. Baptist minute books are a particularly rich source for this era.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census was 1790. Virginia's 1790 schedules were destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814 — they do not survive. The 1800 census is the earliest complete federal enumeration for Virginia.
- **State/provincial census:** Virginia did not take a state census during the Revolutionary War period.
- **Other enumerations:** The 1782, 1783, 1784, and 1785 personal property tax lists are the primary substitute for the missing 1790 census. They survive for most Virginia counties and list free white male tithables by name. FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850" (ID 1456723) covers the earliest of these lists. A FamilySearch-digitized volume of state enumerations/tax lists (image group 005301449, 87 images, 1782-1799) is full-text searchable but NOT name-indexed — it can be searched by text string but not by browsing a name index.
- **Access:** The tax-list collection (1456723) is indexed and searchable by name.

### Military records (the core of this survey)

#### Continental Army
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Military Records, 1775-1783" (ID 1945678) — searchable by name on FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678)
- **NARA Record Group 93:** Continental Line service records and muster rolls are held at the National Archives. Per the FamilySearch Wiki's Virginia Military Records article (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War), Virginia contributed more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony; service records are at NARA RG 93.
- **Online access:** Fold3.com (https://www.fold3.com/) holds digitized NARA Revolutionary War records including compiled service records and pension files.

#### Virginia Militia
- Virginia militia records are held at the Library of Virginia in Richmond. Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War), these are distinct from Continental Line records. Not all militia records have been digitized.

#### Virginia State Navy
- Published records of the Virginia State Navy exist and are cited in the FamilySearch Wiki. Check the Library of Virginia for published rosters.

#### Pension and Bounty-Land Warrant Files
- NARA Record Group 15 holds pension and bounty-land warrant application files. Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War), these are a primary genealogical source — pension files often include family depositions, marriage dates, children's names, and place of residence. They are among the richest genealogical sources for Revolutionary-era Virginia families.
- Fold3.com (https://www.fold3.com/) has digitized pension files online.
- The National Archives (https://www.archives.gov/) holds originals.

#### Post-War Bounty Lands (Virginia Military District of Ohio)
- Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands), Virginia granted bounty lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio after the war. Warrant and survey records at the Library of Virginia connect veterans to their land claims.
- FamilySearch-digitized volume (image group 005301447, 341 images, 1779-1800) covers Revolutionary War land bounty warrants. **This volume is browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) — it must be browsed image by image.**

#### Loyalist Records
- Virginia Loyalists (those who sided with the Crown) may appear in Virginia confiscation and escheat records, British claims commission files (held at The National Archives, Kew, England, AO 12/13), and published lists of attainted persons. These are an overlooked source for families on both sides of the conflict.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, inventories, estate administrations, guardianship bonds, county court order books
- **Date range:** County courts have been operating since the 1630s in older Virginia counties
- **Where held:** County courthouses and the Library of Virginia. FamilySearch collection "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920" (ID 2134567) covers this period. The Augusta County court order books (image group 005301448, 158 images, 1775-1795) are 61% name-indexed — a partially searchable example of county military and civil business recorded in court minutes.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900" (ID 1734285) also covers wills and marriage bonds from this period and is searchable.
- **Note on wartime wills:** Soldiers leaving for service frequently wrote or updated wills; wartime probate filings spike in most Virginia counties 1775-1783.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Virginia is a state-land state, not a federal-land state)

# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775-1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Virginia was one of the original Thirteen Colonies; it ratified the U.S. Constitution in 1788, but its county-level record-keeping infrastructure dates to the 1630s.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Richmond (state capital from 1780; Williamsburg before that)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Colony of Great Britain until independence declared July 4, 1776; Commonwealth of Virginia thereafter
- **Population during period:** Virginia was the most populous of the original states; the 1790 federal census (which survived only partially, as the Virginia schedules were destroyed) documented approximately 747,000 free persons plus an enslaved population of roughly 293,000 — the Revolutionary-era population was somewhat smaller.
- **Economy:** Tobacco planting, mixed farming, maritime trade (especially in the Tidewater), iron works, and frontier land speculation in the western counties
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English colonial stock; substantial Scots-Irish and German settlers in the Shenandoah Valley and western Piedmont; significant enslaved African population throughout
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican/Church of England (established church, disestablished 1776 and reorganized as Protestant Episcopal); Presbyterian (especially Scots-Irish settlers); Baptist (growing rapidly through the Revolution); Methodist; Quaker (particularly in the Northern Neck and Piedmont); Lutheran and German Reformed (Valley counties)
- **Key historical events:** Declaration of Independence 1776; Virginia's colonial government disestablished the Anglican Church 1776; Dunmore's Proclamation (1775) offered freedom to enslaved persons who joined the British, creating complex records; battles at Great Bridge (1775) and Guilford Court House (just across the NC border, 1781); siege of Yorktown (1781) ended major fighting

## Boundary changes
- Virginia's county boundaries were fluid throughout this period. New counties were carved from existing ones regularly. Always identify the specific county that existed at the event date.
- Kentucky County was created from Fincastle County in 1776; Kentucky District was organized in 1780. Records for families in what is now Kentucky before those dates are held under the parent Virginia counties.
- West Virginia did not separate until 1863; families in that territory in 1775-1783 were Virginia residents.
- The Virginia Military District of Ohio (post-war bounty lands) lies entirely outside Virginia's current borders but produces Virginia-created warrant and survey records.

- **What exists for 1775-1783:** No civil birth, marriage, or death registers at the state level exist for this period. County court marriage bonds and consents survive for many counties and are the closest civil equivalent to marriage registration.
- **Where held:** County courthouses and the Library of Virginia, Richmond. Many have been microfilmed by FamilySearch.
- **Gaps:** Extensive — civil vital registration simply did not exist in this period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Anglican/Episcopal parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the primary substitute; county court marriage bonds are the main marriage source.

### Church records

- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929" (collection ID 1598230) covers this period and is searchable by name. Original registers are held at the Library of Virginia, individual parishes, and diocesan archives. Many Anglican registers were transferred to county courthouses after disestablishment.
- **Language:** English throughout
- **Note:** After Anglican disestablishment in 1776, many dissenting congregations began their own record-keeping. Baptist minute books are a particularly rich source for this era.

### Census records

- **State/provincial census:** Virginia did not take a state census during the Revolutionary War period.
- **Other enumerations:** The 1782, 1783, 1784, and 1785 personal property tax lists are the primary substitute for the missing 1790 census. - **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Military Records, 1775-1783" (ID 1945678) — searchable by name on FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678)

Here is what the locality guide returned:

---

**New Orleans, Early 1800s — Records, Disasters, and Substitutes**

New Orleans is one of the most record-rich but also record-complicated cities in American genealogy. Here's what you need to know:

**The Disasters**
The city suffered two catastrophic fires — in **1788 and 1794** — that destroyed much of the French Quarter and many colonial records.

**What Survived and Why**
Several critical record series came through because they were stored separately from the most damaged structures:
- **St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers** (baptisms, marriages, burials from **1731**, with some gaps) survived and are the primary source for vital events in the early 1800s.
- **New Orleans Notarial Archives** (over 30 million pages of legal acts dating to **1734**) survived — these are the functional substitutes for birth, marriage, and death certificates since Louisiana had no statewide civil vital registration in the early 1800s.

**What to Search**
Because there are no birth/marriage/death certificates for this era, researchers rely on:
1. **Church registers** — St. Louis Cathedral registers, accessible through FamilySearch and the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives
2. **Notarial acts** — legal records covering property transfers, contracts, wills, and family agreements; FamilySearch has one digitized (browse-only) volume of Orleans Parish notarial acts from 1803–1820
3. **Successions (probate)** — Louisiana calls probate "successions" and guardianship "tutorships" (French/Spanish civil law tradition)
4. **FamilySearch collections** — four Louisiana-level collections covering church records, parish marriages, probate, and a death index

**Language Warning**
Many pre-1830 records are in **French or Spanish**, requiring language skills or a specialist.

**Key Physical Repositories**
- Notarial Archives Research Center
- Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives
- Louisiana State Archives
- Historic New Orleans Collection

---

The guide suggests the logical next step is building a research plan that sequences these sources against the specific ancestors you're tracing. Would you like to do that?

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800-1860)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Orleans was founded by France in 1718; Orleans Parish was established as the jurisdictional unit.
- **County seat / administrative center:** New Orleans (the parish seat of Orleans Parish; Louisiana uses civil parishes, not counties).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** During 1800-1812: Orleans Territory (U.S.); from 1812: State of Louisiana.
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place_population tool for this query; the city was one of the largest in the United States by 1840, with a highly diverse population.
- **Economy:** Port commerce (the mouth of the Mississippi River made New Orleans the dominant export hub for the interior), cotton and sugar trade, shipping, skilled trades, and domestic service.
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creoles, Spanish Creoles, American Anglo migrants (especially after 1803), free people of color (a large and documented class unique in the antebellum South), enslaved African Americans, Irish and German immigrants (heavy arrival 1830s-1850s), and smaller numbers from the Caribbean.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant, with St. Louis Cathedral as the seat), Episcopal, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Jewish congregations by the 1840s-1850s.
- **Key historical events:** Louisiana Purchase (1803); Louisiana statehood (1812); Battle of New Orleans (1815); repeated yellow fever epidemics (1832, 1853 most severe); hurricanes and seasonal flooding; fires of 1788 and 1794 (colonial era, but shaped record survival into the 19th century).

## Boundary changes
- 1718: New Orleans founded under French authority.
- 1763-1800: Spanish colonial authority; records shift to Spanish-language administration.
- 1800-1803: Briefly returned to France.
- 1803: Louisiana Purchase; Orleans Territory organized 1804.
- 1812: Louisiana achieves statehood; Orleans Parish is one of the original state parishes.
- The parish boundaries of Orleans were essentially stable throughout the 1800-1860 period. Jefferson Parish lies immediately across the river; families straddling the boundary may have records in both parishes.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Louisiana did not have a statewide civil registration system during 1800-1860. The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content for the Louisiana_Vital_Records page during this survey; no specific start date for statewide registration was returned by any tool.
- **What exists:** No mandatory statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths existed in this period. The functional substitutes are (1) sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral and other congregations, and (2) notarial acts recording marriage contracts and other family events.
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives; New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center; Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge).
- **Gaps:** Significant gaps in church registers exist, especially for the colonial and early territorial eras, partly due to the 1788 and 1794 fires. Records for enslaved persons were kept inconsistently and are often fragmentary.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials, 1731 onward with gaps); notarial marriage contracts; newspaper marriage and death notices; death records in the Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819-1964 (FamilySearch collection 1543892, name-indexed, no images).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (St. Louis Cathedral, the primary register keeper for most of the 1800-1860 period); Episcopal, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Jewish congregations documented by the 1840s-1850s.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and confirmations. The sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral survive from 1731 with gaps and are the single most important surviving vital-record series for early New Orleans. According to wiki_search result from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters, these registers survived the 1788 and 1794 fires.
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives; FamilySearch collection 1612905 (Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925) covers this period with 987,654 indexed records and images.
- **Language:** Records from 1718-1803 are predominantly in French; Spanish-language records appear in the 1763-1803 period; English becomes more common after 1803 but French remained in use in Catholic registers well into the 1820s-1830s. Researchers must be prepared to read French and Spanish originals.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** Federal census enumerations were taken in 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850, and 1860. The 1810 and 1820 enumerations covered Orleans Territory/State. The 1850 and 1860 censuses are the most detailed for individuals (naming all household members with ages). The 1890 census was largely destroyed by fire in Washington, D.C. (post-period).
- **State/provincial census:** Louisiana held some state/territorial census enumerations; the FamilySearch Wiki page for Louisiana_Census returned only generic content during this survey — consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly for specifics.
- **Other enumerations:** Spanish colonial censuses (padrones) survive for the late 18th century and may name individuals whose descendants appear in the early 1800s.
- **Access:** Federal censuses for 1850 and 1860 are indexed and available on FamilySearch and Ancestry. Earlier censuses (1810, 1820, 1830, 1840) are indexed at the head-of-household level only.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Louisiana calls probate 'successions' (not wills and administrations, as in common-law states). Intestate succession and testate succession both go through the district court. Tutorships (guardianship of minors) and interdictions (incompetency proceedings) are related record types.
- **Date range:** From the territorial period (1804) through the entire 1800-1860 window.
- **Where held:** Orleans Parish Civil District Court; Louisiana State Archives. FamilySearch collection 2078341 (Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984) covers this period with 456,789 indexed records and images.
- **Note:** Because Louisiana uses civil law, succession records often contain detailed inventories of property (including names of enslaved persons), family trees prepared by the notary, and marriage contracts — far more genealogical detail than a common-law will.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Louisiana uses a French long-lot system in many areas (narrow rectangular lots extending back from a waterfront), not the rectangular township-and-range system of federal-land states. The Bureau of Land Management General Land Office records cover U.S.-period federal land grants after 1803.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Under French and Spanish rule, land grants (concessions) were issued by the colonial government. After 1803, the U.S. General Land Office administered public land; the Louisiana State Land Office holds state-issued patents. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Louisiana_Land_and_Property returned only generic content during this survey.
- **Types:** Notarial acts of sale and mortgage (the primary conveyancing instrument in Louisiana, held at the New Orleans Notarial Archives), U.S. federal land patents (BLM GLO website), tax assessments.
- **Date range:** Notarial records of land transactions survive from 1734.
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (30+ million pages of notarial acts); BLM GLO website for federal patents post-1803; Louisiana State Land Office (Baton Rouge).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 / Battle of New Orleans (1815); Mexican-American War (1846-1848); early Civil War (1861, just outside the target window).
- **Record types:** U.S. service records, pension files, bounty land warrants at NARA; Louisiana militia records at the Louisiana State Archives; Battle of New Orleans muster rolls.
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C. and its regional facilities); Louisiana State Archives; Fold3 (subscription) for digitized military records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (1789), St. Louis Cemetery No. 2 (1823), St. Louis Cemetery No. 3 (1854), Lafayette Cemetery No. 1 (1833, Garden District). Above-ground tombs are characteristic of New Orleans due to the high water table.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has substantial coverage of New Orleans cemeteries. Save Our Cemeteries organization maintains additional records.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers held by the Archdiocese of New Orleans and by the City of New Orleans.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The New Orleans Bee (L'Abeille de la Nouvelle-Orléans, French/English bilingual), the Louisiana Gazette, and the Daily Picayune (founded 1837) all published during the early 1800s. Newspapers routinely printed marriage notices, death notices, legal notices (succession sales, property auctions), and ship arrivals.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Library; Historic New Orleans Collection; Newspapers.com (subscription) and Chronicling America (free, Library of Congress) for digitized holdings.
- **Content value:** For the 1800-1860 period, newspaper notices often provide the only surviving record of a death, marriage, or legal transaction that was not captured in a surviving register.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was the second-largest port of entry in the United States after New York during this period. Irish and German immigrants arrived in very large numbers in the 1830s-1850s.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists (NARA Microfilm Series M259, covering New Orleans arrivals 1820-1902); naturalization records (filed in Orleans Parish district courts and U.S. district courts before 1906); border crossing records.
- **Where held:** NARA; Ancestry.com (New Orleans passenger lists are indexed and available); FamilySearch.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members. Post-1893 lists include birthplace, last residence, and destination — earlier lists are less detailed but still name each passenger.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Louisiana property tax assessment rolls; city of New Orleans tax records.
- **Date range:** Assessment rolls survive from the territorial period.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives; New Orleans City Archives.
- **Substitute value:** Tax rolls can place an individual in Orleans Parish in years between censuses and may name property (including enslaved persons in the antebellum period).

### Notarial records (unique to Louisiana)
- **This record type has no direct equivalent in other U.S. states and deserves its own section.** Under Louisiana civil law, virtually every significant transaction — property sale, mortgage, marriage contract, business agreement, manumission of an enslaved person, act of emancipation, tutorship, succession inventory — was executed before a licensed notary and retained in the notary's permanent protocol.
- **Date range:** Records survive from 1734.
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center. Volume_search returned 1 digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 004990115), covering Orleans Parish notarial acts 1803-1820, with 167 images, in French and English. This volume is browse-only: 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — it must be read image by image.
- **Access:** The Notarial Archives Research Center is accessible in person; their website also provides some finding aids.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records 1718-1925 (coll. 1612905); Louisiana, Parish Marriages 1837-1957 (coll. 1798054); Louisiana, Probate Records 1756-1984 (coll. 2078341); Louisiana, Statewide Death Index 1819-1964 (coll. 1543892); Orleans Parish notarial acts 1803-1820 (browse-only images, vol. 004990115) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | New Orleans passenger arrival lists; U.S. Federal Census (1810-1860) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military service records and pension files | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records including New Orleans cemeteries | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including New Orleans titles | Subscription |
| NARA / Chronicling America | Federal records; digitized newspapers | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume_search returned 1 digitized volume matching New Orleans / Orleans Parish for 1800-1820. Only 1 result was returned (totalResults: 1), so the returned page appears to be the complete result set for that query window. The collections_search returned 4 Louisiana-level collections. The external_links_search returned 6 curated links, all generic (U.S.-wide) rather than New Orleans-specific.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30+ million pages of notarial acts, 1734-present | In-person; some finding aids online |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials, 1731+); other parish registers | In-person or written request |
| Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge) | Territorial and state records; succession records; tax rolls; militia records | In-person; some digitized |
| Historic New Orleans Collection | Manuscripts, maps, photographs, newspapers | In-person; some digitized |
| New Orleans Public Library, Louisiana Division | City records, newspapers, local history | In-person |
| NARA Southeast Region (Atlanta) | Federal court records, naturalization files, census originals | In-person or online request |

## Records NOT online

- The bulk of the New Orleans Notarial Archives (30+ million pages) is not indexed online; the 1 digitized FamilySearch volume covering 1803-1820 is browse-only with no name index.
- Most pre-statehood (pre-1812) church registers beyond the St. Louis Cathedral series are held physically at the Archdiocese.
- City of New Orleans tax assessment rolls are largely physical-only.
- Orleans Parish Civil District Court succession files (physical originals) require in-person or written access at the courthouse or Louisiana State Archives.
- Spanish colonial records (padrones, land concessions, church records in Spanish) are held in part at the Louisiana State Archives, the Historic New Orleans Collection, and in part at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, Spain — a portion have been microfilmed by the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.

## Known record losses

- **Great New Orleans Fire of 1788:** Destroyed approximately 856 buildings in the French Quarter; many colonial administrative and church records were lost.
- **Great New Orleans Fire of 1794:** A second major fire destroyed much of what had been rebuilt, causing further record loss.
- **Effect on genealogical record survival:** According to the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters), sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral survive from 1731 despite these fires, though with gaps. Notarial records also survived in significant volume because the notarial protocols were held separately.
- **Yellow fever epidemics:** The epidemics of 1832 and especially 1853 killed tens of thousands of New Orleans residents; mortality records from these periods are incomplete, and many families lost members whose deaths were never formally recorded.
- **Flooding and hurricane damage:** Recurring storm and flood events over the 19th century caused localized record losses at individual repositories.
- **Substitute sources for lost records:** Notarial acts (marriages, property transactions, succession inventories); newspaper death and marriage notices; sacramental registers of congregations other than St. Louis Cathedral; federal census enumerations; passenger lists; free people of color registers; tax assessment rolls.

## Research tips

- **Louisiana's civil law system means different vocabulary.** Search for 'successions' rather than 'probate,' 'tutorships' rather than 'guardianship.' Locality guide written as loc_001.

---

New Orleans in the early 1800s is one of the most record-rich but also record-complicated cities in American genealogy. The city suffered two catastrophic fires in 1788 and 1794 that destroyed much of the French Quarter and many colonial records, yet several key record series survived: the sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral (baptisms, marriages, and burials from 1731, with gaps) and the New Orleans Notarial Archives (over 30 million pages of legal acts dating to 1734) both came through because they were kept separately from the most damaged structures. There was no statewide civil vital registration in Louisiana during the early 1800s, so those notarial acts and church registers are the functional substitutes for birth, marriage, and death certificates; FamilySearch holds four Louisiana-level collections covering church records, parish marriages, probate, and a death index, plus one digitized but entirely browse-only volume of Orleans Parish notarial acts from 1803 to 1820. Louisiana's civil law tradition (inherited from France and Spain) also means records use different names than other states — probate is called "successions," guardianship is "tutorships" — and many pre-1830 records are written in French or Spanish, requiring either language skills or a specialist. Physical repositories including the Notarial Archives Research Center, the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives, the Louisiana State Archives, and the Historic New Orleans Collection hold the bulk of what survives and are not fully accessible online.

The next step is to build a research plan that sequences these sources against the specific ancestors you are trying to trace.

added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800-1860)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Orleans was founded by France in 1718; Orleans Parish was established as the jurisdictional unit.
- **County seat / administrative center:** New Orleans (the parish seat of Orleans Parish; Louisiana uses civil parishes, not counties).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** During 1800-1812: Orleans Territory (U.S.); from 1812: State of Louisiana.
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place_population tool for this query; the city was one of the largest in the United States by 1840, with a highly diverse population.
- **Economy:** Port commerce (the mouth of the Mississippi River made New Orleans the dominant export hub for the interior), cotton and sugar trade, shipping, skilled trades, and domestic service.
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creoles, Spanish Creoles, American Anglo migrants (especially after 1803), free people of color (a large and documented class unique in the antebellum South), enslaved African Americans, Irish and German immigrants (heavy arrival 1830s-1850s), and smaller numbers from the Caribbean.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant, with St. Louis Cathedral as the seat), Episcopal, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Jewish congregations by the 1840s-1850s.
- **Key historical events:** Louisiana Purchase (1803); Louisiana statehood (1812); Battle of New Orleans (1815); repeated yellow fever epidemics (1832, 1853 most severe); hurricanes and seasonal flooding; fires of 1788 and 1794 (colonial era, but shaped record survival into the 19th century).

## Boundary changes
- 1718: New Orleans founded under French authority.
- 1763-1800: Spanish colonial authority; records shift to Spanish-language administration.
- 1800-1803: Briefly returned to France.
- 1803: Louisiana Purchase; Orleans Territory organized 1804.
- 1812: Louisiana achieves statehood; Orleans Parish is one of the original state parishes.
- The parish boundaries of Orleans were essentially stable throughout the 1800-1860 period. Jefferson Parish lies immediately across the river; families straddling the boundary may have records in both parishes.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Louisiana did not have a statewide civil registration system during 1800-1860. The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content for the Louisiana_Vital_Records page during this survey; no specific start date for statewide registration was returned by any tool.
- **What exists:** No mandatory statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths existed in this period. The functional substitutes are (1) sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral and other congregations, and (2) notarial acts recording marriage contracts and other family events.
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives; New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center; Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge).
- **Gaps:** Significant gaps in church registers exist, especially for the colonial and early territorial eras, partly due to the 1788 and 1794 fires. Records for enslaved persons were kept inconsistently and are often fragmentary.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials, 1731 onward with gaps); notarial marriage contracts; newspaper marriage and death notices; death records in the Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819-1964 (FamilySearch collection 1543892, name-indexed, no images).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (St. Louis Cathedral, the primary register keeper for most of the 1800-1860 period); Episcopal, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Jewish congregations documented by the 1840s-1850s.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and confirmations. The sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral survive from 1731 with gaps and are the single most important surviving vital-record series for early New Orleans. According to wiki_search result from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters, these registers survived the 1788 and 1794 fires.
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives; FamilySearch collection 1612905 (Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925) covers this period with 987,654 indexed records and images.
- **Language:** Records from 1718-1803 are predominantly in French; Spanish-language records appear in the 1763-1803 period; English becomes more common after 1803 but French remained in use in Catholic registers well into the 1820s-1830s. Researchers must be prepared to read French and Spanish originals.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** Federal census enumerations were taken in 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850, and 1860. The 1810 and 1820 enumerations covered Orleans Territory/State. The 1850 and 1860 censuses are the most detailed for individuals (naming all household members with ages). The 1890 census was largely destroyed by fire in Washington, D.C. (post-period).
- **State/provincial census:** Louisiana held some state/territorial census enumerations; the FamilySearch Wiki page for Louisiana_Census returned only generic content during this survey — consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly for specifics.
- **Other enumerations:** Spanish colonial censuses (padrones) survive for the late 18th century and may name individuals whose descendants appear in the early 1800s.
- **Access:** Federal censuses for 1850 and 1860 are indexed and available on FamilySearch and Ancestry. Earlier censuses (1810, 1820, 1830, 1840) are indexed at the head-of-household level only.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Louisiana calls probate 'successions' (not wills and administrations, as in common-law states). Intestate succession and testate succession both go through the district court. Tutorships (guardianship of minors) and interdictions (incompetency proceedings) are related record types.
- **Date range:** From the territorial period (1804) through the entire 1800-1860 window.
- **Where held:** Orleans Parish Civil District Court; Louisiana State Archives. FamilySearch collection 2078341 (Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984) covers this period with 456,789 indexed records and images.
- **Note:** Because Louisiana uses civil law, succession records often contain detailed inventories of property (including names of enslaved persons), family trees prepared by the notary, and marriage contracts — far more genealogical detail than a common-law will.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Louisiana uses a French long-lot system in many areas (narrow rectangular lots extending back from a waterfront), not the rectangular township-and-range system of federal-land states. The Bureau of Land Management General Land Office records cover U.S.-period federal land grants after 1803.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Under French and Spanish rule, land grants (concessions) were issued by the colonial government. After 1803, the U.S. General Land Office administered public land; the Louisiana State Land Office holds state-issued patents. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Louisiana_Land_and_Property returned only generic content during this survey.
- **Types:** Notarial acts of sale and mortgage (the primary conveyancing instrument in Louisiana, held at the New Orleans Notarial Archives), U.S. federal land patents (BLM GLO website), tax assessments.
- **Date range:** Notarial records of land transactions survive from 1734.
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (30+ million pages of notarial acts); BLM GLO website for federal patents post-1803; Louisiana State Land Office (Baton Rouge).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 / Battle of New Orleans (1815); Mexican-American War (1846-1848); early Civil War (1861, just outside the target window).
- **Record types:** U.S. service records, pension files, bounty land warrants at NARA; Louisiana militia records at the Louisiana State Archives; Battle of New Orleans muster rolls.
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C. and its regional facilities); Louisiana State Archives; Fold3 (subscription) for digitized military records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (1789), St. Louis Cemetery No. 2 (1823), St. Louis Cemetery No. 3 (1854), Lafayette Cemetery No. 1 (1833, Garden District). Above-ground tombs are characteristic of New Orleans due to the high water table.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has substantial coverage of New Orleans cemeteries. Save Our Cemeteries organization maintains additional records.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers held by the Archdiocese of New Orleans and by the City of New Orleans.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The New Orleans Bee (L'Abeille de la Nouvelle-Orléans, French/English bilingual), the Louisiana Gazette, and the Daily Picayune (founded 1837) all published during the early 1800s. Newspapers routinely printed marriage notices, death notices, legal notices (succession sales, property auctions), and ship arrivals.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Library; Historic New Orleans Collection; Newspapers.com (subscription) and Chronicling America (free, Library of Congress) for digitized holdings.
- **Content value:** For the 1800-1860 period, newspaper notices often provide the only surviving record of a death, marriage, or legal transaction that was not captured in a surviving register.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was the second-largest port of entry in the United States after New York during this period. Irish and German immigrants arrived in very large numbers in the 1830s-1850s.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists (NARA Microfilm Series M259, covering New Orleans arrivals 1820-1902); naturalization records (filed in Orleans Parish district courts and U.S. district courts before 1906); border crossing records.
- **Where held:** NARA; Ancestry.com (New Orleans passenger lists are indexed and available); FamilySearch.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members. Post-1893 lists include birthplace, last residence, and destination — earlier lists are less detailed but still name each passenger.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Louisiana property tax assessment rolls; city of New Orleans tax records.
- **Date range:** Assessment rolls survive from the territorial period.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives; New Orleans City Archives.
- **Substitute value:** Tax rolls can place an individual in Orleans Parish in years between censuses and may name property (including enslaved persons in the antebellum period).

### Notarial records (unique to Louisiana)
- **This record type has no direct equivalent in other U.S. states and deserves its own section.** Under Louisiana civil law, virtually every significant transaction — property sale, mortgage, marriage contract, business agreement, manumission of an enslaved person, act of emancipation, tutorship, succession inventory — was executed before a licensed notary and retained in the notary's permanent protocol.
- **Date range:** Records survive from 1734.
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center. Volume_search returned 1 digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 004990115), covering Orleans Parish notarial acts 1803-1820, with 167 images, in French and English. This volume is browse-only: 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — it must be read image by image.
- **Access:** The Notarial Archives Research Center is accessible in person; their website also provides some finding aids.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records 1718-1925 (coll. 1612905); Louisiana, Parish Marriages 1837-1957 (coll. 1798054); Louisiana, Probate Records 1756-1984 (coll. 2078341); Louisiana, Statewide Death Index 1819-1964 (coll. 1543892); Orleans Parish notarial acts 1803-1820 (browse-only images, vol. 004990115) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | New Orleans passenger arrival lists; U.S. Federal Census (1810-1860) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military service records and pension files | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records including New Orleans cemeteries | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including New Orleans titles | Subscription |
| NARA / Chronicling America | Federal records; digitized newspapers | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume_search returned 1 digitized volume matching New Orleans / Orleans Parish for 1800-1820. Only 1 result was returned (totalResults: 1), so the returned page appears to be the complete result set for that query window. The collections_search returned 4 Louisiana-level collections. The external_links_search returned 6 curated links, all generic (U.S.-wide) rather than New Orleans-specific.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30+ million pages of notarial acts, 1734-present | In-person; some finding aids online |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials, 1731+); other parish registers | In-person or written request |
| Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge) | Territorial and state records; succession records; tax rolls; militia records | In-person; some digitized |
| Historic New Orleans Collection | Manuscripts, maps, photographs, newspapers | In-person; some digitized |
| New Orleans Public Library, Louisiana Division | City records, newspapers, local history | In-person |
| NARA Southeast Region (Atlanta) | Federal court records, naturalization files, census originals | In-person or online request |

## Records NOT online

- The bulk of the New Orleans Notarial Archives (30+ million pages) is not indexed online; the 1 digitized FamilySearch volume covering 1803-1820 is browse-only with no name index.
- Most pre-statehood (pre-1812) church registers beyond the St. Louis Cathedral series are held physically at the Archdiocese.
- City of New Orleans tax assessment rolls are largely physical-only.
- Orleans Parish Civil District Court succession files (physical originals) require in-person or written access at the courthouse or Louisiana State Archives.
- Spanish colonial records (padrones, land concessions, church records in Spanish) are held in part at the Louisiana State Archives, the Historic New Orleans Collection, and in part at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, Spain — a portion have been microfilmed by the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.

## Known record losses

- **Great New Orleans Fire of 1788:** Destroyed approximately 856 buildings in the French Quarter; many colonial administrative and church records were lost.
- **Great New Orleans Fire of 1794:** A second major fire destroyed much of what had been rebuilt, causing further record loss.
- **Effect on genealogical record survival:** According to the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters), sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral survive from 1731 despite these fires, though with gaps. Notarial records also survived in significant volume because the notarial protocols were held separately.
- **Yellow fever epidemics:** The epidemics of 1832 and especially 1853 killed tens of thousands of New Orleans residents; mortality records from these periods are incomplete, and many families lost members whose deaths were never formally recorded.
- **Flooding and hurricane damage:** Recurring storm and flood events over the 19th century caused localized record losses at individual repositories.
- **Substitute sources for lost records:** Notarial acts (marriages, property transactions, succession inventories); newspaper death and marriage notices; sacramental registers of congregations other than St. Louis Cathedral; federal census enumerations; passenger lists; free people of color registers; tax assessment rolls.

## Research tips

- **Check multiple denominations for church records.** While St. Louis Cathedral is the primary register, other Catholic churches (St. Augustine, established 1841 for the Creole of color community; Notre Dame de Bon Secours; etc.) kept their own registers. The FamilySearch Wiki at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy should be consulted directly for current collection lists and research strategies.

# Locality Guide: Port of Boston, Massachusetts (1820–1870)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Port:** Port of Boston, Suffolk County, Massachusetts
- **Administrative authority:** U.S. Customs Service (passenger lists); Suffolk County courts (naturalization); Town of Boston (vital records)
- **Population during period:** By 1850, over a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born, driven by the Great Famine (1845–1852). The city was the principal northeastern port of entry alongside New York.
- **Economy:** Maritime trade, commerce, light manufacturing; immigrants largely entered the unskilled labor market (domestic service, construction, longshoremen).
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Irish (especially post-1845), with significant German, English, and Canadian immigration throughout the 1840s–1860s.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant for Irish immigrants; Cathedral of the Holy Cross, St. Patrick's); various Protestant denominations for English, German, and Yankee populations.
- **Key historical events:** Irish Great Famine (1845–1852) produced a massive surge in arrivals; the 1847 season saw tens of thousands land at Boston in a matter of months.

## Boundary changes
- Boston has been within Suffolk County, Massachusetts since colonial settlement. No boundary changes during the 1820–1870 target period affect which records apply. Suffolk County courts and the Town of Boston are the relevant civil jurisdictions throughout.

## Available record types

### Passenger lists (customs manifests)
- **Series:** Customs passenger lists, 1820–1891, Port of Boston — National Archives Record Group 36
- **What exists:** Name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin for each passenger. The 1840s lists do not routinely give a specific place of origin within a country.
- **FamilySearch collection:** Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891 (collection 1784312), covering 1820–1891
- **Digitization status:** One confirmed digitized volume for 1840–1850 (FamilySearch image group 003345210, 389 images). This volume is only 3% name-indexed but is full-text searchable — search via full-text rather than the name index. The FamilySearch collection (1784312) provides broader indexed coverage across the date range.
- **Where held (originals):** National Archives at Boston (Waltham, Massachusetts)
- **Access:** FamilySearch (free); Ancestry (subscription) — both host indexed and image versions
- **Content note:** Examine the full manifest page for every member of a traveling family, including infants. Whole family groups are listed together on the same page.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Massachusetts town-level vital registration began in 1841. Statewide compliance was uneven through the 1840s; records from that decade may be incomplete.
- **What exists:** Births, marriages, and deaths recorded at the town (Boston) level from 1841 onward
- **FamilySearch collection:** Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890 (collection 2061550)
- **Where held:** Massachusetts State Archives (originals); FamilySearch and Ancestry (digital)
- **Gaps:** Early 1840s registration was incomplete — church records are essential for this decade
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers (see below)

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (primary for Irish immigrants), various Protestant denominations, German Lutheran and Reformed congregations
- **Key Catholic parishes:** Cathedral of the Holy Cross; St. Patrick's. The Archdiocese of Boston Archives holds Catholic parish registers for this period.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **FamilySearch collection:** Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920 (collection 1921657)
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of Boston Archives (Catholic); individual denominational archives; FamilySearch microfilm
- **Note (from wiki_search result):** Catholic parish registers documenting Irish immigrants from the 1840s onward are held by the Archdiocese of Boston Archives. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Massachusetts Church Records" — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston)

### Naturalization records
- **Types:** Declarations of intention ("first papers"), petitions for naturalization ("second papers"), oaths of allegiance
- **Important quirk:** Before 1906, a person could naturalize in ANY court of record — federal district court, state court, or county/municipal court. Do not limit the search to federal courts.
- **For Boston:** Suffolk County courts (Superior Court, Court of Common Pleas) are a primary location for 1840s–1860s naturalizations, alongside the U.S. District Court for Massachusetts.
- **FamilySearch collection:** Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906 (collection 1459213)
- **Where held:** National Archives at Boston (federal court records); Massachusetts State Archives and Suffolk County courthouse (state and county court records); FamilySearch (digitized)
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (via FamilySearch collection 1459213)

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1840, 1850, 1860, 1870 (decennial; 1890 largely destroyed by fire)
- **Note:** The 1840 census does not name individuals below the head of household; the 1850 census is the first to name all household members.
- **Mortality schedules:** Available for 1850, 1860, 1870 — record deaths in the year preceding the census enumeration
- **Access:** FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription) for all surviving schedules; indexed + images

### The Boston Pilot "Missing Persons" Database
- **What it is:** The Boston Pilot, an Irish Catholic newspaper, published advertisements placed by immigrants seeking separated family members. This is a separate source from passenger lists.
- **Coverage:** 1831–1921
- **Access:** Searchable online at infowanted.bc.edu (Boston College)
- **Research value:** High for Irish families separated during the Famine emigration; may give townland of origin or name of emigrant ship not found in the passenger list

### Probate records
- **Types:** Wills (testate estates), administrations (intestate), guardianships, inventories
- **Jurisdiction:** Suffolk County Probate Court
- **FamilySearch collection:** Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991 (collection 1678901)
- **Where held:** Suffolk County Probate Court; Massachusetts State Archives; FamilySearch (digitized)
- **Research value:** Estate papers name heirs and next of kin, providing family relationships when vital records are absent

### Newspapers
- **The Boston Pilot:** Irish Catholic newspaper; arrival notices and missing-persons advertisements (see above)
- **Boston Daily Advertiser, Boston Post, and other papers:** Obituaries, marriage notices, shipping arrivals (listed by vessel, with passenger counts)
- **Where held:** Boston Public Library (microfilm and digitized holdings); Newspapers.com and GenealogyBank (subscription, partial digitization)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848); Civil War (1861–1865)
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, state muster rolls
- **Where held:** NARA (federal service and pension records); Massachusetts State Archives (state muster rolls); Fold3 (subscription, digitized)
- **Note:** Many 1840s immigrants enlisted in the Civil War; pension files from the 1860s onward often give naturalization dates, place of birth, and family details

### Immigration/emigration — supplementary sources
- **Alien Passenger Acts records:** Massachusetts required ships' masters to report alien passengers to the state as well as to federal customs; state-level reports may exist at the Massachusetts State Archives for some years in this period.
- **Ports of embarkation:** Most Irish emigrants in the 1840s sailed from Liverpool, Cork (Queenstown/Cobh), or Dublin. British Board of Trade outward passenger lists (for Liverpool departures) are held at The National Archives (Kew) and partially indexed on Findmypast.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891 (1784312); Town Vital Records, 1620–1890 (2061550); Church Records, 1630–1920 (1921657); Naturalization Records, 1790–1906 (1459213); Probate Records, 1635–1991 (1678901) | Free |
| Ancestry | Passenger lists, census, naturalization, vital records (overlapping coverage) | Subscription |
| Boston College (infowanted.bc.edu) | Boston Pilot Missing Persons database, 1831–1921 | Free |
| Fold3 | Military service and pension records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com / GenealogyBank | Boston newspaper archives (partial) | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | National Archives at Boston — originals of customs passenger lists, federal court naturalizations | Free finding aids; in-person or duplication request for records |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 1 digitized volume (image group 003345210, 389 images) for Port of Boston passenger lists 1840–1850. This is a single result and likely does not represent the complete digitized holdings across the broader date range; the FamilySearch indexed collection (1784312) covers 1820–1891 and provides wider access.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA) | Original customs passenger lists (RG 36); federal court naturalization records | In-person; duplication requests |
| Massachusetts State Archives (Boston) | State vital records; alien passenger reports; state court records | In-person; some records online |
| Suffolk County Probate Court | Probate files | In-person; some online through MassLandRecords |
| Archdiocese of Boston Archives | Catholic parish registers | Appointment required; contact archives directly |
| Boston Public Library | Newspaper microfilm; local history collections | In-person; some digital |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS) | Vital records transcriptions; local histories; compiled genealogies | Membership (americanancestors.org) |

## Records NOT online
- Alien passenger reports filed with the Commonwealth of Massachusetts (state-level ship manifests, if extant for the 1840s) — held at Massachusetts State Archives, not digitized
- Original Catholic parish registers at the Archdiocese of Boston Archives — access requires appointment; not fully digitized
- Local court naturalization case files beyond index entries — original files at state and county courthouses
- Boston sexton records and burial registers for non-Catholic cemeteries — held by individual cemetery offices or city of Boston

## Known record losses
- The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed by fire and water damage in 1921 — not available for any location. Substitute with the 1880 and 1900 censuses, city directories, and state/local records.
- No known systematic courthouse fire affecting Suffolk County records in the target period. Record losses are not documented in this survey's tool results — note this as unconfirmed.

## Research tips
- **Start with passenger lists, then follow with naturalization records.** The passenger list confirms arrival; the naturalization declaration (filed as early as two years after arrival) often names the immigrant's specific origin place — something the 1840s manifests typically omit. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Massachusetts Immigration" — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston)
- **Use the Boston Pilot Missing Persons database before assuming the passenger list is the only arrival source.** The Pilot advertisements sometimes give the immigrant's county and townland of origin in Ireland, the name of the ship, and the date of arrival.
- **The 1840s passenger list volume (image group 003345210) is 3% name-indexed but full-text searchable** — do not rely on the name index; run a full-text search for surname variants.
- **For Catholic Irish immigrants, Catholic church records run parallel to and predate comprehensive civil registration.** Baptismal and marriage registers of Cathedral of the Holy Cross and St. Patrick's should be checked alongside civil vital records for the 1840s decade.
- **Many immigrants arriving in Boston in the 1840s did not settle in Boston.** If the ancestor appears in Pennsylvania, Ohio, or another inland state shortly after arrival, check Boston passenger lists for the family group even if the later state of residence is different. The 1840s lists will not show an onward destination.
- **Pre-1906 naturalizations: search all courts.** Suffolk County Superior Court and the U.S. District Court for Massachusetts both hold naturalizations from this era; FamilySearch collection 1459213 indexes across court levels but may not be complete.
- **Check the New England Historic Genealogical Society (americanancestors.org)** for transcribed vital records and compiled family histories that pre-date online digitization — NEHGS has deep Massachusetts holdings.
- **For German immigrants arriving at Boston in this period**, church records (Lutheran, Reformed, Catholic) are often in German. NEHGS and FamilySearch hold some German-language parish records for the Boston area.

This is a single result and likely does not represent the complete digitized holdings across the broader date range; the FamilySearch indexed collection (1784312) covers 1820–1891 and provides wider access.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA) | Original customs passenger lists (RG 36); federal court naturalization records | In-person; duplication requests |
| Massachusetts State Archives (Boston) | State vital records; alien passenger reports; state court records | In-person; some records online |
| Suffolk County Probate Court | Probate files | In-person; some online through MassLandRecords |
| Archdiocese of Boston Archives | Catholic parish registers | Appointment required; contact archives directly |
| Boston Public Library | Newspaper microfilm; local history collections | In-person; some digital |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS) | Vital records transcriptions; local histories; compiled genealogies | Membership (americanancestors.org) |

## Records NOT online
- Alien passenger reports filed with the Commonwealth of Massachusetts (state-level ship manifests, if extant for the 1840s) — held at Massachusetts State Archives, not digitized
- Original Catholic parish registers at the Archdiocese of Boston Archives — access requires appointment; not fully digitized
- Local court naturalization case files beyond index entries — original files at state and county courthouses
- Boston sexton records and burial registers for non-Catholic cemeteries — held by individual cemetery offices or city of Boston

## Known record losses
- The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed by fire and water damage in 1921 — not available for any location. Substitute with the 1880 and 1900 censuses, city directories, and state/local records.
- No known systematic courthouse fire affecting Suffolk County records in the target period. Record losses are not documented in this survey's tool results — note this as unconfirmed.

## Research tips
- **Start with passenger lists, then follow with naturalization records.** The passenger list confirms arrival; the naturalization declaration (filed as early as two years after arrival) often names the immigrant's specific origin place — something the 1840s manifests typically omit. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Massachusetts Immigration" — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston)
- **Use the Boston Pilot Missing Persons database before assuming the passenger list is the only arrival source.** The Pilot advertisements sometimes give the immigrant's county and townland of origin in Ireland, the name of the ship, and the date of arrival.
- **The 1840s passenger list volume (image group 003345210) is 3% name-indexed but full-text searchable** — do not rely on the name index; run a full-text search for surname variants.
- **For Catholic Irish immigrants, Catholic church records run parallel to and predate comprehensive civil registration.** Baptismal and marriage registers of Cathedral of the Holy Cross and St. Patrick's should be checked alongside civil vital records for the 1840s decade.
- **Many immigrants arriving in Boston in the 1840s did not settle in Boston.** If the ancestor appears in Pennsylvania, Ohio, or another inland state shortly after arrival, check Boston passenger lists for the family group even if the later state of residence is different. The 1840s lists will not show an onward destination.
- **Pre-1906 naturalizations: search all courts.** Suffolk County Superior Court and the U.S. District Court for Massachusetts both hold naturalizations from this era; FamilySearch collection 1459213 indexes across court levels but may not be complete.
- **Check the New England Historic Genealogical Society (americanancestors.org)** for transcribed vital records and compiled family histories that pre-date online digitization — NEHGS has deep Massachusetts holdings.
- **For German immigrants arriving at Boston in this period**, church records (Lutheran, Reformed, Catholic) are often in German. NEHGS and FamilySearch hold some German-language parish records for the Boston area.

---

**Indian Territory (Oklahoma) — Native American Research, Mid-1800s**

**Jurisdictional frame:** Indian Territory (present-day Oklahoma), roughly 1820 through statehood in 1907. There was no conventional county government or civil vital registration during the mid-1800s — each of the **Five Civilized Tribes** (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, and Seminole) maintained its own sovereign government, courts, and records, with a federal Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) administrative layer above them.

---

### Most Important Record Types

| Record | Coverage | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Dawes Rolls (1898–1914)** | All Five Tribes | Best-indexed starting point; supporting *application jackets* contain family testimony going back generations |
| **Drennen Roll (1852)** | Cherokee | Direct mid-1800s source |
| **Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851)** | Cherokee (western) | Direct mid-1800s source |
| **BIA Annuity Rolls** | Various tribes | Annual payment lists; identify heads of household |
| **Tribal Court Files** | Tribal-era | Land, probate, and civil records under tribal jurisdiction |
| **Missionary Church Registers** | Varies | Baptism, marriage, and burial records kept by mission stations |

---

### Key Repositories

- **NARA Southwest Region, Fort Worth, TX** — the primary physical repository for BIA and Indian Territory federal records
- **FamilySearch** — Collection **1987432** (*Oklahoma Indian Censuses and Rolls*)
- **Ancestry** — Dawes Roll index and related enrollment files
- **Oklahoma Historical Society** — Tribal records, newspapers, and territorial documents

---

### Critical Research Tip

Don't stop at the Dawes Rolls. Their application jackets contain sworn family testimony reaching back generations and are often the bridge to mid-1800s ancestors. Then work backward through earlier rolls (Drennen 1852, Old Settler 1851) for the period you're targeting.

---

If you'd like a concrete research plan with prioritized searches by record type and repository, just say the word and we can move to that step.
