- **Key historical events:** The Homestead Strike of 1892 (Carnegie Steel) generated court, newspaper, and union records. The mill towns along the Monongahela (Homestead, Braddock, Duquesne, McKeesport) expanded rapidly through this period.

## Boundary changes
- Allegheny County boundaries have been stable since 1800.
- **Allegheny City** (North Side of Pittsburgh today) was a separate municipality with its own records until Pittsburgh annexed it in 1907. Ancestors living in Allegheny City generated records filed under that city, not Pittsburgh.
- The mill towns of Homestead, Braddock, Duquesne, McKeesport, and Munhall were independent municipalities within Allegheny County — their records are separate from Pittsburgh's city records.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date — county level:** Allegheny County recorded births and deaths from approximately 1870, earlier than the statewide mandate. Per the wiki search result from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records: Pennsylvania did not require statewide civil registration until 1906.
- **What exists:** County-level birth and death registrations from ca. 1870–1905 (held at the Allegheny County Health Department / Pennsylvania State Archives). Statewide death certificates from 1906 onward are available on FamilySearch (collection 2255317, 4,218,763 records, indexed + images).
- **Marriage records:** Marriage licenses at the county level from 1885 (Allegheny County Courthouse). FamilySearch collections covering Pennsylvania county marriages 1885–1950 (collection 1921317, 524,189 records, indexed + images) and civil marriages 1677–1950 (collection 1571957, 312,045 records) cover this period.
- **Gaps:** Before 1870, there is no county-level civil registration of births or deaths. Church records are the primary substitute. The FamilySearch Wiki does not state a specific date for earlier Allegheny County birth registration beyond ca. 1870.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptismal, marriage, and burial registers; family Bibles; newspaper death notices.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (multiple ethnic parishes — Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian, Irish); Presbyterian, Methodist, Lutheran, Episcopal, Baptist; Greek/Byzantine Catholic; Jewish congregations.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. Catholic parish registers are especially valuable because each ethnic parish served a defined immigrant community.
- **Where held:** Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives holds many originals. FamilySearch has microfilmed some registers. Individual parishes retain others. The Heinz History Center has select collections.
- **Key quirk:** Identify the specific ethnic parish for your ancestor's national/religious background before searching Catholic records — a Polish family attended a Polish parish, not an Irish or Italian one. Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records, Catholic parishes kept registers from the 1840s onward.
- **Language:** Records of Slovak, Polish, Croatian, and other non-English parishes may be in Latin (sacramental entries) with vernacular marginalia. The FamilySearch volume search returned one volume covering Pennsylvania naturalization records 1790–1915 in English and German (imageGroupNumber 008120443, 15% name-indexed); German Lutheran records in the region may also use German.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Available for Allegheny County from 1800. Fully indexed years for the target period: 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900. The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed by fire — only a fragment survives nationally.
- **Value for industrial research:** The 1880 census records occupation and birthplace of parents. The 1900 census adds immigration year and years in the United States — critical for connecting steel workers to their home countries and villages. Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Census, these two censuses are particularly valuable for tracing industrial workers.
- **Mortality schedules:** The 1850–1885 mortality schedules (recording deaths in the year preceding each census) are available through FamilySearch and Ancestry and serve as a pre-1906 death record substitute.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct a separate statewide population census during this period.
- **Access:** Federal censuses 1860–1900 are indexed and searchable on FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription). Ancestry also offers full-image access.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships, estate distributions — filed at the Allegheny County Register of Wills from the county's formation in 1788.
- **Access on FamilySearch:** Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (collection 1999196) has 3,200,560 images but 0 indexed records — browse-only images, must be navigated image by image with no name search. The volume search returned one browse-only probate volume (imageGroupNumber 008120441, 1,180 images, 0% indexed, covering Pennsylvania 1683–1994).
- **Physical holdings:** Allegheny County Courthouse, Register of Wills office. Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) holds some older series.
- **Occupational relevance:** Probate inventories itemize personal property and sometimes name an employer or note stock in an industrial company.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Pennsylvania is a state-land (not federal-land) state — original grants come from William Penn and the Commonwealth, not the BLM. The Pennsylvania Land Office (Harrisburg) holds warrant, survey, and patent records from 1681. Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records.
- **County deeds:** Recorded at the Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds from 1788 onward. Mill workers who owned homes generated deed records; renters do not appear.
- **Tax records:** Assessment lists and tax duplicates survive for Allegheny County and serve as intercensal locating tools. Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records, Pennsylvania tax records survive from the 1690s in some counties.
- **Access:** Allegheny County deed books are held at the county courthouse. Some are accessible through the county's online portal. FamilySearch has microfilmed portions.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) is the dominant military event in this period. Spanish-American War (1898) for later ancestors.
- **Record types:** Civil War service and pension records at NARA (Washington, D.C., and online via Fold3 and Ancestry). Pennsylvania adjutant general records at the Pennsylvania State Archives. WWI draft registration (1917–1918) just outside the period but useful for men born in the 1870s–1890s.
- **Occupational overlap:** Pension application files often contain detailed biographical information including pre-war and post-war occupation and employer.
- **Access:** Fold3 (subscription) has Civil War pension index and many case files. Ancestry has pension and service records. NARA holds originals.

### Naturalization records
- **Repository:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record. The primary Allegheny County record set is the Court of Common Pleas (1798–1930), held at the **National Archives at Philadelphia** (NARA Mid-Atlantic Region). Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Census.
- **FamilySearch digitization:** One volume of Pennsylvania naturalization records 1790–1915 (imageGroupNumber 008120443, 351 images) is 15% name-indexed and partially searchable; the remainder must be browsed.
- **What they contain:** Declaration of intention (first papers) and petition for naturalization (second papers). Post-1906 petitions include place of birth, physical description, occupation, and employer.
- **Key quirk for steel workers:** Many immigrant steel workers filed their first papers to demonstrate intention to naturalize but never completed the process. Search for declarations as well as full petitions.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Most Eastern European steel workers arrived through the Port of New York (Ellis Island, 1892 onward; Castle Garden before that) or Baltimore. Some came via Philadelphia.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests (NARA, digitized on Ancestry, FamilySearch, and Statue of Liberty-Ellis Island Foundation website). After 1895, manifests list last residence and contact in country of origin — valuable for identifying home villages.
- **Access:** Ancestry and FamilySearch have indexed passenger lists for 1820–1957. The Ellis Island database (free, elislandapp.org) covers 1892–1957.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members — a steel worker who sent for his family may appear on a later manifest with wife and children.
- **Occupational data:** Post-1907 manifests include occupation and whether the immigrant had a job arranged — often naming an employer or contact in Pittsburgh.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Allegheny Cemetery (est. 1844), St. Mary Cemetery (Catholic), Homewood Cemetery, and numerous ethnic Catholic and Orthodox cemeteries throughout the county.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) has extensive transcriptions for Allegheny County cemeteries. BillionGraves covers some additional sites.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for major cemeteries are often held by the cemetery office or the Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives.
- **Ethnic cemeteries:** Many ethnic parishes maintained their own burial grounds; identify the parish first.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Pittsburgh Post-Gazette (est. 1786, still publishing), Pittsburgh Dispatch, Pittsburgh Press, Pittsburgh Leader, and ethnic-language papers (Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Yiddish) published from the 1880s onward.
- **Ethnic press:** Slovak and Polish newspapers carried death notices, marriage announcements, and letters from readers — often more detailed than English-language notices for immigrant families.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com and ProQuest Historical Newspapers (subscription) have Pittsburgh dailies. The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh and the Heinz History Center hold microfilm of local papers. Ethnic papers may be at university libraries (e.g., Balch Institute collections, now part of the Historical Society of Pennsylvania).
- **Content value:** Obituaries (especially post-1880) frequently name survivors, employer, length of residence, and home country.

### Industrial and occupational records (the key focus for this research)
- **Company employment records:** Fragmentary. Some Carnegie Steel / U.S. Steel employment records survive at the **Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh) and the **Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area** archives (Homestead, PA). These are not uniformly indexed or digitized; contact the repositories directly.
- **Pennsylvania State Factory Inspector Reports:** The state began inspecting factories from 1889. Annual reports list establishments, number of employees, and sometimes names of foremen or managers. Held at the Pennsylvania State Archives and in bound volumes at major research libraries.
- **Union records:** The Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers kept membership rolls; records are fragmentary but some survive at the Pennsylvania State Archives and the Historical Society of Western Pennsylvania (Heinz History Center).
- **City directories:** Pittsburgh city directories begin in 1813 and list residents by name with occupation and address. From the 1870s onward, reverse directories (street address to name) are available. Held at the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh; some years digitized at Ancestry and Internet Archive.
- **Federal census occupation data:** The 1880 and 1900 censuses record specific occupation (e.g., "puddler," "roller," "laborer in steel mill") and are the most systematic occupational source available for the full working population.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property assessment lists (tax duplicates) survive at the Allegheny County Recorder and Pennsylvania State Archives. These run annually and can place a family in a specific ward or township between census years.
- **Access:** Largely physical only at county or state level; some years microfilmed by FamilySearch.

### Other record types
- **City directories (as a research tool):** Described under Industrial records above — critical for this research focus.
- **Town and county histories:** Published county and neighborhood histories from the 1880s–1900s often include biographical sketches of prominent residents and workers. The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh and the Heinz History Center hold extensive local history collections.
- **School records:** Pittsburgh public school enrollment records exist for some periods; held by the Pittsburgh Public Schools archive and the Pittsburgh City Archives.
- **Social and fraternal organization records:** Ethnic mutual aid societies (e.g., the Slovak Catholic Sokol, Polish National Alliance) maintained membership lists. These are often at the organization's national headquarters or at the Balch Institute / Historical Society of Pennsylvania.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania County Marriages 1885–1950 (524,189 records, indexed); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (312,045 records); Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (3.2 million images, browse-only); Pennsylvania Death Certificates 1906–1968 (4.2 million records, indexed); Naturalization Records 1790–1915 (351 images, 15% indexed); passenger arrival lists | Free |
| Ancestry | Federal censuses 1860–1900 (indexed + images); Civil War pension files; passenger lists; city directories; some Pennsylvania vital records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Civil War service and pension records; military records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery transcriptions for Allegheny County | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Pittsburgh daily newspapers | Subscription |
| National Archives (archives.gov) | NARA finding aids; online naturalization indexes | Free / Fee for copies |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `volume_search` returned 3 digitized volumes statewide (total 3 results, no `nextPageToken`); these represent the full volume-search result for this place and period at the Pennsylvania level. City-level or Allegheny-County-level volume results were not differentiated by the tool, which resolved both to the state scope.

### Physical repositories

| Heinz History Center (Pittsburgh) | Industrial / employment records; union records; local history; ethnic community collections | In-person; contact for research services |
| Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area (Homestead) | Steel industry records; mill town history | In-person; contact for access |
| Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh | City directories from 1813; local newspapers on microfilm; local history books | In-person; some digitized |
| Allegheny County Courthouse (Pittsburgh) | Deeds, marriage licenses (1885+), court records, naturalization petitions | In-person / online portal for deeds |
| Allegheny County Register of Wills | Probate records from 1788 | In-person |
| National Archives at Philadelphia (NARA Mid-Atlantic) | Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas naturalization records 1798–1930; federal court records | In-person; some records on Ancestry/FamilySearch |
| Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives | Catholic parish registers; diocesan records | Contact for access; some records at Heinz History Center |
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) | County birth/death records (pre-1906); factory inspector reports; adjutant general records; tax duplicates | In-person / mail requests |
| Historical Society of Western Pennsylvania (at Heinz) | Manuscript collections; union records; community organization records | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Company employment records for Carnegie Steel / U.S. Steel (fragmentary; Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel)
- Pennsylvania State Factory Inspector annual reports (Pennsylvania State Archives)
- Union membership rolls of the Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers (fragmentary; Pennsylvania State Archives, Heinz History Center)
- Most Allegheny County pre-1870 county-level vital records
- Ethnic fraternal and mutual aid society membership lists
- Pittsburgh City Archives school enrollment records
- Many Catholic ethnic parish registers (Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives)
- Most county tax assessment duplicates (Pennsylvania State Archives)

## Known record losses
- The **1890 federal census** was largely destroyed by fire and water damage in 1921. Only a fragment survives nationally; Allegheny County is not among the surviving fragments. Use 1889 or 1891 city directories, tax records, and state factory inspector reports as substitutes.
- No known courthouse fire destroyed Allegheny County records during this period — the county records appear largely intact, which is fortunate compared to many Pennsylvania counties.

## Research tips
- **Vital records registration levels matter:** Pennsylvania had no statewide birth/death registration before 1906. Allegheny County recorded births and deaths from approximately 1870 at the county level. Before 1870, church registers are the only systematic vital record source. Marriage records are at the county level from the colonial period. (Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records.)
- **Start with city directories:** Pittsburgh directories beginning in 1813, held at the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh, are the fastest way to pin an ancestor to a specific address, occupation, and employer in the years between censuses. (Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records.)
- **Identify the ethnic parish first:** For Catholic immigrants, the specific parish determines which register to search. A Polish family would not be in an Irish or Slovak parish register. Contact the Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives to identify which parish served a given neighborhood in a given decade. (Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records.)
- **Naturalization records cross institutional lines:** Pre-1906 declarations could be filed in any court — state, county, or federal. Search the Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas records at the National Archives at Philadelphia, and also the federal district court records. (Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Census.)
- **Use the 1900 census immigration year field:** The 1900 census is the single most useful document for connecting a steel-era immigrant to a home country and approximate arrival date, enabling a passenger list search.
- **Allegheny City records are separate:** If your ancestor lived in Allegheny City (North Side) before 1907, search Allegheny City records, not Pittsburgh city records. Annexation was in 1907.
- **Search neighboring mill towns carefully:** Homestead, Braddock, McKeesport, and Duquesne were separate municipalities in Allegheny County. Vital and court records for residents of those towns were not filed with Pittsburgh. Confirm the municipality of residence from a census or directory before routing a search.
- **Cross-border research:** Allegheny County borders Washington County (south), Westmoreland County (east), Butler County (north), Beaver County (northwest), and Lawrence County (north). The neighboring-counties table was not returned by the wiki tools in this run, so this list is drawn from geographic context rather than a returned wiki table. Families near county lines may have generated records in adjoining counties, particularly Washington and Westmoreland (both older counties with their own record series).
- **The Homestead Strike of 1892** generated newspaper coverage, court records, and Pinkerton agency reports that can document individual workers. Check the Heinz History Center and the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh for Homestead Strike collections.

# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania — 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic (Focus: 1780–1820)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Philadelphia County formed 1682; Philadelphia City and County became coextensive after the Act of Consolidation of 1854 (outside the target period, but note the dual naming in older records).
- **County seat / administrative center:** Philadelphia
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Approximately 50,000 residents in 1793, making it the largest city in the United States and the national capital at the time. The 1790 federal census is the nearest population enumeration.
- **Economy:** Seaport commerce, merchant trade, crafts, shipping, printing, and early manufacturing. The city's port meant a cosmopolitan mix of residents and regular arrivals of sailors and immigrants.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English Quaker founding stock, with significant German, Scots-Irish, Welsh, and African American communities. A sizable free Black community was active in epidemic relief efforts.
- **Religious denominations:** Society of Friends (Quakers), Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church, St. Peter's), Presbyterian, Lutheran, German Reformed, Methodist, Baptist, Roman Catholic, and African Methodist Episcopal (founded 1793 by Absalom Jones and Richard Allen).
- **Key historical events:** The 1793 yellow fever epidemic (August–November 1793) killed roughly 5,000 residents — one-tenth of the city's population. The federal government and thousands of residents fled. The epidemic generated a concentrated burst of burial, probate, and relief records.

## Boundary changes
- Philadelphia County has been stable since its 1682 formation. The city and county became coextensive by the 1854 Consolidation Act, well after the target period. For 1793 research, the city and county were distinct jurisdictions, but the same courthouse and record-keeping offices served both.
- No boundary changes directly affecting record creation during 1780–1820.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not require statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths until **1906** at the state level. No civil birth, marriage, or death certificates exist for 1793.
- **What exists:** No state-level vital records for this period. The collections_search result confirms the earliest Pennsylvania Death Certificates collection begins in 1906 (FamilySearch collection 2255317).
- **Where held:** Not applicable for this period.
- **Gaps:** The entire 1793 period is a civil registration gap. The Philadelphia City Archives holds some early city-level health board records, but these are not a complete substitute.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church burial registers are the primary death record. The Mathew Carey published list of epidemic dead (1793) is a key supplement. See Church Records below.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Quakers (Society of Friends), Episcopal (Christ Church, St. Peter's, St. Paul's), Presbyterian, Lutheran, German Reformed, Methodist, Baptist, Roman Catholic (St. Mary's), and the newly formed African Methodist Episcopal congregation.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and confirmations. Burial registers from August–November 1793 are the most direct documentary evidence of epidemic deaths.
- **Where held:**
  - **Christ Church (Episcopal):** Burial registers held by Christ Church; transcripts and microfilm at FamilySearch and the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania (GSP).
  - **Gloria Dei (Old Swedes' Church):** One of the oldest surviving churches; records held at the church and on FamilySearch microfilm.
  - **Society of Friends (Quakers):** Philadelphia Yearly Meeting records held by the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Archives. FamilySearch has one digitized volume of Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (imageGroupNumber 001188322) — **browse-only, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable**.
  - **Other denominations:** Records scattered across individual congregations, the Presbyterian Historical Society, and the Lutheran Archives Center at Philadelphia.
  - **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania:** Holds indexes to many Philadelphia church records — consult these first.
- **Language:** Most records are in English; German Lutheran and Reformed records may be in German.
- **Digitization level:** Varies. Quaker minutes: browse-only images (FamilySearch). Many other church registers: physical or microfilm only at the GSP or denominational archives.

### Epidemic-specific primary sources
These sources are unique to the 1793 outbreak and have no parallel in ordinary record series:

- **Mathew Carey, 'A Short Account of the Malignant Fever' (1793):** A published pamphlet containing a named list of the dead. Widely reprinted and digitized; available via HathiTrust and Google Books. A genealogical source, not a government record.
- **Committee of Philadelphia minutes and reports:** The citizens' relief committee (appointed by Mayor Matthew Clarkson) kept minutes and distribution lists naming residents who received aid. Manuscript copies held at the **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)**. Not online.
- **Bush Hill hospital records:** The epidemic hospital at Bush Hill kept patient registers. Held at the **Historical Society of Pennsylvania**. Not online.
- **Philadelphia Board of Health records:** The city health board began more systematic record-keeping after 1793. Some early records held at the **Philadelphia City Archives**.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1790 federal census is the closest pre-epidemic enumeration; the 1800 census captures the post-epidemic population. Both are indexed and available on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **State/provincial census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct a state census during this period.
- **Other enumerations:** The 1793 relief committee lists function as a partial census of epidemic-affected households.
- **Access:** 1790 and 1800 federal censuses: indexed and online (FamilySearch, Ancestry). Relief lists: physical only at HSP.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations (intestate), guardianships, inventories, estate distributions.
- **Date range:** Philadelphia County probate records run continuously from the colonial period. The FamilySearch collection Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (collection ID 1999196) covers this period with 3,200,560 images — **browse-only** (0 indexed records, images must be browsed by date/volume).
- **Epidemic relevance:** The spike in deaths August–November 1793 produced a corresponding spike in probate filings that autumn and winter. Searching probate records filed in late 1793 and early 1794 is a targeted way to find epidemic fatalities, particularly for property-owning families.
- **Testate vs. intestate:** Families whose breadwinner died suddenly in an epidemic often died intestate (no will) — search administration records as well as wills.
- **Where held:** Register of Wills, Philadelphia; FamilySearch microfilm (browse-only online via collection 1999196).

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state; the Commonwealth, not the federal government, granted land).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Pennsylvania Land Office (now the Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg) holds the original land grants and patents. County deed books held at the Philadelphia County Recorder of Deeds.
- **Types:** Deeds, warrants, surveys, patents, mortgages, ground rents (Philadelphia was heavily ground-rent encumbered in the 18th century).
- **Date range:** Deed books from 1682 forward.
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City/County Recorder of Deeds for deeds; Pennsylvania State Archives for warrants and patents. Some records available through FamilySearch microfilm.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War (concluded 1783, just before the target window); the Quasi-War with France (1798–1800); the War of 1812 (1812–1815).
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records and pension files (NARA, many indexed on Fold3 and FamilySearch); War of 1812 service and pension records (NARA); Pennsylvania militia records (Pennsylvania State Archives).
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C. and regional facilities); Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; online via Fold3 and FamilySearch.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:**
  - Christ Church Burial Ground (Episcopal) — notably used during the epidemic
  - Gloria Dei Churchyard (Old Swedes')
  - St. Peter's Churchyard (Episcopal)
  - Friends (Quaker) burial grounds (multiple, non-marked)
  - African American burial grounds (several, some lost)
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has partial coverage of Philadelphia's historic cemeteries, with variable completeness for the 1793 period.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers held by individual congregations or their archives. The epidemic created hasty burials that were not always fully documented.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Pennsylvania Gazette, Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser, and Claypoole's American Daily Advertiser all published during 1793. Several carried epidemic-related notices, death notices, and lists of the dead.
- **Where held:** Historical Society of Pennsylvania; Library Company of Philadelphia; digitized collections at Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and Accessible Archives.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, death notices, official announcements by the relief committee, lists of the dead, and notices of property for sale by estates.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was a major port of entry. Passenger arrival lists are held at NARA.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests), declarations of intention, naturalization records. Pre-1820 passenger lists are incomplete — systematic recording began with the Steerage Act of 1819.
- **Where held:** NARA; FamilySearch and Ancestry hold digitized/indexed passenger lists. Pre-1820 coverage is sparse.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children. When researching an immigrant family affected by the epidemic, examine the full manifest for all traveling members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Pennsylvania provincial and state tax records; county-level property and personal property assessments.
- **Date range:** Tax lists survive from the colonial period. The 1779, 1782, 1793, and 1798 Philadelphia County tax lists are important for this window.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; Philadelphia City Archives; some transcribed records at the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania. Some lists digitized on Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists from 1793 and surrounding years can confirm a person's presence in (or absence from) Philadelphia before and after the epidemic, and can document property that then appears in probate.

### Other record types
- **Relief and institutional records:** The Bush Hill hospital registers and committee distribution lists name individuals not captured in church or probate records, including poor and working-class residents who owned no property. Held at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania; physical access only.
- **African American records:** The Free African Society (founded 1787) kept membership records. Richard Allen's and Absalom Jones's congregations also kept records from 1793 onward. The African Methodist Episcopal Church Archives and the HSP are key repositories.
- **City directories:** The Philadelphia city directory began publication in the 1780s. Directories for 1793–1794 can confirm a person's address before and after the epidemic and show which households disappeared. Available on Ancestry and in facsimile at the HSP and Library Company of Philadelphia.
- **Quaker meeting records:** Beyond the Yearly Meeting minutes, individual monthly meeting records (births, marriages, deaths, disownments) are held by the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Archives and are among the most thorough pre-1800 vital series in the city.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683–1994 (browse-only images, collection 1999196); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (collection 1571957); Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (collection 1502909); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (imageGroupNumber 001188322, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | 1790 and 1800 federal census (indexed); Philadelphia city directories; some Pennsylvania tax lists and church records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Philadelphia newspapers including 1793 epidemic coverage | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War and War of 1812 pension and service records | Subscription |
| HathiTrust / Google Books | Mathew Carey's 'A Short Account of the Malignant Fever' (1793) — digitized and free | Free |
| FindAGrave | Partial cemetery transcriptions for Philadelphia historic churchyards | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume for Philadelphia County in this period (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, browse-only). This is almost certainly not the complete set of digitized material — the collections_search and volume_search returned limited results, indicating further pages were not examined. The FamilySearch catalog and physical microfilm holdings at the Family History Library are likely to contain additional Philadelphia records not surfaced by these results.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP) | Committee of Philadelphia minutes; Bush Hill hospital records; manuscript church records; newspapers; city directories | In-person; some materials by appointment |
| Philadelphia City Archives | City health board records; municipal records from the 1790s | In-person; written requests |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Land warrants and patents; provincial and state tax records; militia records | In-person; some online finding aids |
| Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania | Indexes to Philadelphia church records; compiled genealogies | In-person; published indexes |
| Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Archives | Quaker monthly and quarterly meeting records (births, marriages, deaths, disownments) | In-person or written inquiry |
| Lutheran Archives Center at Philadelphia | Lutheran church records for colonial and early national period | In-person |
| Presbyterian Historical Society | Philadelphia-area Presbyterian church records | In-person |
| Library Company of Philadelphia | Historical newspapers; city directories; published accounts of the epidemic | In-person; some digital holdings |
| NARA (Philadelphia region) | Federal records including passenger lists, naturalization records, military pension records | In-person at NARA Philadelphia; online via Ancestry/FamilySearch for indexed series |

## Records NOT online

- Committee of Philadelphia relief minutes and distribution lists (1793) — HSP, physical only
- Bush Hill hospital patient registers — HSP, physical only
- Philadelphia Board of Health early records — Philadelphia City Archives, physical only
- Most individual congregation burial registers not covered by FamilySearch microfilm — held by individual churches or denominational archives
- Free African Society membership records — HSP and AME archives, physical only
- Philadelphia County deed books (original volumes) — Recorder of Deeds, Philadelphia, physical access

## Known record losses

- No major courthouse fire destroyed Philadelphia County records (unlike many Pennsylvania county courthouses). The county seat remained intact through the period.
- Hasty epidemic burials in August–November 1793 were not always recorded in church registers — some deaths went undocumented or were recorded only in the Mathew Carey list.
- Pre-1820 passenger arrival records are incomplete by law: systematic manifests were not required until the Steerage Act of 1819. Earlier arrivals may appear only in port entry books, if at all.
- Some African American community records from this period were never formally archived and are effectively lost.

## Research tips

- **Start with the Mathew Carey pamphlet.** Carey's 'A Short Account of the Malignant Fever' (1793) contains a named list of the dead and is freely digitized on HathiTrust and Google Books. It is the quickest check for whether a person's name appears among documented epidemic fatalities. [Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Philadelphia Genealogy — Yellow Fever 1793, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793]
- **Check probate records filed in late 1793 and early 1794.** A sudden mass-death event leaves a documentary trail in the Register of Wills. Browsing the Philadelphia probate volumes (FamilySearch collection 1999196) by date range is more efficient than searching by name for this period, given the browse-only status.
- **Use the church burial registers as your death certificate.** Pennsylvania had no civil death registration in 1793. Church burial entries — especially from Christ Church, Gloria Dei, and the Catholic and German congregations — are the equivalent record for this period. [Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Philadelphia Genealogy — Church Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records]
- **Cross-check city directories for 1792, 1793, and 1794.** A name present in the 1792 directory but absent in 1794 is circumstantial evidence of epidemic death, flight, or family disruption. Available on Ancestry and at the HSP.
- **Search surrounding counties for families who fled.** Thousands of residents left Philadelphia during August–November 1793. They may appear in the tax lists, church records, or court records of Montgomery, Bucks, Chester, and Delaware counties during that year.
- **The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania's indexes are a required first stop** before pulling original church registers. They have compiled name indexes to many Philadelphia church record series that are otherwise browse-only.
- **Quaker records are unusually complete.** If your ancestor was a Quaker, the Philadelphia Monthly Meeting records held by the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Archives document births, marriages, deaths, and disownments with a level of detail rarely matched by other denominations in this period.
- **Do not overlook African American records.** The epidemic disproportionately involved Philadelphia's free Black community, both as victims and as the primary caregivers who staffed the relief effort. The Free African Society records, AME congregation records, and the accounts by Absalom Jones and Richard Allen are specific sources for this community.
- **The 1793 relief committee records are genealogically underused.** The distribution lists name ordinary working-class and poor residents who owned no property and therefore left no probate trail. They are held at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and require an in-person visit.

  - Christ Church Burial Ground (Episcopal) — notably used during the epidemic
  - Gloria Dei Churchyard (Old Swedes')
  - St. Peter's Churchyard (Episcopal)
  - Friends (Quaker) burial grounds (multiple, non-marked)
  - African American burial grounds (several, some lost)
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has partial coverage of Philadelphia's historic cemeteries, with variable completeness for the 1793 period.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers held by individual congregations or their archives. The epidemic created hasty burials that were not always fully documented.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Pennsylvania Gazette, Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser, and Claypoole's American Daily Advertiser all published during 1793. Several carried epidemic-related notices, death notices, and lists of the dead.
- **Where held:** Historical Society of Pennsylvania; Library Company of Philadelphia; digitized collections at Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and Accessible Archives.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, death notices, official announcements by the relief committee, lists of the dead, and notices of property for sale by estates.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was a major port of entry. Passenger arrival lists are held at NARA.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests), declarations of intention, naturalization records. Pre-1820 passenger lists are incomplete — systematic recording began with the Steerage Act of 1819.
- **Where held:** NARA; FamilySearch and Ancestry hold digitized/indexed passenger lists. Pre-1820 coverage is sparse.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children. When researching an immigrant family affected by the epidemic, examine the full manifest for all traveling members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Pennsylvania provincial and state tax records; county-level property and personal property assessments.
- **Date range:** Tax lists survive from the colonial period. The 1779, 1782, 1793, and 1798 Philadelphia County tax lists are important for this window.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; Philadelphia City Archives; some transcribed records at the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania. Some lists digitized on Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists from 1793 and surrounding years can confirm a person's presence in (or absence from) Philadelphia before and after the epidemic, and can document property that then appears in probate.

### Other record types
- **Relief and institutional records:** The Bush Hill hospital registers and committee distribution lists name individuals not captured in church or probate records, including poor and working-class residents who owned no property. Held at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania; physical access only.
- **African American records:** The Free African Society (founded 1787) kept membership records. Richard Allen's and Absalom Jones's congregations also kept records from 1793 onward. The African Methodist Episcopal Church Archives and the HSP are key repositories.
- **City directories:** The Philadelphia city directory began publication in the 1780s. Directories for 1793–1794 can confirm a person's address before and after the epidemic and show which households disappeared. Available on Ancestry and in facsimile at the HSP and Library Company of Philadelphia.
- **Quaker meeting records:** Beyond the Yearly Meeting minutes, individual monthly meeting records (births, marriages, deaths, disownments) are held by the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Archives and are among the most thorough pre-1800 vital series in the city.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683–1994 (browse-only images, collection 1999196); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (collection 1571957); Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (collection 1502909); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (imageGroupNumber 001188322, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | 1790 and 1800 federal census (indexed); Philadelphia city directories; some Pennsylvania tax lists and church records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Philadelphia newspapers including 1793 epidemic coverage | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War and War of 1812 pension and service records | Subscription |
| HathiTrust / Google Books | Mathew Carey's 'A Short Account of the Malignant Fever' (1793) — digitized and free | Free |
| FindAGrave | Partial cemetery transcriptions for Philadelphia historic churchyards | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume for Philadelphia County in this period (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, browse-only). This is almost certainly not the complete set of digitized material — the collections_search and volume_search returned limited results, indicating further pages were not examined. The FamilySearch catalog and physical microfilm holdings at the Family History Library are likely to contain additional Philadelphia records not surfaced by these results.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP) | Committee of Philadelphia minutes; Bush Hill hospital records; manuscript church records; newspapers; city directories | In-person; some materials by appointment |
| Philadelphia City Archives | City health board records; municipal records from the 1790s | In-person; written requests |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Land warrants and patents; provincial and state tax records; militia records | In-person; some online finding aids |
| Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania | Indexes to Philadelphia church records; compiled genealogies | In-person; published indexes |
| Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Archives | Quaker monthly and quarterly meeting records (births, marriages, deaths, disownments) | In-person or written inquiry |
| Lutheran Archives Center at Philadelphia | Lutheran church records for colonial and early national period | In-person |
| Presbyterian Historical Society | Philadelphia-area Presbyterian church records | In-person |
| Library Company of Philadelphia | Historical newspapers; city directories; published accounts of the epidemic | In-person; some digital holdings |
| NARA (Philadelphia region) | Federal records including passenger lists, naturalization records, military pension records | In-person at NARA Philadelphia; online via Ancestry/FamilySearch for indexed series |

## Records NOT online

- Committee of Philadelphia relief minutes and distribution lists (1793) — HSP, physical only
- Bush Hill hospital patient registers — HSP, physical only
- Philadelphia Board of Health early records — Philadelphia City Archives, physical only
- Most individual congregation burial registers not covered by FamilySearch microfilm — held by individual churches or denominational archives
- Free African Society membership records — HSP and AME archives, physical only
- Philadelphia County deed books (original volumes) — Recorder of Deeds, Philadelphia, physical access

## Known record losses

- No major courthouse fire destroyed Philadelphia County records (unlike many Pennsylvania county courthouses). The county seat remained intact through the period.
- Hasty epidemic burials in August–November 1793 were not always recorded in church registers — some deaths went undocumented or were recorded only in the Mathew Carey list.
- Pre-1820 passenger arrival records are incomplete by law: systematic manifests were not required until the Steerage Act of 1819. Earlier arrivals may appear only in port entry books, if at all.
- Some African American community records from this period were never formally archived and are effectively lost.

## Research tips

- **Start with the Mathew Carey pamphlet.** Carey's 'A Short Account of the Malignant Fever' (1793) contains a named list of the dead and is freely digitized on HathiTrust and Google Books. It is the quickest check for whether a person's name appears among documented epidemic fatalities. [Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Philadelphia Genealogy — Yellow Fever 1793, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793]
- **Check probate records filed in late 1793 and early 1794.** A sudden mass-death event leaves a documentary trail in the Register of Wills. Browsing the Philadelphia probate volumes (FamilySearch collection 1999196) by date range is more efficient than searching by name for this period, given the browse-only status.
- **Use the church burial registers as your death certificate.** Pennsylvania had no civil death registration in 1793. Church burial entries — especially from Christ Church, Gloria Dei, and the Catholic and German congregations — are the equivalent record for this period. [Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Philadelphia Genealogy — Church Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records]
- **Cross-check city directories for 1792, 1793, and 1794.** A name present in the 1792 directory but absent in 1794 is circumstantial evidence of epidemic death, flight, or family disruption. Available on Ancestry and at the HSP.
- **Search surrounding counties for families who fled.** Thousands of residents left Philadelphia during August–November 1793. They may appear in the tax lists, church records, or court records of Montgomery, Bucks, Chester, and Delaware counties during that year.
- **The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania's indexes are a required first stop** before pulling original church registers. They have compiled name indexes to many Philadelphia church record series that are otherwise browse-only.
- **Quaker records are unusually complete.** If your ancestor was a Quaker, the Philadelphia Monthly Meeting records held by the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Archives document births, marriages, deaths, and disownments with a level of detail rarely matched by other denominations in this period.
- **Do not overlook African American records.** The epidemic disproportionately involved Philadelphia's free Black community, both as victims and as the primary caregivers who staffed the relief effort. The Free African Society records, AME congregation records, and the accounts by Absalom Jones and Richard Allen are specific sources for this community.
- **The 1793 relief committee records are genealogically underused.** The distribution lists name ordinary working-class and poor residents who owned no property and therefore left no probate trail. They are held at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and require an in-person visit.

## Chicago, Cook County, Illinois — Great Fire Research Guide (1860–1885)

### The Core Challenge

The **Great Chicago Fire of October 8–10, 1871** destroyed the Cook County Courthouse and with it the vast majority of pre-fire records:

- Court records (including naturalization papers)
- Tax rolls
- Many church registers

Because originals were in Washington, D.C., federal records survived intact. FamilySearch holds four indexed Illinois/Chicago collections beginning in 1871:
- **Birth certificates** — 1.45 million records

| Record Type | Where to Find It |
|---|---|
| 1850, 1860, 1870 federal censuses | FamilySearch / Ancestry (originals in Washington — survived) |

| Federal land patents | BLM General Land Office website |

quirks: The Great Chicago Fire of October 8-10, 1871 destroyed the Cook County Courthouse and most pre-fire records including deeds, probate files, court records, tax rolls, and many church registers — treat 1871 as a hard break and pivot to substitute sources for anything before that date.

The Burnt Record Act of 1872 required property owners to re-register their deeds; these reconstructed deed filings are the primary substitute for pre-fire land records and are held by the Chicago Title and Trust Company collection at the Chicago History Museum.

Federal census schedules for 1850, 1860, and 1870 survived the fire because the originals were held in Washington D.C. — the 1870 Chicago enumeration in particular is a key pre-fire population snapshot.

Civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths at the Cook County level effectively begins in 1871 (post-fire); no statewide Illinois registration existed during this period — the FamilySearch Wiki generic page did not state a start date for Illinois statewide registration, so do not assume one.

City directories from the 1840s onward survived and are held at the Newberry Library — these are indispensable substitutes for locating individuals between census years and in the immediate post-fire period.

Catholic parish registers are held by the Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives; some parishes were destroyed in the fire but registers may survive from parishes on the outskirts or from re-established parishes.

Illinois is a federal-land state; pre-fire land grants and patents are available through the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM GLO) website and were not stored in the Cook County Courthouse.

Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record — circuit court, probate court, or federal district court — so search all three series, not just one, especially since some Cook County court records were destroyed in 1871.

Two FamilySearch digitized volumes cover this period: DGS 009982110 (38 images, pre-fire reconstructed court records 1865-1871, 0% name-indexed, browse-only) and DGS 009982111 (112 images, post-fire property re-recordings 1871-1880, 41% name-indexed). Volume_search returned 2 total results — these are the complete set.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois (1860-1885)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Cook County formed in 1831; Chicago incorporated as a town 1833, as a city 1837
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chicago
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Illinois (state)
- **Population during period:** Population data tool returned no figures for this place; per Wikipedia, Chicago grew from approximately 109,000 (1860) to 503,000 (1880) as a major industrial and rail hub
- **Economy:** Rail terminus, meatpacking, grain trading, lumber, manufacturing; attracted massive immigrant labor
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish, German, Scandinavian, Polish, Bohemian, and native-born American populations; smaller African American community
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant among Irish, Polish, German, Bohemian immigrants), Lutheran (German, Scandinavian), Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, Episcopalian, Jewish congregations
- **Key historical events:** Great Chicago Fire, October 8-10, 1871 — destroyed roughly 3.3 square miles of the city, killed approximately 300 people, left over 100,000 homeless, and destroyed the Cook County Courthouse and the majority of pre-fire official records

## Boundary changes
- Cook County boundaries were stable during this period
- Chicago city limits expanded through annexations (notably in 1889, just outside the target window), but for 1860-1885 the city and county are the operative jurisdictions
- No record-custody split requiring a different parent jurisdiction

## The record break of 1871

The Great Chicago Fire is the single most important fact for this research. According to Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire), the fire destroyed the Cook County Courthouse, which housed deeds, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls. The FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire) confirms that probate files and many church registers were also lost. Every record type below must be assessed against this break: records before October 1871 are presumed destroyed unless a specific survival is documented; records from late 1871 onward begin fresh series.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Cook County civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths begins effectively with the post-fire period (late 1871 onward). The Illinois-specific Vital Records wiki page did not return content in this session, so no statewide Illinois registration start date can be confirmed from tool results — do not assume one without checking the FamilySearch Wiki directly
- **What exists (FamilySearch collections):**
  - Birth Certificates, 1871-1940 — 1,450,000 records (collection ID 2024189)
  - Death Records, 1871-1947 — 980,000 records (collection ID 1913456)
  - Marriage Records, 1871-1920 — 620,000 records (collection ID 1756321)
- **Digitization level:** These are FamilySearch indexed collections — indexed + images
- **Where held:** Cook County Clerk's office (originals); FamilySearch (online)
- **Gaps:** No pre-fire civil vital records survive for Chicago/Cook County. Pre-1871 events must be documented through church registers, the 1850/1860/1870 census, or city directories
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptismal, marriage, and burial registers; federal census mortality schedules (1850-1880 list deaths in the prior year)

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic, Lutheran (German and Scandinavian congregations), Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, Episcopalian, Jewish congregations, Bohemian and Polish ethnic parishes
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **FamilySearch collection:** Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833-1925 — 285,000 records (collection ID 1803978; indexed + images for the indexed portion)
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives (Catholic registers); denominational archives for Protestant denominations; FamilySearch has microfilmed many post-fire registers. The FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories) names the Bernardin Archives specifically
- **Fire impact:** Many downtown parish registers were destroyed. Parishes on the periphery and suburban parishes were more likely to survive. For destroyed parishes, check whether neighboring parishes absorbed the congregation and continued a combined register
- **Language:** German, Polish, Bohemian (Czech), and Scandinavian registers will be in those languages; Latin is common in pre-Vatican II Catholic sacramental records

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1860, 1870 — SURVIVED the fire (originals held in Washington D.C., per Wikipedia). The 1880 federal census is also available. The 1890 federal census was destroyed in a Washington fire (1921) nationally
- **State census:** Illinois conducted state censuses in 1855 and 1865; survival and digitization status not confirmed by a specific wiki page in this session — check the Illinois State Archives
- **Mortality schedules:** Available 1850-1880, recording deaths in the year preceding the census; the 1870 mortality schedule captures some deaths near the fire period
- **Access:** 1860, 1870, 1880 federal censuses are indexed + images on FamilySearch and Ancestry
- **Key point:** The 1870 Chicago census, taken before the October fire, is the most important pre-fire population snapshot for locating families

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, inventories, naturalization petitions, civil and criminal cases
- **Fire impact:** Pre-1871 Cook County probate and court records were largely destroyed in the courthouse fire, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)

- **Economy:** Rail terminus, meatpacking, grain trading, lumber, manufacturing; attracted massive immigrant labor
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish, German, Scandinavian, Polish, Bohemian, and native-born American populations; smaller African American community
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant among Irish, Polish, German, Bohemian immigrants), Lutheran (German, Scandinavian), Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, Episcopalian, Jewish congregations

## Boundary changes

- **Naming conventions:** German, Scandinavian, and Slavic immigrants often anglicized surnames; Irish names were sometimes phonetically respelled. Search variant spellings, especially for the 1860 and 1870 censuses where enumerators recorded names as heard

quirks: The entire 1700s period falls under colonial rule — French (1699-1762) then Spanish (1762-1800) then briefly French again (1800-1803). There was NO civil vital registration; the Catholic Church was the only legally recognized church, and Catholic sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the primary vital record source for all free and enslaved persons.
The Code Noir required baptism of all enslaved persons in the Catholic Church, so sacramental registers record enslaved individuals — search them for any family in the colony, not only free settlers.

The Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur), the colony's governing body, kept court, land grant, contract, and estate records from 1712. These records are held at the Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) and are partially digitized. They do not overlap with parish registers.

Louisiana is a civil-law (not common-law) state, inherited from French and Spanish legal traditions. Notarial acts — not deeds recorded at a courthouse — are how property transfers, wills, marriage contracts, and many other transactions were documented. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds notarial records from the 1730s onward.

FamilySearch has 2 digitized volumes covering this period (image groups 004330991 and 004330992). Both are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — they must be browsed image-by-image. Records are in French and Spanish; a reading knowledge of both languages is needed.

The Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France holds the metropolitan administrative correspondence and census rolls for the French colonial period. This is a physical/correspondence-access repository not covered by FamilySearch.

Louisiana did not become a U.S. state until 1812. Federal census coverage begins in 1810 for Orleans Territory. There are no federal censuses for the French or Spanish colonial period — colonial censuses (recensements) were conducted by the colonial government and are held at ANOM and the Louisiana Historical Center.

Land grants in colonial Louisiana followed French concession and Spanish grant systems, not the U.S. rectangular survey. Colonial land claims were adjudicated after the Louisiana Purchase and are documented in the American State Papers: Public Lands series and at the Louisiana State Land Office.

Parish (ecclesiastical) and parish (civil/county equivalent) are two entirely different things in Louisiana. Civil parishes — Louisiana's county equivalent — did not exist until after 1807; do not conflate them with Catholic parishes, which are the relevant ecclesiastical unit for the 1700s.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Louisiana, United States — French Colonial Period (1699-1803)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** French presence established 1699; formal colony proclaimed 1712 under the Company of the Indies. New Orleans founded 1718. France ceded western Louisiana to Spain by the Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762), ratified 1764. Spain administered the colony until 1800; Napoleon retroceded it to France, then sold it to the United States in the Louisiana Purchase (1803).
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (founded 1718) served as the colonial capital throughout the period.
- **Parent jurisdiction (French era):** New France / Company of the Indies
- **Parent jurisdiction (Spanish era):** Viceroyalty of New Spain, Captaincy General of Cuba
- **Population during period:** No FamilySearch population data was returned for this period. Wikipedia and the FamilySearch wiki_search result note a small, slowly growing settler population through the early 18th century, augmented by enslaved Africans and later Acadian exiles (1755-1785). A colonial census (recensement) from the French period survives and is held at ANOM, Aix-en-Provence.
- **Economy:** Fur trade, indigo cultivation, later sugar cane and cotton; river commerce on the Mississippi. Plantation agriculture dependent on enslaved labor.
- **Ethnic composition:** French settlers (metropolitan and Canadian), German immigrants (Côte des Allemands settlement), Acadian exiles from 1755, Spanish settlers after 1762, free people of color (gens de couleur libres), and a large population of enslaved Africans and their descendants.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (exclusively legally recognized). Capuchin and Jesuit missionaries served the colonial population. The Diocese of Louisiana was established 1793 under Spanish rule.
- **Key historical events:** Founding of New Orleans 1718; Natchez Massacre 1729; Treaty of Fontainebleau 1762 (cession to Spain); Acadian exile and resettlement 1755-1785; Spanish period 1762-1800; Louisiana Purchase 1803.

## Boundary changes
- **1699-1762:** French colonial territory, enormous and loosely defined, covering the Mississippi basin. Administered through a series of concession companies before direct royal control.
- **1762 (Treaty of Fontainebleau):** France ceded the portion west of the Mississippi River (and the Isle of Orleans) to Spain. Britain received the eastern portion (West Florida). Records created before 1762 remain in both French and Spanish colonial archives regardless of later boundary.
- **1763 (Treaty of Paris):** The eastern portion of Louisiana (east of the Mississippi) passed to Britain as West Florida. Families in that zone generated records under British administration after 1763.
- **1800-1803:** Napoleon retroceded Louisiana to France briefly; the Louisiana Purchase transferred it to the United States 1803.
- **1812:** Louisiana became the 18th U.S. state. Civil parishes were established 1807.
- **Key implication:** A family living anywhere in colonial Louisiana in the 1700s may have records created under French administration (at ANOM or the Louisiana Historical Center), Spanish administration (also at the Louisiana Historical Center and Archivo General de Indias, Seville), or both depending on which side of 1762 the events fall.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** There was NO civil vital registration in colonial Louisiana during the 1700s. The Louisiana FamilySearch Wiki pages for vital records returned only a generic page rather than state-specific content, so a definitive statewide civil registration date cannot be stated from that source. The FamilySearch Louisiana collections search shows the Statewide Death Index beginning 1819, and Parish Marriages beginning 1837 — both well after the colonial period.
- **What exists for the colonial period:** Catholic sacramental registers are the functional substitute for civil vital records. They record baptisms (which doubled as birth registration), marriages, and burials for the entire colonial period. The Code Noir mandated baptism of all enslaved persons, so these registers extend to the enslaved population as well.
- **Where held:** St. Louis Cathedral registers from 1720 are held at the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives. FamilySearch collection 1612905, "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925," covers this material. FamilySearch also holds 2 digitized volumes of sacramental registers for the Archdiocese of New Orleans (image group 004330991, 264 images, covering 1720-1803).
- **Gaps:** The earliest registers (before 1720) were not consistently kept. Records from rural posts and missions outside New Orleans are spottier.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** The Superior Council records (see Court Records below) contain incidental vital information in estate inventories, succession proceedings, and contracts.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic exclusively (the only legally recognized religion under both French and Spanish colonial law).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. Marriage dispensation files (held in diocesan archives) can be genealogically rich.
- **Where held:**
  - Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives: original sacramental registers
  - FamilySearch collection 1612905 ("Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925"): indexed + images, date range covers the colonial period
  - FamilySearch digitized volume 004330991: 264 browse-only images, 0% name-indexed, NOT full-text searchable — must be browsed page by page
- **Language:** French (French colonial period) and Spanish (Spanish colonial period, 1762-1800). A reading knowledge of both is required to use the browse-only volume.
- **Access classification:** The FamilySearch indexed collection (1612905) is indexed + images. The raw digitized volume (004330991) is browse-only, non-name-indexed, in French and Spanish.

### Census records
- **Colonial censuses (recensements):** The French colonial government conducted periodic population counts. These are NOT the U.S. federal census. The Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France holds colonial census rolls for Louisiana. These are physical/correspondence-access only.
- **U.S. federal census:** The first federal census covering Louisiana was 1810 (Orleans Territory), which falls outside the 1699-1803 colonial scope. These censuses are background context for families that continued into the American period.
- **Access:** Colonial census rolls at ANOM — physical or correspondence access only (not digitized on FamilySearch for the colonial period). The U.S. federal censuses from 1810 onward are fully indexed and online.

### Probate and court records
- **The Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur):** This was the colony's governing judicial and administrative body, 1712-1769 under French administration. It kept records of land grants (concessions), court proceedings, contracts, marriage settlements, and estate inventories. These records are genealogically rich and name settlers, free people of color, and enslaved persons.
- **Where held:** Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans. Partially digitized. FamilySearch has digitized volume 004330992 (149 images, covering French colonial notarial acts and Superior Council records 1699-1769), but this volume is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only, in French.
- **FamilySearch collection 2078341** ("Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984") overlaps the late colonial period beginning 1756.
- **Spanish period courts:** After 1769, Spanish courts replaced the Superior Council. Records of the Cabildo (the Spanish governing council in New Orleans) and the Spanish notarial system are held at the Louisiana Historical Center and the City Archives of New Orleans.
- **Access:** Browse-only for the colonial-era digitized volume. The indexed FamilySearch probate collection (2078341) is indexed + images and covers from 1756.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** French concession grants and Spanish land grants — NOT the U.S. rectangular survey system. Louisiana's land was distributed in long-lot (arpent) strips running back from waterways.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** French colonial concessions were granted by the Company of the Indies and later the Crown. Spanish grants were issued by Spanish colonial governors. After the Louisiana Purchase, all colonial land claims had to be adjudicated before U.S. patent could be issued.
- **Types:** Concessions (French), Spanish land grants, notarial contracts recording property transfers, post-Purchase U.S. adjudicated claims in the American State Papers: Public Lands series.
- **Where held:**
  - New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center: notarial acts from the 1730s onward (contracts, sales, donations, wills, marriage contracts) — physical access, in New Orleans.
  - Louisiana State Land Office: records of colonial grants and post-Purchase patent adjudications.
  - American State Papers: Public Lands series — published, available at major libraries and digitized online.
  - ANOM (Aix-en-Provence): original French colonial concession documents.
- **Access:** Per the FamilySearch wiki_search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants), notarial archives are the primary source; the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center provides public access.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War / Seven Years' War (1754-1763), American Revolution (colonial Louisiana under Spain was involved peripherally — Governor Bernardo de Gálvez led campaigns 1779-1781).
- **Record types:** Muster rolls, officer commissions, and military correspondence are in the colonial administrative records at ANOM (French period) and the Archivo General de Indias, Seville (Spanish period). Post-1803 U.S. military records are at NARA.
- **Where held:** ANOM (Aix-en-Provence) for French colonial military; Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Spain) for Spanish colonial military; NARA for post-Purchase U.S. service records.
- **Access:** Physical or correspondence access only for the colonial-era repositories.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (New Orleans, opened 1789, Spanish colonial period) is the oldest surviving Catholic cemetery. Earlier burials were often in church yards, many of which no longer survive.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has some New Orleans colonial-era entries but coverage is thin for the 1700s.
- **Physical records:** Burial registers overlap with sacramental registers (burials are recorded in the church books). Sexton records for colonial-era cemeteries are largely not available separately.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The first Louisiana newspaper, Le Moniteur de la Louisiane, began publication in 1794 — near the very end of the colonial period. Coverage is extremely limited before 1803.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State University Libraries and the Historic New Orleans Collection hold early newspaper runs. Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) has limited Louisiana colonial-era coverage.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant arrivals:** Ship passenger lists for colonial-era arrivals are preserved in the Company of the Indies records and royal administrative correspondence, held at ANOM. The Acadian exile and resettlement (1755-1785) is documented in both French/Spanish colonial records and in Canadian archives.
- **Record types:** Passenger and settler lists, concession applications, engagé contracts (indentured servant agreements).
- **Where held:** ANOM (Aix-en-Provence) for French colonial arrivals; Spanish colonial records at Archivo General de Indias (Seville) for the 1762-1800 period.
- **Post-1803:** NARA holds U.S.-era passenger lists.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists and settler rolls record every person named, including family members. Engagé contracts (agreements for indentured labor) name both the employer and the laborer.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Colonial-era tax and revenue records were maintained by the colonial administration, not at the parish/county level. They are held at ANOM and the Louisiana Historical Center.
- **Substitute value:** Colonial censuses and notarial records serve the same substitute function as tax lists for missing enumerations.

### Notarial records (unique to Louisiana)
- **This is a record type with no direct equivalent in common-law states.** Under French and Spanish law, notaries authenticated virtually all legal transactions: wills, property sales, donations, marriage contracts, manumissions (freeing of enslaved persons), apprenticeships, and business agreements.
- **Date range:** From the 1730s onward.
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (public access, New Orleans). Earlier notarial acts are embedded in the Superior Council records at the Louisiana Historical Center.
- **Access:** Physical access. Not fully digitized on FamilySearch for the colonial period.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925 (collection 1612905) | Free |
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984 (collection 2078341) | Free |
| FamilySearch | Digitized browse-only volume: Sacramental registers, Archdiocese of New Orleans, 1720-1803 (image group 004330991, 264 images) | Free — browse only |
| FamilySearch | Digitized browse-only volume: French colonial notarial acts / Superior Council records, 1699-1769 (image group 004330992, 149 images) | Free — browse only |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (post-1803 only for Louisiana) | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records (thin coverage for 1700s) | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Post-1803 records only | Free/in-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** 2 digitized volumes match this place and period in FamilySearch volume_search; both are detailed above and represent the complete result set returned.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans | Superior Council records 1712-1769; Spanish Cabildo records 1769-1803; colonial court records; partially digitized | In-person or written inquiry |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Original sacramental registers from 1720; marriage dispensation files | In-person or written inquiry |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Notarial acts from 1730s onward (contracts, wills, marriage settlements, manumissions) | In-person, New Orleans |
| Louisiana State Land Office | Colonial land grants and post-Purchase adjudicated claims | In-person or online search portal |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial administrative correspondence, census rolls, military records, settler/concession files | In-person or correspondence; partial digitization at archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr |
