# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — Anthracite Coal Region (1860–1890)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties
- **County seat:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:**
  - 1860: 89,510
  - 1870: 116,428
  - 1880: 129,974
  (Source: U.S. Census via FamilySearch place_population)
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated; related occupations include mine laborer, loader, breaker boy, mule driver, colliery engineer, blacksmith, and company-store clerk. The region's coal powered much of the northeastern industrial economy in this era.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish immigrant and Irish-American population, especially after the Famine migrations of the late 1840s and 1850s. Welsh, English, and German miners were also numerous; Eastern European immigration (Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak) began growing in the 1880s.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant among Irish), Welsh Congregationalist and Baptist, Methodist Episcopal, Lutheran (German), and Episcopal. Catholic parishes were established between 1840 and 1870 across the region.
- **Key historical events:** Molly Maguires trials (1875-1877) involving Irish miners; major strikes and labor unrest throughout the period; rapid growth of company towns (patches); railroad expansion by the Philadelphia and Reading Railroad.

## Boundary changes
- Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties. Its boundaries were stable throughout the 1860–1890 research window.
- Records predating 1811 are held by Berks County (county seat: Reading) and Northampton County (county seat: Easton).
- The coal region spans five counties: Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, and Carbon. A miner's family may have moved among them. Each county has its own court and record series — a Schuylkill-only search misses records generated in those neighboring counties.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date and level:** Pennsylvania did not have a functioning statewide civil registration system during most of the 1860–1890 window. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Vital Records returned only generic content in this survey run and did not state a specific statewide start date; confirm the exact year and level via https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records before assuming any state-issued birth or death certificate exists. The 1893 statewide registration act is frequently cited in secondary literature, but that date could not be verified from the pages fetched here.
- **What exists:** Civil marriage records were kept at the county level throughout this period by the Register of Wills / Orphans' Court. FamilySearch digitized volume 007936753 covers Schuylkill County Marriage Records 1870–1910 (94 images); it is 0% name-indexed and must be browsed image by image.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Courthouse (Register of Wills, Pottsville); Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) holds some transcribed series.
- **Gaps:** Statewide birth and death registration is absent or unreliable for most of 1860–1890. Civil death certificates are not a reliable primary source for this window.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic baptismal registers and burial registers are the best substitutes for births and deaths; see Church Records below.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (Irish and later Eastern European parishes established 1840–1870+), Welsh Baptist and Congregationalist, Methodist Episcopal, German Lutheran, Episcopal.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and confirmations (confirmations are a separately dated event occurring years after baptism — they carry their own date and sponsor names).
- **Diocesan jurisdiction (critical for locating records):** Before 1868, all five anthracite counties — including Schuylkill — fell under the Roman Catholic Diocese of Philadelphia. From 1868, Luzerne and Lackawanna transferred to the new Diocese of Scranton, and Northumberland to the Diocese of Harrisburg. Schuylkill and Carbon remained under the Diocese of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. For an Irish Catholic ancestor in Schuylkill County 1860–1890, the controlling diocese is Philadelphia (pre-1961). Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records
- **Where held:** Diocesan archives (Diocese of Philadelphia, 222 N. 17th St., Philadelphia) hold many registers; some parishes retain their own. FamilySearch digitized volume 007936751 covers Church Records 1842–1895 (187 images), in English and German; 0% name-indexed, browse-only. The SYNTH-PA-CHURCH collection (test fixture, 1,245,830 records) covers Schuylkill County church records 1708–1985 — verify this collection's status on FamilySearch before relying on it, as it is flagged as a synthetic test fixture.
- **Language:** Records are in English for Irish-origin parishes. German-congregation registers in volume 007936751 require ability to read German script.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Schuylkill County appears in federal censuses 1860, 1870, 1880, and 1900 (all within or adjacent to the target window). The 1890 population schedules are almost entirely destroyed nationwide — this is a firm gap.
- **What each census provides:** The 1880 census is the first to record the relationship of each household member to the head of household, making it especially valuable for proving family relationships. The 1870 and 1900 censuses provide complementary evidence for families with children. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania,_United_States_Genealogy#Census_Records
- **Mortality schedules:** The 1860, 1870, and 1880 federal mortality schedules record persons who died in the twelve months preceding the census enumeration — these partially fill the gap left by absent civil death registration.
- **State/other enumerations:** Pennsylvania state tax assessors enumerated coal-region residents triennially from 1853. The assessment ledgers list householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity — a strong substitute for the missing 1890 census and for off-census years. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records
- **Access:** Federal censuses 1860–1880 are indexed and image-viewable on FamilySearch and Ancestry. The 1900 Ancestry collection (collection 1276) was returned by external_links_search for Schuylkill County. State tax assessments are largely physical or microfilm.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills (testate), letters of administration (intestate), guardianship files, estate inventories, and estate distributions. Naturalization petitions and declarations of intent are filed in court and are essential for Irish immigrants.
- **Testate vs. intestate:** A miner who left a will (testate) generates a will and executor's account; one who died without a will (intestate) generates letters of administration. Search both the will books and the administration dockets, as laboring-class men often died intestate.
- **Date range:** Probate records begin with county formation in 1811. FamilySearch digitized volume 007936749 covers Schuylkill County Probate Records 1851–1930 (412 images); 0% name-indexed, browse-only. FamilySearch collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994) covers the same material at the state level with 3,200,560 images; 0 records indexed (browse-only).
- **Naturalization records:** Before 1906, declarations of intent and petitions for naturalization in Schuylkill County were filed in the Quarter Sessions Court, Common Pleas Court, or Orphans' Court — search all three. These records name country of origin and are critical for confirming Irish birth. FamilySearch digitized volume 007936750 covers Schuylkill County Naturalization Records 1849–1915 (298 images); 0% name-indexed, browse-only. After September 1906, naturalizations centralized in federal courts; NARA's Philadelphia facility holds eastern Pennsylvania files. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Naturalization_Records
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Courthouse (Orphans' Court, Register of Wills, Clerk of Courts); Pennsylvania State Archives.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state — land was distributed by the Commonwealth, not the federal government).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania distributed land through the Commonwealth's land office (now at the Pennsylvania State Archives). County deed books record subsequent transfers; the Recorder of Deeds at the Schuylkill County Courthouse holds deed books.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, and tax records. Many coal-region miners lived in company-owned patch towns and never owned land — absence from deed records does not mean absence from the county.
- **Date range:** Deed records begin with county formation 1811. FamilySearch digitized volume 007936752 covers Deed Records 1815–1900 (543 images); 22% name-indexed — the best-indexed Schuylkill digitized volume; the remaining 78% must be browsed image by image.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds (Pottsville); Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) holds original land warrants and surveys.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) is the dominant conflict for this window. Schuylkill County contributed heavily to Pennsylvania volunteer regiments. Draft registration (1863) covers all men 20–45.
- **Record types:** Civil War service records and compiled military service records (CMSR) at NARA; pension files at NARA (pension index on FamilySearch and Ancestry); Civil War draft registrations (Consolidated Lists of Civil War Draft Registrations) on Ancestry and FamilySearch; Pennsylvania regimental history records at the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Irish soldiers:** Irish-born soldiers often appear under anglicized or phonetically spelled names — search variant spellings.
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington DC and St. Louis); Pennsylvania State Archives (Military Records Section, Harrisburg).

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Catholic cemeteries associated with Pottsville-area parishes; miners' cemeteries in individual patch towns (many small and denominationally affiliated).
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) and BillionGraves index many Schuylkill County cemeteries; coverage is uneven for smaller patch-town cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers are held by individual parishes and cemeteries. Catholic burial registers are at the parish level (some transferred to the Diocese of Philadelphia archive).

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Miners' Journal (Pottsville) is the premier newspaper of the anthracite region and published continuously from 1825. It carried obituaries, marriage notices, inquest reports on mining accidents, and legal notices.
- **Where held:** The Miners' Journal archive is available on microfilm at the Schuylkill County Historical Society (Pottsville) and partially digitized through newspaper aggregators. Check Newspapers.com and Chronicling America (Library of Congress, chroniclingamerica.loc.gov).
- **Content value:** Mining accident reports in the Miners' Journal name individual victims and witnesses; these are often the only contemporaneous record of an immigrant miner's death before civil death registration was reliable.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia (the dominant port for Irish immigrants to this region) and New York (Castle Garden, then Ellis Island after 1892). Many Schuylkill County Irish arrived via Philadelphia in the 1840s–1860s.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests (Philadelphia and New York lists on FamilySearch and Ancestry); declarations of intent and naturalization petitions (see Court Records); alien registration records.
- **Where held:** NARA (Philadelphia and Washington DC facilities); FamilySearch has indexed many Philadelphia and New York passenger lists for this period.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed. For pre-1895 lists, Irish passengers are often recorded only by name, age, sex, and occupation; origin county in Ireland is rarely given.

### Coal-region specialized indexes
- **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855–1898:** Names approximately 41,000 colliery workers across the lower anthracite field, drawn from company payroll books. Entries include occupation (loader, breaker boy, mule driver), wage rate, and parish of origin where stated. Note: this index covers the Lackawanna Valley primarily; Schuylkill County researchers should verify whether their ancestor's colliery falls within its scope. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records
- **Mine inspection and accident reports:** Organized by colliery, not by person — useful for confirming that an ancestor worked at a specific colliery, but not a name index. Use payroll indexes first.
- **Triennial state tax assessments from 1853:** Cover all five anthracite counties; ledgers list householder, occupation, real estate value, and sometimes nativity. Especially valuable as a 1890-census substitute and for locating men in inter-census years. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records

### Tax records
- **Types:** Triennial state assessment ledgers (from 1853); county property and personal property tax records.
- **Date range:** State triennial assessments begin 1853; county tax records begin with county formation 1811.
- **Where held:** County tax records at the Schuylkill County Courthouse; state assessment records at the Pennsylvania State Archives and potentially on microfilm.
- **Substitute value:** The triennial assessments from 1853 onward are the strongest substitute for the missing 1890 census in the anthracite counties.

### Other record types
- **Company store records / patch-town records:** Many miners lived and traded exclusively in company towns. Philadelphia and Reading Railroad and individual coal companies kept employment rolls and store ledgers. These records, where they survive, are held at the Pennsylvania State Archives, the Hagley Museum and Library (Wilmington, Delaware), and university special collections.
- **Labor and union records:** The Workingmen's Benevolent Association (WBA) and the Miners' and Laborers' Amalgamated Association were active in Schuylkill County. If fraternal or union membership records survive, they may name members' origins. Check with the United Mine Workers of America archive and the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Molly Maguires court records:** The 1875–1877 trials generated extensive court records naming Irish miners and their associates. These records are at the Schuylkill County Courthouse and have been studied by historians; published transcripts exist.

- **Search all five anthracite counties.** A miner's family may have lived in Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, or Carbon at different times. Each county has its own court and record series. Guides for those four counties have not yet been produced and should be the next locality surveys.
- **Neighboring counties:** Berks County (Reading) and Northampton County (Easton) are the parent counties of Schuylkill; Dauphin, Lebanon, and Columbia are adjacent. Families near those borders may have generated records on either side.

Here is what the locality-guide agent produced for you:

---

## Vermont Pre-Statehood Locality Research Guide

This guide covers Vermont in the **late 1700s before statehood (1791)**. During that window Vermont passed through three distinct identities:

1. **The New Hampshire Grants** — land granted by Governor Benning Wentworth of New Hampshire
2. **Disputed New York colonial territory** — New York asserted competing jurisdiction over the same land
3. **The Vermont Republic (1777–1791)** — a self-declared independent republic until admission as the 14th state

---

### Record Availability for the Pre-Statehood Period

Because none of those governments established a modern vital records system, **births, marriages, and deaths from this period were almost never recorded by any official authority.** The records that *do* survive are:

| Record Type | What It Contains | Where Held |
|---|---|---|
| **Land grant documents** | Two competing systems — New Hampshire grants and New York patents | Vermont State Archives; FamilySearch |
| **Town proprietors' records** | Early land divisions, lot assignments, settler names | Individual town offices and Vermont State Archives |
| **Town-level tax lists** | Lists of taxable residents, useful as census substitutes | Town clerks; Vermont State Archives |
| **Church registers** | Baptisms, marriages, burials (where a congregation existed) | Individual churches; VT Historical Society |
| **Revolutionary War military files** | Service records, pension files | National Archives (NARA); Fold3 |
| **1771 Grant Survey Schedule** | Names ~1,800 grant holders — the earliest systematic resident list | Vermont State Papers |

---

### Key Finding Aids

- **Vermont State Papers** — the printed multi-volume series includes land grant schedules and early legislative records
- **FamilySearch Vermont collections** — land and tax records, early vital records by town
- **Vermont Historical Society** — manuscripts, church registers, town histories
- **National Archives** — Revolutionary War pension and bounty-land warrant files (often the richest source of biographical detail for men of this era)

---

### Critical Caveat: Town-Level Research

Vermont's record-keeping was **entirely town-based** throughout this period. The next step in your research is to identify the specific Vermont town your ancestor lived in. Once that town is known, a focused plan can be built around:
- Its town clerk's land and proprietors' records
- Any surviving church registers for that congregation
- The relevant New Hampshire or New York land-grant series

---

*A locality entry (`loc_001`) has been written to your project's research log for future reference.*

quirks: No statewide civil vital registration existed before 1857 (statewide level). Town clerk vital records survive for some towns back to the 1770s but coverage is uneven — contact each town clerk individually.

The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule, prepared under New York colonial authority, enumerates approximately 1,800 grantees of New Hampshire grants New York refused to recognize. It is the earliest systematic resident list for the future state and predates any civil registration.

Land grants were issued by two competing authorities: New Hampshire (Benning Wentworth grants, 1749–1764) and New York (post-1764). Researchers must search both grant series; the same settler may appear in both or in records disputing one against the other.

Vermont declared itself an independent republic in 1777 and was not admitted to the Union until 1791. Federal records (census, military pensions) begin only at statehood; for pre-1791 events, there is no federal record infrastructure.
The first federal census to include Vermont was 1790 (taken after admission). Vermont was not enumerated in any earlier federal census.

Town-level government was the primary civil record-keeping unit throughout the pre-statehood period. Vital events, land transfers, and proprietors' records were kept at the town level, not at a county level.

Nineteenth-century town histories (most published 1860–1900) often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records otherwise difficult to access — these are a critical finding aid per the FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy).

Vermont borders New Hampshire (east, across the Connecticut River), New York (west), Massachusetts (south), and Quebec, Canada (north). Families near these borders generated records on both sides — search New Hampshire towns across the Connecticut River and New York counties across Lake Champlain and the Taconic range.

The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Vermont Vital Records, Land and Property, Church Records, Probate Records, Census, and Naming Customs all resolved to a generic Genealogy Records page rather than Vermont-specific content — these are digitization/coverage gaps in the wiki, not evidence that those record types do not exist.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Vermont, United States (ca. 1760–1791, Pre-Statehood)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Vermont was admitted as the 14th U.S. state on March 4, 1791. Before statehood it existed as the self-declared Vermont Republic (1777–1791). Before that, the territory was known as the New Hampshire Grants (ca. 1749–1764) and was then disputed between New Hampshire and New York colonial authority (1764–1777).
- **County seat / administrative center:** No single capital equivalent during the Vermont Republic era; Montpelier became the state capital after 1791. The town was the primary administrative unit throughout the pre-statehood period.
- **Parent jurisdictions:** New Hampshire (Wentworth grants, ca. 1749–1764), Province of New York (contested jurisdiction, 1764–1777), then the self-governing Vermont Republic (1777–1791).
- **Population during period:** Population data for this exact pre-statehood window was not returned by the place_population tool. Vermont's population at the 1790 federal census (the first to include Vermont after admission in March 1791) was approximately 85,000. Settlement was sparse and largely limited to the river valleys and western lowlands in the earlier part of this window.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, frontier land clearing, some fur trade, and small-scale milling. The land disputes between New Hampshire grant holders and New York claimants dominated economic and legal life.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English-stock New Englanders migrating north from Connecticut, Massachusetts, and Rhode Island. Small numbers of French Canadians in the northern counties.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist (dominant among New England settlers), Baptist, Methodist, and Episcopal (Anglican). Quaker meetings existed in some communities. Many early frontier settlements had no established church and relied on itinerant ministers.
- **Key historical events:** Benning Wentworth's New Hampshire grants (1749–1764) drew the first wave of settlers; New York's assertion of authority (1764) created the land disputes that animated the entire period; Ethan Allen and the Green Mountain Boys resisted New York authority through the 1770s; Vermont declared independence in 1777 and operated as an autonomous republic until U.S. admission in 1791. The Revolutionary War (1775–1783) ran through the entire middle of this window, including the Battle of Bennington (1777).

## Boundary changes
- The territory that became Vermont passed through three successive jurisdictional identities during the target window:
  - **New Hampshire Grants (ca. 1749–1764):** Governor Benning Wentworth of New Hampshire issued township grants to settlers. Records from this period sit partly in New Hampshire colonial records.
  - **Province of New York (1764–1777):** The British Crown confirmed New York's authority west of the Connecticut River. New York then attempted to issue its own grants over the same land, creating a competing and overlapping grant system. New York colonial records from this period are relevant.
  - **Vermont Republic (1777–1791):** Vermont declared independence from both New York and Britain in January 1777, held its own constitutional convention, and functioned as a self-governing republic for 14 years. Land records, court records, and town records from this period are Vermont's own.
- The Connecticut River forms the eastern boundary with New Hampshire throughout the period. Records of towns on both banks may be relevant.
- County structure within Vermont was rudimentary in the early Republic years; the town remained the operative record-keeping level.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Statewide civil registration began in Vermont in 1857 (statewide level). This is decades after the target window.
- **What exists for the target window:** There was no civil vital registration during the pre-statehood period. Some town clerks recorded births, marriages, and deaths voluntarily from the 1770s onward, but this was not required and coverage is deeply uneven. The FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki page ([Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)) confirms that earlier town clerk records survive for some towns back to the 1770s.
- **Where held:** Individual town clerk offices. There is no centralized pre-1857 vital record repository. Contact each relevant town clerk directly.
- **Gaps:** For the pre-statehood period (before 1791), and even for the decades after statehood until 1857, the near-total absence of civil vital registration is the defining research challenge.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the primary substitute. Family bibles, cemetery inscriptions, probate inventories naming heirs, and newspaper notices are secondary substitutes.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregationalist, Baptist, Methodist, Episcopal/Anglican, and Quaker. Many frontier communities had no organized church in the early settlement years.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and (for some denominations) confirmations. Some churches also kept membership rolls and disciplinary records.
- **Where held:** Local parish offices and denominational archives. The Congregational records are often held by the individual church or by the Vermont Conference of the United Church of Christ. Episcopal records are at the Diocese of Vermont. The Vermont Historical Society (Montpelier) holds some deposited church registers.
- **Language:** English throughout.
- **Access:** Coverage is uneven. Many early frontier churches kept no registers, or registers have been lost. For the earliest settlement years (1760s–1770s), church records may be entirely absent for a given community. Itinerant ministers sometimes recorded marriages and baptisms in personal diaries or circuit notebooks rather than formal registers.
- **Digitization level:** Varies by collection; many church registers survive only as physical originals or microfilm at the Vermont Historical Society or FamilySearch Library.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census was 1790. Vermont was admitted in March 1791 and appears in the 1790 enumeration. The 1790 census is the only federal census touching this period, and it is a household-level head-of-household count, not a full name list for all members.
- **Pre-1790 enumerations:** There was no federal census before 1790, and Vermont had no state-level census during the Republic period. Tax lists and militia musters serve as the closest functional equivalents.
- **Other enumerations:** The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule (see Land Records below) is the earliest systematic list of residents, enumerating approximately 1,800 New Hampshire grant holders. It predates any census and is the closest thing to a pre-statehood population list.
- **Access:** The 1790 federal census for Vermont is indexed and available on Ancestry.com and FamilySearch (indexed + images).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, inventories, and estate distributions.
- **Date range:** Vermont's county probate courts were established as the Republic organized its government beginning around 1778–1779. Before that, any probate would have fallen under New York colonial court authority.
- **Where held:** Vermont probate district courts at the county level (Vermont uses probate districts, not all of which align with county lines). The Vermont State Archives holds some historical probate records. Town-level probate records for the Republic period may be at individual county courthouses.
- **Digitization level:** The FamilySearch Wiki topic-specific pages for Vermont Probate Records did not return Vermont-specific content — those records' digitization status cannot be confirmed from this survey. The Vermont State Archives and county probate courts hold physical records.
- **Testate vs. intestate:** Both wills (testate) and administrations (intestate) were filed. Probate files name heirs, creditors, and neighbors — valuable for reconstructing family relationships when vital records are absent.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes-and-bounds survey within township grants. Vermont is a state-land state — land was distributed by the colonial proprietors (New Hampshire and, later, competing New York grants) rather than the federal General Land Office.
- **Land-distribution authority:** Two competing grant systems operated:
  - New Hampshire grants (Benning Wentworth, 1749–1764): Original township grants issued by New Hampshire. Records sit in New Hampshire colonial and state records.
  - New York grants (post-1764): New York's competing grants over the same townships. Records are in New York colonial records.
  - Vermont Republic grants (post-1777): After independence, Vermont's own General Assembly issued confirmatory grants and new grants. These are in the Vermont State Archives.
- **Types:** Township grants, land patents, deeds, tax lists, bounty land warrants (for Revolutionary War service), proprietors' records.
- **The 1771 Grant Survey Schedule:** Prepared under New York colonial authority, this schedule enumerates approximately 1,800 grantees of New Hampshire grants that New York refused to recognize. Per the FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki page ([Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)), each entry lists grantee, township grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status. It is the earliest systematic resident list for the future state.
- **Where held:** Vermont State Archives (Montpelier) for Republic-era and post-statehood land records. New Hampshire State Archives for the Wentworth grants. New York State Archives for the competing New York grants.

- **Parent jurisdictions:** New Hampshire (Wentworth grants, ca. 1749–1764), Province of New York (contested jurisdiction, 1764–1777), then the self-governing Vermont Republic (1777–1791).

Vermont's population at the 1790 federal census (the first to include Vermont after admission in March 1791) was approximately 85,000. Per the FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki page ([Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)), this is the earliest systematic resident list for the future state, enumerating approximately 1,800 grantees.

# Locality Guide: Vermont, United States (ca. 1760–1791, Pre-Statehood)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Vermont was admitted as the 14th U.S. state on March 4, 1791. Before statehood it existed as the self-declared Vermont Republic (1777–1791). Before that, the territory was known as the New Hampshire Grants (ca. 1749–1764) and was then disputed between New Hampshire and New York colonial authority (1764–1777).
- **County seat / administrative center:** No single capital equivalent during the Vermont Republic era; Montpelier became the state capital after 1791. The town was the primary administrative unit throughout the pre-statehood period.
- **Parent jurisdictions:** New Hampshire (Wentworth grants, ca. 1749–1764), Province of New York (contested jurisdiction, 1764–1777), then the self-governing Vermont Republic (1777–1791).
- **Population during period:** Population data for this exact pre-statehood window was not returned by the place_population tool. Vermont's population at the 1790 federal census (the first to include Vermont after admission in March 1791) was approximately 85,000. Settlement was sparse and largely limited to the river valleys and western lowlands in the earlier part of this window.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, frontier land clearing, some fur trade, and small-scale milling. The land disputes between New Hampshire grant holders and New York claimants dominated economic and legal life.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English-stock New Englanders migrating north from Connecticut, Massachusetts, and Rhode Island. Small numbers of French Canadians in the northern counties.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist (dominant among New England settlers), Baptist, Methodist, and Episcopal (Anglican). Quaker meetings existed in some communities. Many early frontier settlements had no established church and relied on itinerant ministers.
- **Key historical events:** Benning Wentworth's New Hampshire grants (1749–1764) drew the first wave of settlers; New York's assertion of authority (1764) created the land disputes that animated the entire period; Ethan Allen and the Green Mountain Boys resisted New York authority through the 1770s; Vermont declared independence in 1777 and operated as an autonomous republic until U.S. admission in 1791. The Revolutionary War (1775–1783) ran through the entire middle of this window, including the Battle of Bennington (1777).

## Boundary changes
- The territory that became Vermont passed through three successive jurisdictional identities during the target window:
  - **New Hampshire Grants (ca. 1749–1764):** Governor Benning Wentworth of New Hampshire issued township grants to settlers. Records from this period sit partly in New Hampshire colonial records.
  - **Province of New York (1764–1777):** The British Crown confirmed New York's authority west of the Connecticut River. New York then attempted to issue its own grants over the same land, creating a competing and overlapping grant system. New York colonial records from this period are relevant.
  - **Vermont Republic (1777–1791):** Vermont declared independence from both New York and Britain in January 1777, held its own constitutional convention, and functioned as a self-governing republic for 14 years. Land records, court records, and town records from this period are Vermont's own.
- The Connecticut River forms the eastern boundary with New Hampshire throughout the period. Records of towns on both banks may be relevant.
- County structure within Vermont was rudimentary in the early Republic years; the town remained the operative record-keeping level.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Statewide civil registration began in Vermont in 1857 (statewide level). This is decades after the target window.
- **What exists for the target window:** There was no civil vital registration during the pre-statehood period. Some town clerks recorded births, marriages, and deaths voluntarily from the 1770s onward, but this was not required and coverage is deeply uneven. The FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki page ([Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)) confirms that earlier town clerk records survive for some towns back to the 1770s.
- **Where held:** Individual town clerk offices. There is no centralized pre-1857 vital record repository. Contact each relevant town clerk directly.
- **Gaps:** For the pre-statehood period (before 1791), and even for the decades after statehood until 1857, the near-total absence of civil vital registration is the defining research challenge.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the primary substitute. Family bibles, cemetery inscriptions, probate inventories naming heirs, and newspaper notices are secondary substitutes.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregationalist, Baptist, Methodist, Episcopal/Anglican, and Quaker. Many frontier communities had no organized church in the early settlement years.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and (for some denominations) confirmations. Some churches also kept membership rolls and disciplinary records.
- **Where held:** Local parish offices and denominational archives. The Congregational records are often held by the individual church or by the Vermont Conference of the United Church of Christ. Episcopal records are at the Diocese of Vermont. The Vermont Historical Society (Montpelier) holds some deposited church registers.
- **Language:** English throughout.
- **Access:** Coverage is uneven. Many early frontier churches kept no registers, or registers have been lost. For the earliest settlement years (1760s–1770s), church records may be entirely absent for a given community. Itinerant ministers sometimes recorded marriages and baptisms in personal diaries or circuit notebooks rather than formal registers.
- **Digitization level:** Varies by collection; many church registers survive only as physical originals or microfilm at the Vermont Historical Society or FamilySearch Library.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census was 1790. Vermont was admitted in March 1791 and appears in the 1790 enumeration. The 1790 census is the only federal census touching this period, and it is a household-level head-of-household count, not a full name list for all members.
- **Pre-1790 enumerations:** There was no federal census before 1790, and Vermont had no state-level census during the Republic period. Tax lists and militia musters serve as the closest functional equivalents.
- **Other enumerations:** The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule (see Land Records below) is the earliest systematic list of residents, enumerating approximately 1,800 New Hampshire grant holders. It predates any census and is the closest thing to a pre-statehood population list.
- **Access:** The 1790 federal census for Vermont is indexed and available on Ancestry.com and FamilySearch (indexed + images).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, inventories, and estate distributions.
- **Date range:** Vermont's county probate courts were established as the Republic organized its government beginning around 1778–1779. Before that, any probate would have fallen under New York colonial court authority.
- **Where held:** Vermont probate district courts at the county level (Vermont uses probate districts, not all of which align with county lines). The Vermont State Archives holds some historical probate records. Town-level probate records for the Republic period may be at individual county courthouses.
- **Digitization level:** The FamilySearch Wiki topic-specific pages for Vermont Probate Records did not return Vermont-specific content — those records' digitization status cannot be confirmed from this survey. The Vermont State Archives and county probate courts hold physical records.
- **Testate vs. intestate:** Both wills (testate) and administrations (intestate) were filed. Probate files name heirs, creditors, and neighbors — valuable for reconstructing family relationships when vital records are absent.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes-and-bounds survey within township grants. Vermont is a state-land state — land was distributed by the colonial proprietors (New Hampshire and, later, competing New York grants) rather than the federal General Land Office.
- **Land-distribution authority:** Two competing grant systems operated:
  - New Hampshire grants (Benning Wentworth, 1749–1764): Original township grants issued by New Hampshire. Records sit in New Hampshire colonial and state records.
  - New York grants (post-1764): New York's competing grants over the same townships. Records are in New York colonial records.
  - Vermont Republic grants (post-1777): After independence, Vermont's own General Assembly issued confirmatory grants and new grants. These are in the Vermont State Archives.
- **Types:** Township grants, land patents, deeds, tax lists, bounty land warrants (for Revolutionary War service), proprietors' records.
- **The 1771 Grant Survey Schedule:** Prepared under New York colonial authority, this schedule enumerates approximately 1,800 grantees of New Hampshire grants that New York refused to recognize. Per the FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki page ([Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)), each entry lists grantee, township grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status. It is the earliest systematic resident list for the future state.
- **Where held:** Vermont State Archives (Montpelier) for Republic-era and post-statehood land records. New Hampshire State Archives for the Wentworth grants. New York State Archives for the competing New York grants.
- **Town proprietors' records:** Individual town proprietors kept their own records of lot assignments and transfers. These are held by individual town clerks or deposited with historical societies. Nineteenth-century town histories often reprint these.
- **Digitization level:** Varies widely. Some have been microfilmed by FamilySearch; others are physical-only at the Vermont State Archives or town clerk offices.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The French and Indian War (ending 1763) affected the region immediately before the survey window. The Revolutionary War (1775–1783) is the central military event of the period, including the Battle of Bennington (August 1777). Vermont fielded its own militia and sent troops to Continental Army units.
- **Record types:**
  - Revolutionary War service records and pension files (NARA, Washington, D.C.)
  - Bounty land warrants for Revolutionary War service
  - Vermont militia muster rolls (Vermont State Archives)
  - DAR and SAR lineage records often name Vermont Revolutionary War soldiers
- **Where held:** NARA holds federal service records and pension files. Vermont State Archives holds state militia records. Many pension files have been digitized and are available on Fold3 and Ancestry.
- **Digitization level:** Revolutionary War pension files are indexed and partially imaged on Fold3 (subscription) and through the National Archives online catalog.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Vermont has numerous small town cemeteries, many established in the earliest settlement years. The earliest graves (1760s–1780s) are often in private family plots or small community burying grounds.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) has broad Vermont cemetery coverage, though the density of indexed pre-1800 stones varies by town.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for this early period are rare. The Vermont Old Cemetery Association has conducted surveys of historic cemeteries.
- **Note:** Grave markers from the pre-statehood period are often simple slate stones with minimal biographical information.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Vermont's first newspaper, the Vermont Gazette (Bennington), began publication in 1783. A few other papers followed before 1791. Coverage for the very early settlement period (1760s–1770s) is essentially nonexistent.
- **Where held:** Vermont Historical Society and various library microfilm collections hold early Vermont newspaper runs.
- **Content value:** Marriage notices, death notices, legal notices, and land sale advertisements. For the 1783–1791 window specifically, newspapers are worth checking for notices.
- **Digitization level:** Limited digitization of pre-1800 Vermont newspapers. Newspapers.com and Chronicling America may have partial holdings; confirm by searching directly.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Pre-statehood Vermont settlers came primarily overland from southern New England (Connecticut, Massachusetts, Rhode Island) rather than through seaports. Some northern-border traffic with Quebec existed.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists are not relevant for the dominant overland migration pattern. Naturalization records are not applicable to the pre-independence period (these settlers were British subjects). After 1790, declarations of intention and naturalizations could be filed in any Vermont court of record.
- **Border with Canada:** The northern border with Quebec was permeable throughout this period. Some settlers had French-Canadian origins or French-Canadian neighbors; Quebec Catholic parish registers (held by the Bibliothèque et Archives nationales du Québec) are relevant for families with cross-border connections.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists cover arrivals by sea. The overland migration from southern New England that populated Vermont in this period does not appear in passenger manifests.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Vermont Republic and early county-level tax lists. Property tax lists recorded adult male property holders.
- **Date range:** Some Vermont town tax lists survive from the late 1770s onward.
- **Where held:** Vermont State Archives, individual town clerks, and county courthouses. Some have been microfilmed.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists serve as a census substitute, placing a named individual in a specific town at a specific year — crucial for the pre-1790 period when no census exists.

### Other record types
- **Town and county histories:** Nineteenth-century town histories (most published 1860–1900) frequently reprint colonial-era proprietors' records, grant lists, and early settler biographies otherwise inaccessible. Per the FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki page ([Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)), these are a critical finding aid for the pre-statehood period. WorldCat and the FamilySearch Catalog can identify which towns have published histories.
- **Proprietors' records:** Each granted township had a body of proprietors who allocated individual lots. Proprietors' records — meetings, votes, lot assignments — name early settlers. Held by individual town clerks or deposited at the Vermont Historical Society.
- **Vermont Republic General Assembly records:** Vermont's Republic-era legislature produced journals and committee records. Vermont State Archives holds these.
- **Green Mountain Boys and militia records:** Ethan Allen's Green Mountain Boys and subsequent militia units kept muster rolls. Some have been published or microfilmed.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Ancestry.com | 1790 federal census for Vermont (indexed + images); Revolutionary War pension files (partial); some Vermont vital records for post-1857 period | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War service records and pension files | Subscription |
| FamilySearch | 1790 federal census; some microfilmed Vermont records (access via FamilySearch Library or online) | Free |
| Find A Grave | Vermont cemetery inscriptions, variable pre-1800 coverage | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Limited pre-1800 Vermont newspaper holdings | Subscription |
| NARA Online Catalog (archives.gov) | Revolutionary War military records, pension files | Free to browse; some images free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The external_links_search returned 6 curated links for Vermont, all generic national-level repositories (Ancestry census, NARA, Find A Grave, Newspapers.com, Fold3, FamilySearch Wiki vital records category). No Vermont-specific curated collection links were returned for the 1760–1791 window. This is a coverage gap in FamilySearch's curated links, not evidence that Vermont records do not exist online.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Vermont State Archives (Montpelier, VT) | Republic-era land records, General Assembly records, militia records, post-1791 vital records compilations, some tax lists | In-person; some records available by mail request |
| Vermont Historical Society (Montpelier, VT) | Town histories, deposited church registers, genealogical collections, newspaper microfilm, proprietors' records | In-person; some holdings digitized |
| Individual town clerk offices | Town vital records (some back to 1770s), proprietors' records, early land deeds | Contact each town clerk individually |
| New Hampshire State Archives (Concord, NH) | Benning Wentworth township grants (1749–1764), New Hampshire colonial records | In-person; some records online via NH Division of Archives |
| New York State Archives (Albany, NY) | New York colonial grant records (1764–1777), competing New York grants | In-person; some records available remotely |
| National Archives (NARA), Washington, D.C. | Revolutionary War service records, pension files, 1790 census | In-person; many records digitized on Fold3/Ancestry |
| FamilySearch Library (Salt Lake City, UT) | Microfilmed Vermont records including some church registers, probate, and land records | In-person; some available for loan to local FamilySearch centers |

## Records NOT online
- Most pre-1790 Vermont church registers survive only as physical originals at local churches or the Vermont Historical Society, or on microfilm at the FamilySearch Library.
- Town clerk vital records predating statewide registration (pre-1857) — including any surviving pre-1791 entries — are largely not digitized. Each town must be contacted individually.
- Vermont Republic-era tax lists and militia muster rolls are largely physical-only at the Vermont State Archives.
- Proprietors' records for individual townships are largely physical-only at town clerk offices or the Vermont Historical Society.
- New Hampshire Wentworth grant records are in the New Hampshire State Archives and have limited online access.
- New York colonial grant records disputing Vermont township ownership are in the New York State Archives.

## Known record losses
- No catastrophic statewide record loss is documented for Vermont comparable to courthouse fires in some other states. However, the pre-statehood period presents structural gaps rather than disaster losses: records simply were not required to be kept, and many communities had no civil infrastructure to keep them.
- Some individual town clerk offices have experienced losses of early volumes through water damage, fire, or simple neglect.
- The frontier nature of settlement through much of the 1760s–1780s means that many events (births, marriages, deaths) were never recorded by any authority at the time they occurred.

- **Cross the Connecticut River.** Families in eastern Vermont towns often had relatives and land transactions in New Hampshire towns across the river. Search the corresponding New Hampshire county records as well as Vermont's.
- **Cross into New York.** Families in western Vermont had economic and family connections to New York towns across Lake Champlain and the Taconic Range. Relevant New York counties include Essex, Washington, Rensselaer, and Albany.
